Late 1980s.Author: No author
Late 1980s.chunks:
'Aids risk' in surgery rubbish

Children were exposed to a "clinical cocktail of risk" including hepatitis and Aids from waste materials strewn outside a Bradford doctors' surgery, city magistrates were told yesterday.

A girl aged five had gone home crying after pricking her finger on a hypodermic needle and a boy aged three had found a tablet he thought was a sweet, days before a complaint was made to the local Department of Environmental Health, Mr Michael Wilcock, for the prosecution and on behalf of the Health and Safety Executive, said.

Two Bradford doctors were fined £500 each and ordered to pay £49 costs after admitting failing to ensure the safety of the public from waste material at their surgery in Oak Lane, Bradford.

They were Naeemullah Mir, of Malvern Grove, and Syed Muhammad Intiaz, of Box Tree Close, Bradford.

Mr Bob Stewart, the doctors' solicitor, said that they had left the waste in plastic bags outside their premises and it was not their fault that it was later strewn about'Aids risk' in surgery rubbish.
The Times (London, England), Tuesday, March 25, 1986; pg. 3; Issue 62413. (183 words)

Late 1980s.Title: BMA guide on Aids safety
Late 1980s.Author: No author
Late 1980s.chunks:
BMA guide on Aids safety
Advice on how to avoid Aids (acquired immune deficiency syndrome) and recognize symp-toms of the disease is published in a booklet by the British Medical Association today.
The booklet warns readers against having sexual relations with multiple partners and sharing syringes, razors or other skin cutting instruments.
The disease is spread, like hepatitis B and syphilis, by sexual contact, blood transfusion, syringe needles or other sharp instruments contaminated with infected blood, the booklet says.
Symptoms which may mean a person is suffering from Aids include reduced energy, fever, swollen lymph glands, loss of resistance to infections, and some cancers.
Dr Tony Smith, medical editor of the BMA's Family Doctor Publications, said better understanding would help re-duce anxiety and some mis-taken ideas about Aids.
Infectious diseases, by Dr Melvin Ramsay, 95p plus 15p p&p; BMA House, Tavistock Square, LondonBMA guide on Aids safety.

Late 1980s.Author: PHILIPPA TOOMEY
Late 1980s.chunks: Lassa fever is the great frightener but, as Dr Susan Fischer-Hoch points out, in a country like Sierra Leone, where she has just spent six weeks with a large number of cases, only 1 per cent die. Moreover, with 500 patients, barrier nursed and with proper medical care, there were no infections in the staff.The Viral Zoonoses laboratory specializes in rare haemorrhagic fevers which not only affect man, but are the viruses of animals like the rat, conveyed through mosquitoes and ticks.The laboratory provides diagnostic services, research and public education, going out into the field, and collaborating with others, such as Americans, who are doing a lot of advanced work. In London they are a Category p4 centre so they can cope with the highest form of any hazard known, or yet to arrive, to a standard where nothing at all can get out of the laboratory.Virology, she says, is an advancing field - just how close the haemorrhagic fevers are advancing we may not realize, but the Korean variety (3,000 cases in the UN forces in Korea) has appeared in 30 cases in northern France before anyone realised they had it.Exotic strains'We haven't had a serious epidemic of flu since 1969-70,' says Dr Philip Mortimer of the Virus Reference Laboratory. It used to be one every 10 years. Flu, of all viruses, keeps changing, and it is the emergence of a new strain which produces an epidemic. New vaccines must contain the new strain to be effective. 'So we'd go on collecting strains and doing isolates even if there hadn't been a pandemic for 40 years,' he says.The laboratory tends to concentrate on the more exotic and nasty problems: they also keep an eye on the polio vaccines because, as it is a live virus, it is essential to know which is a vaccine strain and which is a live strain - and on viral meningitis, myocarditis (inflamation of the muscles of the heart, which kills babies) the polyoma viruses, which cause various degenerative diseases of the brain and affect those with suppressed immunity. Then there is the group of papilloma viruses, probably implicated in cervical cancers, now on the increase and appearing in younger women. 'The parvovirus was discovered here in 1975 by Dr Cossart and Dr Field, with the South London Blood Transfusion Centre, Tooting. It produces a condition in children called Fifth Disease, and arthritis in their mothers. We're doing two studies on this. 'On Aids, the laboratory has been responsible for setting up national diagnostic system, evaluating the commercial kits, of which there are a number, providing confirmatory testing, and doing about 13,000 diagnostic tests in the course of a year. The routine work will devolve to the other laboratories in the service now that they have the tools for the work, but the important reference function will remain with the laboratory.Hazard of hepatitisThe principal concern of the small Hepatitis Epidemiology Unit is the life and works of the hepatitis B virus. 'Its prevalence is low, but it's nasty,' says Dr Sheila Polakoff. The eradication of infection of dialysis units with hepatitis B, common in the early 1970s, following studies by the unit, was an early success.But the rate of hepatitis B has risen again in the past year of so, a consequence of drug abusers and those in close contact with them. The unit is studying an infection from carrier mother to child, found in women of Chinese, African or Asian origins.It is essential to immunise the child within 48 hours of birth, and the screening for this condition is difficult, needing the help of ante-natal clinics, GPs, pediatricians, community health centres and hospitals, to spot the potential sufferers.The unit is also undertaking a survey of the infection (HCLV 3) in Aids - taking a sample of homosexuals and heterosexuals of both sexes from 12 places in the country to get some better idea of the spread of the disease.Patients found to be positive will be followed up. As Dr Polakoff says:'We can only guess at the number of people who will develop the symptoms. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 1985

The Times (London)

November 30 1989, Thursday

A to E of hepatitis; Medical Briefing

BYLINE: Dr THOMAS STUTTAFORD

SECTION: Issue 63565.

LENGTH: 634 words

 
 The bewitching smile with which the toddler Linda Prime rewarded the staff at Addenbrookes Hospital, Cambridge, as she left after her successful liver transplant, as well as the tragic failure of the battle to save the life of Mrs Aisling Barnett, has highlighted liver disease in general and transplants in particular.
 Mrs Barnett's case was comparatively unusual; she suffered acute liver failure after taking a very properly prescribed drug. Most drugs are detoxified in the liver; unfortunately, in occasional cases the liver tissue is unusually sensitive to them and liver damage, and even necrosis, occurs.
 The great majority of people, excluding those who suffer from alcoholic cirrhosis, who reach the progressive end stage of liver failure the point at which the physician can offer no more help, and only transplant surgery gives a chance of survival are not suffering from an idiosyncratic response to medical treatment, but from the late effects of viral hepatitis or auto-immune chronic liver disease. 
 Three national liver units are funded by central government. They are able to perform about 250 transplant operations a year. Last year the Royal Free Hospital in London, which has had an international reputation for the treatment of liver disease for nearly 40 years, allocated cash from its own resources to help deal with the thousands of patients in this country who are in severe liver failure, and whose only chance of survival depends on a transplant. A team led by Mr Keith Rolles undertook 23 operations 17 patients survived. Of the 23, 21 were suffering from late viral hepatitis or auto-immune disease.
 Transplants can help a few individuals, but the major impact on the death rate from liver failure can only be achieved when heavy drinkers monitor their intake, and when medical science finds ways to limit the spread of hepatitis.
 Until the late 1940s all cases of viral hepatitis were lumped together as catarrhal jaundice, but by the 1950s it was realized that there were at least two separate diseases, infectious hepatitis and serum hepatitis. Doctors now distinguish the many different types of viral hepatitis by assigning them a letter: we already have hepatitis A, B, C, D and E.
 The original infectious hepatitis is hepatitis A, and blood tests have shown 50 per cent of British people have at some time been infected with it, even though many will not have noticed an attack of jaundice. Hepatitis A is caused by a virus related to the polio virus. It is spread by infected sewage, contaminated water and unwashed hands in the kitchen. Hepatitis B is a totally different virus, only related to various animal viruses. It is a serious disease spread by blood and other body fluids including semen; it is endemic in the Third World, where it is transmitted from mother to child soon after birth. In Britain it is commonly found in health care workers, homosexuals and prostitutes. Ten per cent fail to make a full recovery, and may eventually develop cirrhosis or cancer of the liver.
 Hepatitis D is a virus which can exist only in conjunction with an established hepatitis B infection; it enhances the ill effects of the hepatitis B, and may, if the disease has become quiescent, cause a relapse.
 Hepatitis C has recently been isolated; it is usually spread by blood transfusion, probably occasionally by sexual intercourse. When the attack is severe enough to cause jaundice, it will in 50 per cent of cases give rise to chronic hepatitis, progressive liver failure and later, in an alarmingly high proportion, cancer of the liver.
 The hepatitis E virus is related to the yellow fever virus, but is not insect borne but spread by faulty sewage disposal. Outbreaks have occurred recently in Mexico, Delhi and parts of China.

The Times (London)

September 3 1987, Thursday

New drug cure for hospital infections

BYLINE: Our Science Correspondent

SECTION: Issue 62864.

LENGTH: 267 words

 
 A new drug which could be crucial in controlling epidemics of hospital infections is likely to be made available by the end of next year.
 However, leading specialists are urging the Department of Health to speed approval of the drug, mupirocin, because of its importance. 
 The drug can be given to hospital staff and patients to prevent them being infected with methicillin-resistant staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) which has affected about 100 British hospitals.
 The infection is estimated to cost the health service about Pounds 100 million a year.
 Dr Michael Kelsey, consultant microbiologist at the Whittington Hospital, London, said: 'This is the only drug we believe to be effective in eradicating the infection from the nasal membranes of carriers'.
 The drug has been developed by Beecham Pharmaceuticals in Britain and is undergoing trials since it was reformulated for the control of hospital infections.
 After the trials are completed the Government's Committee on the Safety of Medicines has to approve it before made available.
 Hospitals can already use the drug so long as it is done as part of the existing trials.
 The Government has grossly underestimated the spread of hepatitis B in Britain and should launch a drive to vaccinate those most as risk, one of the country's leading experts said yesterday.
 Professor Aris Zuckerman, director of medical microbiology at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, said there were probably 20,000 cases of the potentially fatal disease, 10 times more than the government figures of annual cases.

7 March 1988.Author: JOHN WICKS
7 March 1988.chunks: A breakthrough in the prevention of hepatitis is being claimed by Biocine, a company jointly owned by the Swiss Ciba-Geigy group and the biotechnology concern, Chiron, of Emergyville, California.Scientists working onthe project say they have isolated proteins of the so-called non-A, non-B virus of hepatitis with the aid of genetic engineering. Infection with this blood-borne virus occurs primarily during transfusions.Some 5 per cent of patients receiving blood in the US are said to come into contact with it. Half of them develop chronic hepatitis and a further fifth, cirrhosis of the liver.Biocine's discovery opens the way to a screening test and a vaccine for acute and chronic forms of related liver inflammation.The company has started the scale-up process for biotechnological manufacture of the proteins, permitting the development of immuno-diagnostic agents to screen donor blood and blood products, as well as vaccines to prevent infection. Since this will be a synthetic vaccine, there will be no risk of infection during its manufacture or administration.The next step will be to try to isolate the whole virus to establish its causative role in hepatitis non-A, non-B.An estimated 90 to 95 per cent of all cases of hepatitis arising after blood transfusions are attributed to the non-A, non-B virus, adding up to 150,000 cases annually in the US alone.

Transplant hope as TV host Harty slips into coma
by Jeff Postlewaite and Alan Massam

TV STAR Russell Harty was fighting for his life today suffering from hepatitis and acute liver failure. Doctors expressed grave concern for the 53 year-old BBC presenter and that show host, who is unconscious and in a critical condition. He is being treated in the intensive care unit of St James's University Hospital, Leeds.

Harty spent two weeks last month in Airedeale General Hospital, near his North Yorkshire home, being treated for viral jaundice. A hospital spokesman could not say which strain of hepatitis he is suffering from.

Bachelor Harty, who to TV viewers last saw on BBC's Grand Tour of Europe, could have a liver transplant even though he is so ill a leading specialist said today. Dr Roger Williams, director of the liver unit at King's College Hospital, London, said: 'I imagine that may be being considered.'

'We do a lot of transplants for liver failure at King's and our unit has about a 60-70 per cent survival rate. We do transplants for acute liver failure.' Dr Williams said acute viral hepatitis could be very severe and cause liver failure. About 200 people died as a result each year in Britain.

Hepatitis is an acute inflammation of the liver, which initially causes flu-like symptoms and later progresses to fever, acute fatigue, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and loss of appetite.

There are three types: Type A enters the body through water or food; Type B enters via blood transfusions or injections with contaminated syringes; and Type Non-A, Non-B, which again enters through transfusions. The last two types, by far the most dangerous, are highly infectious, and need to be treated by 'barrier nursing' in hospital. Hepatitis B can also be transmitted by sex practices common among homosexuals.

Harty has never made any secret of his unconventional sex life. But friends say he would rather go to bed with a good book than with a lover.

A BBC spokesman said: 'We are all very distressed to hear of Russell's illness. Our thoughts are with him.'

With his camp mannerisms and downright rudeness, Russell Harty's television interviews at their best contain an element of danger that single him out from Parkinson's chat or Wogan's charm. He is best known for his run in with seagurds Grace Jones. The TV host decided that the statuesque pop singer wasn't worth talking to, so she thought she would get her own back by clouting hapless Harty on the head. The drama was wonderful publicity for both entertain-ers and confirmed Russell Harty's status as a household name.

'I'm like a soldier who sometimes injects a tiny bit of poison into the fly,' he said.

And Harty hasn't melted with age. His recent Harty's Grand Tour of Europe series was the subject of a vituperative attack by The Observer's TV critic John Naughton who was amazed that more people hadn't answered Harty's questions with a punch.

7 March 1988.Author: No author in byline
7 March 1988.chunks: Dr Hans Popper, the Viennese-born doyen of liver pathologists the world over, died in New York on May 6 at the age of 84.For 40 years he worked on all aspects of the subject raising it to a major clinicial and scientific speciality. He made important contributions to the fields of auto-immune drug-induced and alcoholic liver disease.In recent years Popper was particularly interested in viral hepatitis, liver transfers and the mefchanisms underlying the development of cirrhosis. Blood test for rare hepatitis considered

By Our Health Services Correspondent

THE Department of Health is considering 'screening blood supplies for a new form of hepatitis to ensure the greater safety of blood transfusions, it was disclosed yesterday.

A test for the virus responsible for Hepatitis C has been developed in California and is being evaluated in Britain by scientists at the National Blood Transfusion Service.

A Department of Health spokeswoman said Hepatitis C was an extremely rare disease suffered by 0.7 per cent of the population, but the American study had shown the virus responsible was carried by 10 per cent of the population.

She said: "We have not been able to screen blood for this condition until now because no test was available that would identify it. Now that a test has become available, we are considering using it to screen blood supplies to make transfusions even safer than they are at present."

June 1989.Author: Mark Whittet
June 1989.chunks: SCOTLAND'S biggest health board is withholding the opening date of a ward for patients suffering from full-blown Aids and HIV-related diseases for fear of protest demonstrations, writes Mark Whittet.The ward is set to open sometime during August at Ruchill Hospital in Glasgow, but the city's health board has declined to name the day because of concerns over public safety.When the board started a needle exchange at the hospital last year for syringes used by drug addicts, there were public demonstrations.Greater Glasgow Health Board said that the protests proved so damaging that for a year few people used the facility.As a result, it has refused to publicise the opening of the Ruchill ward, but Dr Campbell Love, a consultant in the hopsital's communicable diseases unit, last week confirmed that the purpose-built ward will start ``sometime'' in August.Funded by the Scottish Home and Health Department at a cost of Pounds 500,000, the 15-bed ward will be the first of its kind in the west of Scotland, following a similar 15-bed facility in Edinburgh's City Hospital and another 10-bed unit in Dundee.Love stressed that the Ruchill ward had not been designed specifically for Aids patients.He said: ``There has been a lot of speculation and some misconception about this unit.``Our instructions from the Scottish Home and Health Department were that 15 beds should be made available in Glasgow to cope with the expected increase in west central Scotland in HIV related diseases over the next few years.``This ward is our response to that request. But we are not intending to segregate Aids patients. The unit will also accommodate patients suffering from a number of infectious diseases, including those who are HIV-positive or have hepatitis. ''Love added that the aim of the specialised ward was to promote a better and more efficient service for sufferers, but said that although the statistics were escalating in the Edinburgh area, the increase in Strathclyde had been lower than predicted.Scottish Office figures published last month showed 102 Aids cases in Scotland, which resulted in the deaths of exactly half. Sept 1991.chunks: Did the cost of screening allow a virus to spread? The Blood Transfusion Service has begun mass screening for hepatitis C, a rare blood-borne virus which can cause chronic liver damage and, ultimately, death. Up to 12 sufferers plan to sue the Department of Health because, they believe, screening should have begun nearly two years ago, when a test was first available. They claim cost was a major factor in postponing the screening. The C virus has recently paid out 8 million to 1,200 haemophiliacs infected with HIV from contaminated supplies of Factor VIII. But it could win the proposed action if lawyers can prove that sometimes the health needs of the many outweigh those of the individual. There are two or three cases of post-transfusion hepatitis annually. The obvious symptom is jaundice. Death can result and, 30 years ago, it was a major concern. The virus was hepatitis B, which was not identified until 1965. It took another five years to create a crude laboratory test to identify some of the blood donations which carried the virus and another 15 to give transfusion laboratories the full battery of diagnostics to detect all stages of the disease's progress. Only then could all donations be confidently shown to be clear. Even then, some post-transfusion hepatitis still occurred. Since it was not due to hepatitis B, nor to hepatitis A, which is not blood-borne, it was described as Non-A Non-B hepatitis (NANBH). Transfusion specialists, anxious to determine the incidence of NANBH, examined the medical records of patients with liver disease, but found no obvious correlation except the well-known link with heavy drinking. It took another decade before the nature of NANBH was discovered, after a Californian biotechnology company, Chiron, finally devised a new kind of test. Dr Marcela Contreras, director of the North London Blood Transfusion Service (BTS), and Dr John Barbara, a microbiologist, used the test and found that in 400 blood samples, only two showed raised liver enzyme activities consistent with NANBH. And just one was associated with the virus now called hepatitis C a prevalence of 0-25 per cent. But the new test was prone to cross-reactivity with other antibodies.

11 July 1995.chunks: _F By CELIA HALL. The country's leading charity for sufferers of liver disease yesterday condemned the Government for the "cheap and easy" ways in which it plans to tell thousands of unsuspecting people that they may have the potentially fatal liver disease hepatitis C (HCV). Arrangements to inform about 3,000 people that they may be infected with the "silent" disease, given to them in blood transfusions, were sent to all doctors this month. But Alison Rogers, director of the British Liver Trust, said yesterday: "The Department of Health has taken the cheap and easy way both on the extent of the look-back and, most critically, on the service that is provided for the unfortunate recipients of infected blood." HCV is a slow-acting liver virus which the DoH says may affect up to 1 per cent of the population. Many of these people are believed to be drug addicts. But about 8,000 people have been infected by blood transfusions or by receiving blood products to treat conditions such as haemophilia. It can take 20 or 30 years for symptoms of hepatitis to appear, and in 10 to 20 per cent of cases liver cirrhosis will develop. Following disclosures last year in the Independent that haemophiliac patients were dying, the DoH announced in January that it would instigate a look-back programme to trace patients who had received infected blood transfusions. In the meantime the Haemophilia Society, which says that at least 40 haemophiliacs who received infected blood products have died, is campaigning for compensation. The DoH has decided it will only try to trace patients who it discovered had received infected blood when it began to test donated blood for the virus after 1991. But Ms Rogers says the donor population changes and infected donors may have stopped giving before the testing began. "If someone with hepatitis C was donating blood before 1991 and not afterwards there will be no record of whether they are hepatitis C positive or not, and the recipients of their blood will not be traced," she said. The letter to doctors acknowledges this gap. It says: "Not all those transfused with potentially infectious blood prior to the commencement of testing will, however, be identified by the "look-back" procedure". Once traced, the blood transfusion centres will play a key role in counselling and arranging testing. The British Liver Trust argues that patients need to feel the information they receive is unbiased. "Patients identified by this look-back study need a source of information they perceive as unbiased - not the consultant of a blood transfusion service they may feel is to blame for their infection with hepatitis C," Ms Rogers said. Medicine 'aiding virus'

GENETIC genealogy trees of the hepatitis C virus have shown that modern medicine helped it to become the leading cause of death from liver disease, the association was told.

The genetic blueprint of a virus can be used to create virus family trees that can cast remarkable light on the origins of an epidemic.

Dr Paul Harvey, of Oxford University, said the genetic make up of the hepatitis C virus can show that the virus has been spreading rapidly over the past 30 to 50 years, as a result of vaccination and blood transfusions.

From the known rate of change of one of the genes in the virus, it is possible to tell there was an explosion in the number of varieties — and thus incidence — half-a-century ago. "That really is an impressive finding, because nobody even knew that particular virus existed until 1989," said Dr Harvey.

The virus is spread by blood products. The easiest way is transfusion, he said. Vaccination campaigns are another possibility.

Light has been thrown on the origins of Aids. The most common virus, HIV 1, was thought to have arisen from the green monkey but new findings suggest that chimpanzees may have also been important in its spread.

Scientists have discovered three previously unknown hepatitis viruses in an analysis of blood samples taken from an American doctor who contracted the disease in 1964. The doctor, known as GB, has since died: his blood samples were frozen and stored until researchers at Abbott Laboratories in Chicago had sophisticated techniques to extract the viruses. James Koziarz, vice-president of research and development at Abbott's diagnostics division, said work had started to determine what damage the viruses could cause to the liver. Genetic analysis of the new viruses shows they belong to the same flavivirus family as hepatitis C and yellow fever. Hepatitis - an inflammation of the liver - can be caused by chemicals, as well as viruses. Any or all of the new viruses could be responsible for cases of hepatitis that cannot be diagnosed with currently available tests. In one survey no known virus was found in about 15 per cent of hepatitis cases. Abbott scientists are currently trying to determine the prevalence of the viruses in the population. "Evidence indicates that the GB viruses are not merely types or subtypes within the hepatitis C group of viruses, but rather that they constitute their own distinct category of viruses," Mr Koziarz said. If the new viruses resemble hepatitis C in more than just their structure, they could pose serious health risks. Hepatitis C is causing a silent epidemic with up to 40 per cent of carriers eventually developing chronic active hepatitis.

Tests showed he was suffering from rare forms of hepatitis, including hepatitis B and E. "He was in effect a super carrier," said Miss Foster. He was told he would have to stop performing surgery while he received treatment, but it was later discovered that after September 1990 he had operated at six London hospitals - the Royal London, Guy's, St George's, St Bartholomew's, the London Chest Hospital and Harefield. After being asked for samples of his blood for hepatitis B screening, he submitted samples which were not his - at least one came from a patient. When he finally submitted his own blood in August 1993 it showed he had three forms of hepatitis. Despite further counselling, he performed surgery in four more hospitals - Lewisham, St Peter's, Chertsey, the Bethlem Royal and Maudsley and Crawley Hospital. Miss Foster told the committee: "Here we have a picture of a man who has over a substantial period of time prevaricated in order to continue as a surgeon. 26 March 2001.chunks: CONSUMERS won a landmark victory yesterday when more than 100 patients infected with Hepatitis C through blood transfusions, blood products or transplants won a GBP7million compensation battle in the High Court. Lawyers said the judgment confirmed the existence of a "no fault" regime under the Consumer Protection Act and the EU Product Liability Directive - on which it is based. It protects "anyone damaged by a defective product, in other words a product which is not as safe as the general public is entitled to expect." Anthony Mallen, of Newcastle solicitors Deas Mallen which led the campaign, said: "This is a landmark decision for consumer rights and shows that the effect of the EU directive has been significantly to strengthen product liability law in the UK and throughout Europe. "Producers are not liable for risks which are genuinely unknown to exist, but as soon as the possibly dangerous nature of the product has been discovered by someone somewhere they will be liable if they continue to supply dangerous products." Actor Timothy Pearce, who became infected with the virus after a hip replacement, yesterday spoke of his anger. Mr Pearce, 65, of Highgate, North London, was the only victim to attend court. He said: "I feel bitter that I may have been given a death sentence and that it could have been avoided by the introduction of a screening test that was in use in other countries." During the three-month case Mr Michael Brooke QC, for the claimants, said: "All of these have suffered in one way or another the stigma of being Hepatitis C sufferers. "The fact that a person is infected with HCV attracts stigma which is objectively unwarranted. The public is often confused about HCV and wrongly believes that it is similar to HIV infection. Mr Brooke explained that hepatitis meant inflammation of the liver - Hepatitis C was an illness with a "complex natural history which defies precise prognosis". Nicholas Underhill QC, for the National Blood Authority, told Mr Justice Burton: "As with any other form of medical treatment, blood transfusion cannot be made absolutely risk-free. Claimants sadly suffering this infection from products given in the course of their medical treatment does not of itself mean that they are legally entitled to compensation. The Times (London)

March 27, 2001, Tuesday

 Hepatitis cases land NHS with Pounds 10m bill

BYLINE: Helen Studd

SECTION: Home news

LENGTH: 797 words

 
 THE NHS was facing a Pounds 10 million compensation bill yesterday after more than 100 people who contracted the hepatitis C virus through medical treatment won an unprecedented High Court battle for damages.
 In six lead cases, chosen to give general guidance on damages, the judge awarded sums of up to Pounds 210,000 per person, while leaving the way open for victims to make further claims if their condition deteriorated. The NHS is now preparing itself for a flood of similar claims from sufferers of CJD and recipients of the MMR vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella, who will be able to apply the same criteria to win compensation.
 Yesterday's multi-party hearing is the first time since its introduction in 1988 that the Consumer Protection Act has been tested on medical products in the UK. At least another 2,500 hepatitis C sufferers who contracted the virus after 1988 are believed to be eligible to bring similar cases. 
 Many of the 114 claimants were young children or pregnant when they contracted the potentially fatal liver disease through blood transfusions, blood products or organ transplants following routine operations or road accidents. Some have not yet developed long-term symptoms of the condition, which may limit their life expectancy.
 The other 108 claims are expected to be along similar lines to yesterday's awards and will be decided in coming months. Crucially, however, the arguments behind yesterday's ruling can be applied to any medical product that is deemed to have put people at risk and the NHS is now bracing itself for thousands of new claims from CJD sufferers and recipients of the MMR vaccine who are able to prove that they were infected by defective medical products after 1988.
 Scientists claim that 10,000 people in Britain are harbouring CJD, which can be contracted through surgical instruments, while 2,000 children are estimated to have suffered adverse effects as a result of the MMR vaccine.
 Ruling in favour of the victims, Mr Justice Burton said: "Such infected blood did not provide the safety which persons generally are entitled to expect." He said routine screening "ought to have been introduced by March 1, 1990". It was finally introduced in the UK in April 1991, despite being used in other countries long before this date.
 The initial 114 victims took the action last year against the National Blood Authority and Velindre NHS Trust in Cardiff. They set out to prove the existence of a no-fault regime "for anyone damaged by a defective product".
 Lawyers for the group put the value of their claim at about Pounds 7 million yesterday with Pounds 3 million in costs.
 The initial six claimants included a mother in her mid-thirties who became infected by a blood transfusion during childbirth, and a young man infected after a road accident when he was nine years old.
 A man in his seventies who contracted the disease following heart surgery was awarded Pounds 53,000, while Jane Lindley, 56, a married mother of three, was awarded Pounds 210,000 after becoming infected during routine surgery to remove a cyst.
 Anthony Mallen, the solicitor who led the litigation, said the ruling had been a landmark decision that would open the way for a variety of similar claims.
 He added: "This shows that producers are not liable for risks which are genuinely unknown to exist, but as soon as the possibly dangerous nature of the product has been discovered by someone somewhere, they will be liable if they continue to supply dangerous products. The judgment is an important contribution to both UK and European law."
 The Haemophilia Society said last night that the ruling would give renewed hope to the dependants of the more than 100 people, suffering from haemophilia, who have already died of the infection.
 Mr Justice Burton is due to preside over a preliminary hearing involving another nine claimants including haemophiliacs and a woman who became infected after a heart transplant in May. He will decide whether to grant the National Blood Authority and the Velindre NHS Trust leave to appeal on April 10. A similar case is being prepared in Northern Ireland while one in Scotland has so far been blocked.
 Hepatitis C causes inflammation of the liver that can lead to liver disease, cirrhosis and liver cancer. While some of those infected would, in due course, spontaneously clear the virus from their systems, many others experienced symptoms a number of years after contracting the infection.
 Nicholas Underhill, QC, for the defence, told the court that the risk of patients contracting hepatitis C was tiny and was expected to reduce further with advances in medical science.

April 4, 2001, Wednesday

 Liability for defective blood products

SECTION: Features

LENGTH: 1372 words

 
 QUEEN'S BENCH DIVISION. Published April 4, 2001. A and Others v National Blood Authority and Another. Before Mr Justice Burton. Judgment March 26, 2001.
 When determining, under article 6 of the Product Liability Directive (85/374/EEC), what degree of safety the public were entitled to expect in a product, the impossibility of avoiding a harmful characteristic in the product by taking precautions was irrelevant.
 If the existence of a defect generally was known or should have been known in the light of accessible information, then a producer could not rely on the defence under article 7(e), regardless of whether it was possible to identify in which if any of his products that defect would occur. 
 Mr Justice Burton so held, in the Queen's Bench Division, giving judgment for A and 113 other claimants, on their claims for damages under the Consumer Protection Act 1987, made against the National Blood Authority and Velindre NHS Trust in respect of their infection with hepatitis C contracted from blood and blood products used in blood transfusions.
 Article 6 of the 1985 Directive (OJ 1985 No L210 p29) provides: "1 A product is defective when it does not provide the safety which a person is entitled to expect, taking all circumstances into account..."
 Article 7 provides: "The producer shall not be liable as a result of this Directive if he proves ... (e) that the state of scientific and technical knowledge at the time when he put the product into circulation was not such as to enable the existence of the defect to be discovered."
 Mr Michael Brooke, QC, Mr Stuart Brown, QC, Mr Ian Forrester, QC, of the Scots Bar, and Mr Jalil Asif for the claimants.
 Mr Nicholas Underhill, QC, Mr Philip Brook Smith and Ms Louise Merrett for the defendants.
 MR JUSTICE BURTON said that the 114 claimants had all been infected with the hepatitis C virus as a result of being given infected blood in transfusions for which the defendants were responsible.
 Section 2 of the Consumer Protection Act 1987 imposed strict liability on the producer of a defective product which caused damage.
 The claimants' case was that all those who received blood infected by hepatitis C after the Act came into effect on March 1, 1988 were entitled to recover damages, irrespective of any fault of the defendants.
 It was agreed that although the medical profession had known since the 1970s that there was a problem of infection by hepatitis C in transfused blood, no screening test to discover the presence of the virus in a donor's blood was even known of until Spring 1989.
 Following the introduction of screening tests throughout England and Wales in September 1991 the problem of infection through blood transfusion had been all but eliminated.
 The 1987 Act had been passed in order to implement the Product Liability Directive and, as had been held in European Commission v United Kingdom (re Product Liability Directive) (Case C-300/95) ((1997) ECR I-2649), was to be construed so as to be consistent with the Directive. Consequently both parties during the trial had concentrated on the terms of the Directive itself.
 Article 6 The parties agreed that the question to be resolved, when deciding whether a product was defective within the meaning of article 6.1, was the degree of safety which persons generally were entitled to expect.
 The claimants asserted that the conduct of the producer was irrelevant to that question, and the avoidability of the virus, whether it was possible to take any steps by way of prevention or avoidance, did not arise.
 The defendants argued that avoidability was a relevant circumstance under article 6. They submitted that avoiding the risk had been impossible and it was not legitimate for the public to expect the unattainable; all they were entitled to expect was that all reasonably available precautions had been carried out.
 His Lordship did not consider that the legitimate expectation of the public at large was that legitimately expectable tests would have been carried out or precautions adopted. Their legitimate expectation was as to the safeness of the product (or not). It was inappropriate to propose that the public should not expect the unattainable, in the sense of precautions which were impossible, at least unless it was informed as to what was unattainable or impossible.
 In his Lordship's judgment "all circumstances" in article 6.1 meant all relevant circumstances. It was quite plain that the 1985 Directive was intended to eliminate proof of fault or negligence.
 It was intended to make it easier for claimants to prove their case, so that a consumer would not have to prove that the producer did not take all legitimately expectable steps.
 His Lordship concluded therefore that "avoidability" was not one of the circumstances to be taken into account within article 6, because it was outwith the purpose of the Directive.
 His Lordship set out what he considered to be the structure for consideration under article 6.
 The first step must be to identify the harmful characteristic which caused the injury, article 4.
 The next step would be to conclude whether the product was standard or non-standard, which would be done most easily by comparing the offending product with other products of the same type or series produced by that producer.
 If the respect in which it differed from the series included the harmful characteristic, then it was non-standard.
 If it did not differ, or if the respect in which it differed did not include the harmful characteristic, then it was to be treated as a standard product.
 The primary issue in relation to a non-standard product was whether the public at large accepted the non-standard nature of the product, that is whether they accepted that a proportion of the products would be defective. They did not in this case.
 The question was one of legitimate expectation. The avoidability of the harmful characteristic, the impracticality of taking precautionary measures, and the benefit to society or utility of the product were all irrelevant considerations.
 With a standard product the sole question would be safety for the foreseeable use. "Avoidability" was again irrelevant.
 Article 7(e) The parties agreed that the defence must be based on the most advanced scientific and technical knowledge available to anyone at the time when the product was put into circulation, as long as it was accessible.
 The claimants argued that, in order to establish the defence, it was necessary to show that there was no such knowledge which had identified the problem.
 On that basis, the defendants would have no defence, since it was common ground that the existence of the hepatitis C virus in blood generally was known at all relevant times.
 The defendants argued that it was enough to show that, although the existence of the defect was known, there was no such knowledge which would have enabled a producer to discover the existence of the defect in a particular product.
 In his Lordship's judgment, the analysis of article 7(e) was entirely clear.
 If the existence of the defect was known or should have been known in the light of accessible information, then the producer continued to produce at his own risk.
 It would be inconsistent with the purpose of the 1985 Directive if a producer, in the case of a known risk, continued to supply products simply because he was unable to identify in which if any of his products that defect would occur.
 Result In his Lordship's judgment, the infected bags of blood were non-standard products since they were different from the norm which the producer intended for use by the public.
 They were defective because his Lordship was satsified that the public at large was entitled to expect that the blood transfused to them would be free from infection.
 The defendants had no defence under article 7(e), since the existence of hepatitis C in blood was known at the relevant time. Therefore the claimants succeeded.
 Solicitors: Deas Mallen, Newcastle upon Tyne; DMH, Brighton; Evill & Coleman; Freeth Cartwright, Nottingham and Howard Cohen & Co, Leeds.

26 March 2001.Title: Dublin's record hepatitis payout.
26 March 2001.Author: By John Burns.
26 March 2001.chunks: A WOMAN suffering from hepatitis C has been awarded almost #2.5m in damages, the highest compensation payment ever made to a sufferer. The settlement was made last November by the hepatitis C tribunal, which has paid out a total of #217.8m in compensation to 1,418 women suffering from the incurable disease. The woman was represented by Patrick A Hurley, a Cork solicitor. The previous record award was #1.6m. The tribunal was set up in 1995 after 1,600 women were infected with hepatitis C during pregnancy by a contaminated anti-D blood product. More than #35m has been paid by the state to legal firms representing hepatitis C victims. Almost a third of that figure - #10.7m - was earned by Ivor Fitzpatrick & Co. Figures obtained by The Sunday Times for the past six months reveal that the Fitzpatrick practice earned almost #550,000 in that time, representing 16 clients who got compensation from the tribunal, at an average of #34,375 per case. Fitzpatrick was the first legal firm to represent hepatitis C victims and did all the preliminary research. "The amount of work devoted to this research was enormous in terms of time and staff resources and was carried out at a stage when there was no guarantee of any form of professional remuneration," the firm has said. The #10.7m fees paid to Fitzpatrick include payments to barristers and accountants, as well as actuarial, medical and other professional costs incurred in making a claim to the tribunal or to the High Court on appeal. The next highest earning legal practice is Malcolmson Law, which has been paid #5.1m in fees for representing hepatitis C sufferers. More than #900,000 of this was paid in the past six months for representing 20 clients, at an average of #45,000 per case. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2001.

26 March 2001.Title: Holyrood
26 March 2001.Author: By Fraser Nelson Scottish Political Correspondent.
26 March 2001.chunks: THE Scottish National Party yesterday claimed a small victory in its attempts to secure compensation for haemophiliacs infected with hepatitis C by infected blood products. Malcolm Chisholm, the Deputy Health Minister, headed off an SNP motion in the Scottish Parliament with a promise "to examine constructively the implications" of a recent English High Court judgment. This was taken as a hint that the the Executive may support Scottish victims who may wish to sue the NHS after becoming infected. Nicola Sturgeon, the SNP's Shadow Health Minister, told the Parliament she was "greatly encouraged" by Mr Chisholm's amendment to her motion. She had expected complete opposition, with no undertaking to recognise the award of #2.5 million to six plaintiffs who sued the National Blood Authority in England. "This amendment takes us further than the Scottish Executive have gone before, and I can only encourage this as a step in the right direction," she said. "It is still a fair bit away from where we want to be." Ms Sturgeon was moving a debate on the need for compensation to be paid to haemophiliacs who contracted the disease through NHS treatment during the 1970s and 1980s. She called for a no-fault compensation scheme where all victims would be compensated by the Executive without the need to sue the NHS. This would go a stage further than England, where government compensation is refused. Mr Chisholm said that Ms Sturgeon's proposal would set a dangerous precedent for other legal action to be taken against the NHS. "Would we want to create a climate in our health care system which made it risk averse?" he said. "Would we want to see new treatments denied to people because they might involve a risk?" In England, hepatitis C victims who had contracted the disease through blood transfusion managed to sue, claiming that that contaminated blood should be categorised as a faulty product. Six plaintiffs, on behalf of 114 other victims, had sued under the Consumer Protection Act of 1987 and were awarded average compensation of #24,200. Ms Sturgeon said the ruling should hold good for Scotland, and be taken further into government policy. The Scottish Parliament has been petitioned by a group of hepatitis victims who contracted the disease in the mid-1980s. They cannot sue as they were infected before the Consumer Protection Act came into effect (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2001.

26 March 2001.Title: Compensation for NHS mistakes - Letter.
26 March 2001.Author: No author in byline
26 March 2001.chunks: From Professor John A. DavisSir, With a judge's decision (report, March 27; see also law report, April 4) that the NHS must pay damages to patients infected with the hepatitis C virus by blood transfusions, albeit at the time there was no way of checking for its presence, we have reached an important crossroads in our attitude to such accidents.One road leads to ever-increasing demands for compensation and the attribution of blame, with no great gain to anyone bar lawyers and leading to the practice of defensive medicine and the milking of public money. The other leads to the recognition that, regardless of who or what may have been responsible, persons who suffer loss or injury through no fault of their own should be helped out of public funds as a form of national insurance to recoup the strictly financial costs of their misfortune.When someone clearly was to blame, it would then be up to the relevant authority, not the injured party, to recover some or all of the cost of compensations already claimed and paid out according to need. This would save a lot of time and money for all concerned without in any way diminishing the sense of responsibility of those who hold our lives in their hands, whether they be surgeons, the drivers of motor vehicles or Railtrack.If we do not take the bull by the horns now, we shall be faced in the future with the absurdity of a patient suing a blood or organ donor (or their kin) for illness inadvertently caused by their being carriers of - for instance - BSE. Do we need more doctors or more lawyers?Yours faithfully,JOHN DAVIS,1 Cambridge Road,Great Shelford, Cambridge CB2 5JE.April 5. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2001.

26 March 2001.Title: Health: Infected blood has ruined the lives of many haemophiliacs. So why are they denied the safe, synthetic alternative?
26 March 2001.Author: No author found
26 March 2001.chunks:
The Guardian (London)

February 8, 2001

Health: Infected blood has ruined the lives of many haemophiliacs. So why are they denied the safe, synthetic alternative?

BYLINE: James Meikle

SECTION: Guardian Features Pages, Pg. 15

LENGTH: 682 words

 
 The NHS has accidentally infected 4,800 British haemophiliacs with the hepatitis C virus. Of these, 1,200 have also been infected with HIV; a third of them remain alive. Now there is a theoretical risk that the NHS has infected some of these people with the human form of BSE, the fatal variant CJD.
 No wonder many haemophiliacs are angry. As many as 5,000 people in Britain need a "clotting factor" (made from blood plasma) to treat the painful, excessive bleeding that swells their muscles as a result of haemophilia. Imagine finding out that these products were made from contaminated blood. 
 And it is no wonder adult haemophiliacs in England are demanding the same "safer" synthetic alternative (known as recombinant) that is on offer to child sufferers throughout Britain, and to older patients in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. You might think any government, having seen the effects of two previous mistakes involving tainted blood supplies, would be keen to cough up the extra cash for such treatment.
 But not a bit of it. Ministers, under pressure from the Haemophilia Society's campaign for recombinant and a public inquiry into the overall safety of blood products, appear more worried about the effect "sensationalist" press coverage would have in further distressing patients.
 Decisions on providing recombinant should be made on clinical grounds, not on whether a fuss is made. Haemophilia doctors say recombinant should be on offer, although British-sourced products, which might carry vCJD infection from donors, were replaced by US plasma in 1998. Paul Giangrande, at the Churchill centre in Oxford, says this could cost an extra pounds 23m a year.
 He, like many other centre directors, is ignoring general NHS guidance not to tell patients they have been treated with products that included material donated by someone who went on to develop vCJD. The third warning of this type, relating to treatments given before the switch to US human product, was sent out by the blood service before Christmas. Dr Giangrande has informed 85 of his patients.
 Three years ago, batches involving other vCJD patients had to be recalled. Then, some directors, including Dr Giangrande, told; some did not. Now the NHS is reviewing that don't-tell policy, implemented because vCJD cannot be detected before symptoms are evident. It is also untreatable and incurable. Some haemophiliacs are convinced they have been infected again, and some of the most militant sufferers believe they are acting the canaries in the coal mine in an experiment to see if vCJD can be transmitted through blood.
 Reassurances from officials may have little impact. Sufferers know that the NHS, worried enough to have changed the source of most plasma and to have introduced other blood controls at a combined cost of pounds 83m a year in England and North Wales, has been further alarmed by evidence from an experiment with sheep that showed BSE can be transmitted by transfusion. Now officials are considering whether anyone who has received a blood transfusion should be allowed to donate blood themselves.
 It could be years before we know if there has been human transmission. The incubation period of vCJD is unknown, and the disease has been identified for less than five years. If most of the current 94 victims were infected by cheap meat products in the mid-80s, how much longer before we know the condition's eventual scale?
 Thirteen victims so far have been blood donors, their donations transfused into 23 people, as well as going into blood products used by thousands at home and abroad. The government should be desperately seeking to shore up confidence in blood transfusion, but when it is gearing up to spend pounds 200m on new hospital sterilisation measures, pounds 30m on disposable instruments for tonsillectomies and, if necessary, a great deal more on changing other surgical procedures, can they blame haemophiliacs for thinking another pounds 23m is small change?
 James Meikle is the Guardian's health correspondent. Sarah Boseley is away.

 Victim was told that she had ten years to live
26 March 2001.Author: No author found

The Times (London)

March 27, 2001, Tuesday

 Victim was told that she had ten years to live

BYLINE: Helen Studd

SECTION: Home news

LENGTH: 531 words

 
 WHEN Jane Lindley had a routine operation to remove a cyst 11 years ago she had never heard of hepatitis C and hailed her blood transfusion as a life-saver.
 Four years later she was told that she had ten years to live, the beginnings of cirrhosis of the liver and would need a liver transplant. "No one told me about the risks of a blood transfusion and I had never even heard of hepatitis C," she said. 
 Subsequent medical tests showed that Mrs Lindley, 56, a mother of three children, had cirrhosis of the liver, a condition normally suffered by alcoholics. At a time when hepatitis C was little-known even among the medical profession, her doctor assumed that heavy drinking was to blame.
 It was then in 1994 that doctors told her the prognosis. From contracting the disease she had just ten years to live. She had been living with hepatitis C for four years but despite a painful course of Alfa-Interferon injections to help to suppress the virus, her condition deteriorated.
 By 1998 she was virtually housebound, unable to muster the energy to carry out even the simplest household chores.She suffered from excruciating joint and stomach pain and her skin turned a sallow shade of yellow. That March she was told that she needed a liver transplant or would die.
 Luckily for her the transplant was successful and Mrs Lindley found herself with a new lease of life and the energy to do things on her own for the first time in years.
 Yesterday she was awarded more than Pounds 210,000 in compensation from the National Blood Authority.
 "The prognosis is uncertain and I could start rejecting at any time," she said. "My faith and my family have got me through."
 Less optimistic, however, was Timothy Pearce, 65. As he left the High Court after the hearing yesterday, the bitterness and pain of the past nine years was etched on his face.
 Mr Pearce had broken down as he told how the disease, which he had contracted during a hip operation in 1991, had become an "early death sentence".
 He claims that he has been drained of his vitality. He has lost his job, been inflicted with endless bouts of flu and had been forced to resign as a coach for his local football team.
 Despite previous appearances in the film Jesus of Nazareth, and the television shows Minder and EastEnders, he has also been unable to get a manager to promote his career and more recently has had trouble getting insurance.
 "I am frightened about what the future holds," he said outside the High Court yesterday. "I am not confident that there will ever be a cure.
 "Ever since the operation, I've never really felt like myself. I am just not the person I was before. I have become increasingly tired and lethargic. I am now very susceptible to colds, flu and have massive problems with my teeth."
 Mr Pearce, of Highgate, North London, first became aware of the infection in 1995 when he was traced as part of a "look-back" programme by the National Blood Authority.
 He is one of 30 people who were infected on or after the beginning of April 1991 whose claims were settled shortly before the trial began. Their claims will be assessed later in the hearing.

Haemophiliacs fear it could leave them vulnerable to bloodborne infections. In the past patients have been infected with HIV and hepatitis C from blood products. The development comes just days after it was revealed that 206 non-haemophiliacs in Scotland developed hepatitis C from infected blood transfusions. The victims are currently involved in a dispute with Susan Deacon, the health minister, over compensation. More than 300 haemophiliacs also contracted hepatitis C from blood products. Sufferers were told about the switch in their drug treatment in a letter sent by doctors at haemophilia centres across Scotland. The letter warned that younger Scots may also have to give up the treatment as the shortage takes hold later in the year. Recombinant Factor 8 replaced a less safe, non heat-treated variety of the drug which was derived from human plasma about a decade ago. The new form is manufactured from genetic material so does not carry the same risks as products made from human plasma. Philip Dolan, a haemophiliac from Glasgow who has already contracted hepatitis C, said sufferers were wary of going back to the older form. "I have enough recombinant at home to take when I go to the dentist for a filling to prevent excessive bleeding. After that, I really don't know what to do," said Dolan. Although haemophiliacs have been told the older, plasma-based Factor 8 is safe, they are unconvinced. "We know the Factor 8 which is made in Scotland goes through one viral inactivation process, but it is not heat-treated and we believe this is potentially unsafe," said Dolan. Members of the Haemophilia Society recently told the health and community care committee of the Scottish parliament that they had not been informed of the risks of developing hepatitis C before products were made safer in the late 1980s. Karin Pappenheim, the chief executive of the Haemophilia Society, said the UK health departments were doing all they could to ensure that children and babies continued to get Factor 8. "It's almost like war-time rationing - they're really having to eke it out," she said. The shortage came about because one of the three manufacturers of the product, Bayer, has had production difficulties in America. The other two suppliers, Baxter and Wyeth, are unable to keep up with demand. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2001.

26 March 2001.Title: DOCTOR'S FURY AT BLOOD DEATHS
26 March 2001.Author: MARK BLACKLOCK
26 March 2001.chunks: A DOCTOR yesterday blamed the Government for killing 77 of his patients with infected blood products. Dr Peter Jones, a world haemophilia expert, called for a public inquiry into the scandal of sufferers of the illness who were treated with contaminated supplies from abroad. He said the authorities were responsible because the transfusion service in Britain had been underfunded for decades, forcing doctors to seek products from overseas to meet demand. Thousands of people may have contracted HIV or hepatitis C viruses as a result. Dr Jones, an executive member of the World Federation of Haemophilia, was head of a regional treatment centre at Newcastle upon Tyne's Royal Victoria Infirmary during the Seventies and Eighties. The transfusion service could not meet demand for blood products, and doctors all over the country used imported supplies of the clotting agent Factor VIII. But that was made from blood bought from drunks and drug-addicted prisoners in the United States and from the slums of South Africa. One infected donor could contaminate thousands if suspect blood was used to make the clotting agent. Today only 18 of the 105 patients Dr Jones treated on Tyneside are still alive because 95 of them became infected with HIV and hepatitis C.  "We were all devastated when the true horror of what had happened started to unfold in the mid-Eighties," he said. "At the haemophilia centre we were like one big family and myself and my colleagues had always tried to be completely open and honest with our patients. "The Government promised us that Britain would be self-sufficient in blood products by 1977 but in fact we have never been able to meet demand and we are still importing plasma from the US. "So many of my patients died, as they did at centres across the UK, and as their doctor I felt responsible." Public inquiries into the safety of blood supplies have been started in Ireland, Canada, and Germany. "It is a basic human right that patients have their questions about their treatment answered and that accidents occurring in the course of that treatment are explained," he said. Dr Jones spoke out before addressing the inquiry in Dublin. A Department of Health spokeswoman said the Government did not believe it would be "in anybody's interests" to hold a public inquiry. "Little was known about HIV and Aids at the time and a test did not exist until 1985," she said. "Factor VIII was in great demand from haemophiliacs."

26 March 2001.Title: Hepatitis jabs for court staff as heroin bust junkie is jailed.
26 March 2001.Author: By DONNA CARTON.
26 March 2001.chunks: EXCLUSIVE  A COURTHOUSE went on hepatitis alert last week when it was discovered a heroin junkie had been diagnosed as having the virus. Thomas Morgan was in front of a magistrate facing charges of having heroin. A probation report revealed that he had Hepatitis C and possibily the more dangerous Hepatitis B. His condition was referred to the Northern Ireland Court Service who took medical advice. As a result, all staff at Newtownards Courthouse were told to attend their GP and have injections against both Hepatitis C and B. And the alert was later widened to include police and prison staff who had been in contact with Morgan during the case. A legal source said: "The court staff were advised to visit their GP and receive injections. "Because they are not free on the NHS, the staff each had to pay out #41.50 for the injections. However, they will be reimbursed." Court officials were so concerned about the spread of the virus that anything Morgan touched in court was thrown out. Hepatitis C is the less serious strain of the virus, affecting the liver and be caught from a blood transfusion and injecting from illegal drugs. Hepatitis B, caught in the same way, is regarded as much more serious. Morgan pleaded guilty last Tuesday to having eight grammes of heroin with an estimated street value of around #1,500. Magistrate John Fyffe sentenced Morgan to six months in prison and said he should seek rehabilitation on release. Before being led away, Morgan told the RM: "God sparing, you will not see me within the next 10 years."

26 March 2001.Title: This careless error has wrecked our lives.I'm here for justice
26 March 2001.Author: No author in byline
26 March 2001.chunks: HAEMOPHILIACS infected by hepatitis C through tainted blood products renewed their demands for compensation yesterday as they gave evidence to a committee of MSPs. About 400 haemophiliacs in Scotland have contracted the disease and at least 15 have died in the last 15 years. The Scottish National Blood Transfusion Service insisted there were technical reasons why the service was 18 months behind England in producing treated blood product which eliminates the virus. Its arguments have satisfied Health Minister Susan Deacon but sufferers have waged an angry campaign for compensation. Here we tell the moving story of how a wife has coped with her haemophiliac husband's suffering. PAT McAUGHEY is not fainthearted. She is a nurse. She has seen patients die, burn victims weep in their sleep, children so sick they need tubes to breathe. And although she has done her best to help them all, human misery is nothing new to her. It is something to be borne bravely. But when she tells how her gentle, doting husband cannot dare even to pick up his beloved grandchildren for fear of infecting them with the hepatitis C that courses through his veins, she has to squeeze her eyes to stop herself from crying. She simply feels he has been robbed. John McAughey, 60, was born a haemophiliac. After years of blood infusions and spontaneous, painful bleeding, he had it under control. Once o r twice a month he would visit Ninewells Hospital in Dundee. It was no more than an inconvenience and he felt safe there, knowing his wife was nearby, comforted by the fact that the regular doses of Factor 8 would help his blood clot and ease the agony in his joints. Little did he realise that the very infusions designed to save life would in fact result in destroying it. In 1991 he was, without his knowledge, tested twice for HIV and hepatitis C after an influx of infected blood polluted the health service. He was found positive for the latter on both occasions but, incredibly, he and his family were not told until 12 months later. Fortunately, he did not pass on the virus which is so infectious that a spot of blood can remain 'active' for three months. But he easily could have done. He and his wife have had to practise safe sex ever since and will have to do so forever more. Their one glint of hope is that the haemophilia will die with them. Only men can contract haemophilia, but it is carried by women. The couple's sons John, 32, and Tommy, 33, are safe. Their daughter Wendy, 30, had a 50 per cent chance of passing it on. But her two sons, aged 18 months and four years, were both, joyfully, given the all-clear. Mrs McAughey, 54, travelled to Edinburgh alone from the family home in Perth to give evidence to the Scottish parliament's health and community care committee as part of a bid by the Haemophilia Society for compensation. There are 6,000 haemophiliacs in Britain, 600 in Scotland. And 4,800 300 north of the Border were infected by HIV or hepatitis C, or even both. They are grim statistics, but Mrs McAughey is determined to be more than just a number. She says: 'There is a terrible stigma attached to hepatitis C. People seem to think it's like Aids. It's not. But it's a life sentence all the same. John had enough problems with the haemophilia. But he coped. We coped. 'He should never have been given hepatitis. What makes me even angrier is that measures were brought in south of the Border to screen blood products in 1985, yet nothing was done in Scotland for another two years. That is criminal in my book. 'We don't know when John was infected, but that could have saved him. The cruelty is that we will never know.' Mr McAughey is at home, too sick to travel. The internal bleeding caused by his haemophilia is getting steadily worse because he is now wary of blood infusions. A bad bleed can confine him to bed for up to three weeks, and this occurs on average every other month. He has had to give up his job as an antiques dealer as a result. The bleeds, left unchecked, have given him chronic arthritis, which has crippled his shoulders, fingers, hips, knees and ankles. And the hepatitis is also getting worse as his liver slowly packs up. He has never been a drinker but he cannot now have so much as a glass of wine with a meal because his liver could not cope. The future is uncertain. Cirrhosis is a probability, a transplant possible. Mrs McAughey says: 'John has no appetite. The hepatitis is always there and the symptoms are horrendous headaches, dizziness, loss of concentration, memory lapses, muscular pain, fatigue, anorexia, nausea and insomnia. 'He is tired all the time. He only sleeps for three hours a night. We have been married for 35 years. We are a normal, healthy couple and still share a bed but this thing has disrupted both our lives, and affects the children. Our eldest grandchild is 11 and he is old enough now to understand that his grandad is poorly. 'But it's heartbreaking to see the two younger ones. They'll go bounding up to him but John is nervous. He can't hug them and show affection as he should, as he would like to. If one of them falls over and cuts their knee, he can't help. It's a terrible, terrible disease. And there's such a lot of ignorance surrounding it. Our friends and neighbours have been wonderful, but you hear these terrible stories of the children of infected haemophiliacs being shunned in the playground. Taunted for having "dirty blood". 'At least we haven't had to go through that. But we do want justice. 'Our life has been stolen from us and nothing can ever get it back. At the very least we deserve some compensation, some recognition. 'No amount of money can ever make John well again. But it would help us feel happier about the future. At present we are just living day-today, and that is not easy.' The committee's findings are expected to be released in the next few months, but already 900 of the 4,800 haemophiliacs who were infected in the Seventies and Eighties are dead, and that figure is rising. Mrs McAughey only hopes her husband will still be alive when the hoped-for judgment finally comes. 'It's like playing Russian roulette,' she says sadly, walking away. 'Every day.'

 Race to find patients at risk of CJD
26 March 2001.Author: No author found
26 March 2001.chunks:
The Times (London)

January 30, 2001, Tuesday

 Race to find patients at risk of CJD

BYLINE: David Charter, Health Correspondent

SECTION: Home news

LENGTH: 667 words

 
 THE Government was trying last night to trace scores of haemophiliacs at risk from catching the human form of "mad cow" disease after admitting that NHS patients were treated with blood products from a man who died of vCJD.
 Ministers immediately announced counselling arrangements for patients and their families who will face an agonising wait to learn if they received the infected treatment.
 The admission last night by Lord Hunt of Kings Heath, the junior Health Minister, will alarm Britain's 10,000 haemophiliacs. The incident echoes the 1980s blood contamination scandals when 4,800 haemophiliacs contracted hepatitis C and 1,200 caught HIV. 
 The disclosure came as one of the Government's advisers on vCJD accused ministers of "seriously misleading" the public over the safety of hospital treatment. Michael Banner, the chairman of a group of experts set up to control vCJD, considered quitting the CJD Incidents Panel over his concerns about surgery.
 In a letter to Liam Donaldson, the Chief Medical Officer, he accused the Government of not taking the panel seriously. Civil Service support of the panel was a "shambles", he said. He did not know from one day to the next which official he would be dealing with because none was assigned to the panel. His letter landed on Professor Donaldson's desk as Parliament heard that scientists were combing hospital records to find how many haemophiliacs were given a clotting agent made from a blood donor in 1996 or 1997 who later learnt that he had vCJD.
 The Government banned the use of British plasma in the manufacture of blood products in 1998 as a precautionary measure against the risk that vCJD can be transmitted in this way. Lord Morris of Manchester, the Labour peer who is honorary president of the Haemophilia Society, said: "This has come as a devastating shock to the haemophiliac community who have already been stricken by HIV and hepatitis C infection in the course of NHS treatment."
 He added: "I will be discussing the minister's reply very urgently with the Haemophilia Society. No one seems to know how many people may be affected but the society is doing all it can to counsel families that have cause to believe they were affected. The implications are very serious."
 Lord Hunt admitted that it was too early to tell how many haemophiliacs might have been affected but sought to play down the risks. He said: "We would stress that any risk of transmission of vCJD through blood products is theoretical. There have been no reported cases of vCJD among the haemophilia community."
 Professor Banner, of King's College London, criticised just such reassurances as "seriously misleading" in his letter, saying the incubation period was too long to be at all certain.
 He took issue with a statement from John Denham, the Health Minister, who said: "We have no evidence of any patient being infected with variant CJD in hospital. But while we are still learning about the progress of vCJD we should take precautions to reduce the theoretical risk of transmission."
 Professor Banner said that "simply overlooked" the fact that the vCJD incubation period could be 20 years and was therefore "not as reassuring as it may seem".
 Earlier this month ministers announced Pounds 200 million to improve hospital sterilisation, including Pounds 25 million for disposable instruments for all tonsillectomies. Professor Banner implied that all high-risk operations should be performed with disposable instruments.
 He said: "While no one within the Department of Health would intend to mislead the public, it is a matter of great concern if the public is misled, even as a result of lack of care in setting out the current state of knowledge in a clear and frank form."
 In the letter he added: "The course of events up to this point may suggest to the public that the Department of Health is not taking seriously the very important issues of public health which are the concern of the panel."

After newspaper articles about the service based on information provided by Mr Shayler, the Attorney-General had obtained an injunction prohibiting, pending trial, the publication of any information that Mr Shayler had gained during his employment. Allowing the appeal, the court held that while publication of the article defeated the purpose of the injunction, it had not been shown that S had been aware that it would do so. A proviso to the injunction requiring anyone wishing to publish material within its ambit to obtain the AG's consent was disproportionate to any public interest and contrary to the European Convention on Human Rights 1950 Art. 10. 26 March 2001.Title: Haemophiliacs risk deathin blood treatment protest.
26 March 2001.Author: By LORRAINE FRASERMedical Correspondent.
26 March 2001.chunks: HAEMOPHILIACS are refusing to take a life-saving - though potentially deadly - treatment in protest at the refusal of the NHS to pay for them to receive medication free from the risks of them contracting HIV or vCJD.Dozens of sufferers have stopped using a standard NHS treatment and risk bleeding to death. They say they would rather suffer the pain of their illness or die, than continue to take it.The "treatment strike" only applies to sufferers in England, where health authorities are refusing to find the #23 million a year to switch from blood-derived treatment to a genetically engineered treatment, which is safer.Most of the men on strike are ill with HIV and hepatitis C virus infection, contracted from the contaminated blood clotting treatment they received on the NHS in the 1970s and 1980s. Now many have been told they are among hundreds, including children, to have received treatment made from the blood of a victim of vCJD, the human form of BSE.Marc Payton, 40, from Worcestershire, said last night: "It's time to make a stand. The pain is horrific without treatment and people are afraid to go back to that, but I feel that if we don't nothing will get done. "People with haemophilia are unable to make their own supply of key blood clotting proteins, most commonly Factor VIII, and unless they get this through treatment they can suffer painful bleeding into the joints and potentially fatal internal haemorrhage. A death among the protesters, which is possible, would provoke an outcry.The drastic protest is a measure of the anger many haemophiliacs now feel towards the Government and the NHS. Of 1,200 sufferers who contracted HIV from blood-derived treatment, 800 have died. Hundreds are living with hepatitis C or both viruses, contracted before heat treatment to destroy them was introduced in the mid-1980s.Those who have survived blame the Department of Health for their illnesses, saying it has failed repeatedly to recognise the risks of contamination in the Factor VIII made from human blood plasma, and continues to do so. Even now, blood-derived Factor VIII is known to be contaminated with viruses which can be harmful to individuals with a damaged immune system.Mr Payton, who has HIV and hepatitis C and has had cancer because the Aids virus has damaged his immune system, said the possible vCJD contamination was the last straw. He sent back his supply of plasma-derived Factor VIII to the Queen Elizabeth Hospital, Edgbaston, three weeks ago.He said: "It has destroyed my life and I am not prepared to take any more. Every time you inject it you are injecting something that is supposed to be life-saving but effectively it's a killer. It is slowly poisoning us. "Health ministers are struggling to explain why English haemophiliacs are discriminated against. Lord Hunt, the health minister, met their representatives a fortnight ago but has yet to make an announcement.
