26 March 2001.Title: At last, bad blood victims seem to be getting justice
26 March 2001.Author: Paul Cunningham
26 March 2001.chunks: Tragic stories stun tribunal THE Lindsay Tribunal into the deaths of 75 people from infected blood supplies enters its final stages in the New Year. RTE newsman PAUL CUNNINGHAM has closely monitored evidence presented to the inquiry. Here he examines harrowing cases of suffering as a result of the scandal. One child victim was mercilessly taunted in the playground while a dad contracted AIDS after going into hospital for a routine operation. The inquiry is due to report its findings in May. The State-backed Blood Transfusion Service will be under the spotlight. Cunningham also questions the way Ministers have approached this disturbing national tragedy. TO hear a father talk about the "relief" he felt when his 11-year-old son died is shocking. But it becomes understandable when you hear the pain that the young child had to endure before his death. He was "a pathetic little sight...so thin you'd be afraid to look at him, almost blind, his eyes were like golfballs, his body like something out of Auschwitz". This was just one tragic story out of 43 told to the Lindsay Tribunal this year as it investigated why 220 haemophiliacs got HIV and hepatitis C from contaminated blood products. The clotting agents which were supposed to help haemophiliacs and prevent bleeding ended up killing 75 of them. Delays Their plight captured public attention not just because of that pain but also because the medical profession seemingly didn't care. Haemophiliacs claimed HIV tests were performed without their permission, there were lengthy delays in telling people they were HIV positive and little or no counselling was provided. Even at the end, the bodies were put into black bags and sealed - preventing family members from seeing their loved ones. The horror also extended to family and friends. Karen Stephens spoke of how her father Jerome contracted HIV from blood products then went on to develop AIDS and die. Karen was in school at the time and most of the other pupils wouldn't hold her hands during games and were told by their parents to wash themselves if she made contact with them. The job of the tribunal is to find out why this tragedy happened and establish who was responsible. The main focus so far has been on the Blood Transfusion Service Board (BTSB) - the body which looks after blood supplies in Ireland. Some new information has already come out: While most of the blood products were imported from the U.S., Irish-made clotting agents infected seven haemophiliacs here with HIV, and five have died as a result. The tribunal, led by Judge Alison Lindsay, has also heard that the BTSB was effectively broke in the early 1980s, it had serious management problems a few years later, critical records were destroyed in the early 1990s and a senior employee had a conflict of interest. The BTSB board also took some apparently strange decisions. Once it disregarded the advice of its leading medical officer. On another occasion, it agreed to indemnify a drug firm so that if its product infected anyone it would not be legally responsible. The tribunal's work to date has already thrown light on a hidden tragedy which affected a vulnerable group of people totally reliant on a clean and safe blood supply. In one case, a blood sample was taken from a haemophiliac to conduct an HIV test without his knowledge or permission. On the same day, the doctor advised the man that it would be OK to try to have a family. The man's wife told the tribunal that the test was HIV positive but they were not informed for seven months by which time she was five months' pregnant. She had to wait another six weeks before finding out she was HIV negative. After her husband's death, she had to fight to ensure that AIDS was not written down on the death certificate. This was a man who went into hospital to get an ingrown hair removed from his back and was given a contaminated clotting agent. The Government has recently announced that haemophiliacs who contacted HIV due to contaminated blood products will be able to get money by applying to a Compensation Tribunal. Elections That wasn't always the Government's response. In 1989 Charlie Haughey collapsed a government rather than pay Pounds 400,000 to infected haemophiliacs to help them with their medical expenses. Some money finally began to come through after haemophiliacs put forward candidates for elections on the compensation issue. With a tribunal operating and money now available, it seems that the haemophiliac community is finally getting justice. Yet, no matter who is held responsible and what money is paid it will not bring back the 75 people who died or take away the suffering of those still battling with illness. Paul Cunningham is researching a book into the scandal. It is expected to be published during 2001. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2000

26 March 2001.chunks: THE FOOD Standards Agency demanded an urgent investigation yesterday into lax abattoir procedures in Germany, after discovering pieces of potentially BSE-infected spinal cord in 41 tons of imported beef. The Consumers' Association said the discovery of the shipment from Germany strengthened the case for labelling animal-derived food, especially beef, with the countries in which the animals were born and raised. That will not be required until January 2002, despite demands for its implementation for the past five years. Vets in Northern Ireland impounded the shipment at two meat processing plants in Newry, Co Down, and are expected to destroy it. They discovered pieces of the spinal cord - which, under EU-wide rules implemented in October, should have been removed - still hanging from carcasses. The spinal cord and brain of BSE-infected cows are potentially thousands of times more infective than any other part of the body. In humans, BSE infection is thought to lead to variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (vCJD), a fatal brain disorder with no known cure. Suzi Leather, the deputy chairwoman of the FSA, said: "Consumers have the right to be reassured that European-wide controls are being effectively enforced. We have referred this breach of the EU's BSE controls for an investigation by the German authorities and the European Commission." The FSA said it believed the beef had been shipped to Britain, possibly Liverpool, in sealed containers before completing its journey by sea and road. However, they were unable to say what sort of food the beef would have been used to make. Morris McAllister, director of the FSA in Northern Ireland, said: "None of this meat will get anywhere near the human food chain thanks to decisive action by the FSA and our colleagues in the Northern Ireland Department of Agriculture and Rural Development." A spokeswoman for the Consumers' Association said the discovery pointed up a basic weakness in food labelling standards. "We have been calling for this since August 1995," she said. In a separate development hundreds of British haemophiliacs have been warned they could have been infected with vCJD by plasma made from a blood donor who has subsequently been diagnosed with the disease. The warning came from Bio Products Laboratory (BPL) in Elstree, which has written to centres around the country which treat haemophiliacs with its blood clotting products, which are derived from plasma in donated blood. The letter notes that a person who gave blood in 1997 - a year before the Government ordered BPL to source plasma from the United States - has subsequently been diagnosed with vCJD. However, it insists that "there is no evidence that vCJD has been transmitted by blood products and therefore [the risk of infection in this case] is considered to be a theoretical risk". But the letter does list the potentially infected plasma batches, so centres can trace any patients who may have received transfusions. The news has outraged Britain's haemophiliacs, who have endured earlier problems in the 1980s over contamination of clotting factors used by the NHS. That resulted in 4,800 haemophiliacs being infected with hepatitis C, and 1,200 were also infected with HIV. Chris Hodgson, a haemophiliac who has chaired the Haemophilia Society since 1997, said: "We are so angry because we feel more care should have been taken. We are kept in constant danger. I know it is a theoretical risk but when I read the letter I thought: here we go again. You wonder what's next."

The Times (London)

December 26, 2000, Tuesday

 Patients angry over blood risk in England

BYLINE: Philip Webster

SECTION: Home news

LENGTH: 557 words

 
 THOUSANDS of people suffering from haemophilia are being subjected to unnecessary risk from deadly viruses because the Government has failed to order health authorities to ensure that they have the safest possible treatment, it was claimed last night.
 Renewed fears that vCJD, the human form of "mad cow" disease, may be far more widespread than suspected has increased demands on the Government to end the "scandal" under which treatment for haemophiliacs depends purely on where they live.
 Experts stress that there are no known cases of haemophiliacs suffering from vCJD and the risk is "theoretical". But campaigners say that any risk is completely avoidable and the Government should act. Some people who have contracted vCJD are known to have been blood donors. 
 Many hospitals and doctors across England are treating adult haemophiliacs with products derived from human plasma, which can still transmit blood-borne viruses in spite of big advances since the 1980s when haemophiliacs were infected with HIV, the Aids virus, and hepatitis C.
 In Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland and some health authorities in England, some haemophiliacs have already changed or are on the point of changing to the alternative clotting factors known as "recombinants", which are genetically produced.
 They are much safer but around 30 per cent more expensive. The devolved administrations in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have decided that they should be generally prescribed.
 Some 1,200 people were infected with HIV and 4,000 with hepatitis C from contaminated blood supplies in the 1970s and 1980s.
 The problem with the human-derived treatment is that a massive number of blood donors - between 3,000 and 5,000 - are needed to contribute to a single batch of plasma from which individuals are treated, thus multiplying the potential risk.
 Liam Fox, the Shadow Health Secretary, said that the Government should now act to stop haemophiliacs in England being treated as second-class citizens.
 "We are asking a group of people who have already been through such trauma and pain with HIV and hepatitis to be at greater risk than they need be. It is absolutely intolerable that we should put haemophiliacs at risk purely to save money. The risk is only a theoretical one at the moment but there is no need for any extra risk here. The alternative treatment is available and should be given," he said.
 Haemophilia is a genetic condition. Sufferers are at risk of haemorrhaging because they lack Factor VIII, the protein that causes blood to clot. Treatment involves injection with products containing the missing protein. There are some 6,000 sufferers in the United Kingdom.
 Mark Weaving, a spokesman for the Haemophilia Society, said the Government had honoured a commitment to ensure that all children aged under 16 suffering from haemophilia were treated with recombinants.
 He said that since 1986 plasma had been specially treated to eliminate known viruses such as HIV and hepatitis. "They have not been shown to have been transmitted since then, " he said. He added that there had been no cases of vCJD among haemophilia suffers. However, he said that it was known that some viruses could still get through despite the treatment of the plasma and that it was impossible to eliminate all risk.

26 March 2001.Title: I've lost a brother and an uncle because of contaminated blood, now my son Jordan could ...
26 March 2001.Author: By ALEXANDRA WILLIAMS.
26 March 2001.chunks: I've lost a brother and an uncle because of contaminated blood, now my son Jordan could be dying from vCJD. AN Irish mother who lost two members of her family because of contaminated blood transfusions is living with the fear that her haemophiliac son may have CJD. Eight-year-old Jordan Mc-Envoy was given blood from a man who died from the human form of mad cow disease. Now his mother Susan says he risks contracting the killer illness. And she claims cost-cutting led to him being given inferior treatments in the first place. Susan, 36, said: "I am so angry. This could have been prevented. But now my son's at risk from variant CJD and nobody can tell me for sure that he hasn't contracted it. There's no test for it." Susan's agony is compounded by the fact that three haemo-philiac members of her family were given HIV-contaminated blood in Dublin in 1984. Her eldest brother Gerard died of Aids in 1992 at the age of 33, and her uncle Benny McEnvoy died in 1989. Another brother still in Dublin is being treated with drugs to stave off Aids. Susan, who lives in London, spoke out after haemophiliac Marc Payton from Rubery, Worcestershire, revealed last week that contaminated blood had exposed him to vCJD. Marc, 39, also has hepatitis and HIV. Susan said: "It's like genocide. That man has been cheated out of a life just to save money." Jordan was born in 1992, three months after the death of his uncle Gerard. Haemophilia is a hereditary condition passed through the mother, who has a 50 per cent chance of passing it to her sons. Because the blood is stopped from clotting naturally, a cut can mean bleeding to death and a bruise can lead to internal haemorrhaging. Susan injected Jordan every other day with a clotting factor made from blood plasma. But when he was five she learned that the blood product he had been given from London's Royal Free Hospital came from a vCJD sufferer. Susan, a single mum who moved from Dublin to Clapton 15 years ago, said: "I nearly had a heart attack when the hospital told me. "After what happened with the Aids virus I was scared stiff. "They patronised the life out of me at the hospital. "The doctor was like a robot reading a memo when he told me that the risks of Jordan getting vCJD from the blood were theoretical. "When I asked him how he knew, he couldn't tell me. I want to know the full details. "I was treated like an idiot but it's simple for the doctor to blurt out what he wants when it's not his son." A year before the hospital discovered Jordan had been treated with a contaminated batch they had already switched him to man-made blood products (recombinant). Susan said: "I'm relieved that Jordan has recombinant. The risk of viral infection through a genetically engineered product is greatly reduced. "All haemophiliacs should have it. The British government pumps money into futile projects like the Dome but penny pinches when it comes to health. "I feel like it's a wait and see situation with Jordan's health. "Every time he's ill and it's not a cold I get worried that it could be symptoms of vCJD. If he has a headache I make him lie down because I just don't know what I'm dealing with. I am waiting on tenterhooks until someone develops a test for vCJD." In Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland all haemophiliacs are given recombinant, but in England it is only prescribed to children under the age of 16. A spokesman from The Haemophilia Society, which is campaigning for recombinant and a public inquiry in England into the safety of blood products, said: "It is illogical to make them available for under-16s only. "If cost is the reason it's being withheld then it's a false economy." He said more patients were refusing treatment with a clotting factor from human sources. Instead, they joined networks that allowed patients who do get recombinant to send their doses to others without it. One patient who did this last year forced his health authority to pay for the treatment. There are 10,000 haemophiliacs in Britain. The vCJD scare echoes the 1980s blood contamination scandals when 4,800 haemophiliacs were accidentally infected with the hepatitis C virus. Of these, 1,200 were infected with HIV, and only a third of them are still alive. It could be years before doctors know if there has been human transmission. The incubation period of variant CJD is unknown and the disease has been identified for less than five years. When questioned in January, Britain's Junior Health Minister Lord Hunt said it was too early to assess the extent of any infection. He said: "We would stress that any risk of transmission of vCJD through blood products is theoretical. "There have been no reported cases of vCJD among the haemophiliac community." But Michael Banner, the chair of a group of experts set up to control vCJD, criticised such reassurances as "seriously misleading". Susan said: "I am angry. I have watched my brother die over five years from Aids after he had contaminated blood. It has to stop. It's pure and simple penny-pinching but it could be costing lives." A spokeswoman for Britain's Department of Health said they now have safeguards against vCJD transmission. In 1998 they stopped using plasma from UK donors. She said: "There is no evidence worldwide that vCJD of any type has been transmitted via blood or blood products, although the possibility cannot be ruled out. "Since 1998, as a precaution against this theoretical risk, no blood products have been manufactured using plasma from UK donors. US donors are now used. "All children under 16 and all new patients receive recombinant. "The Haemophilia Society has now asked the government to provide recombinant clotting factors for all haemophiliacs but there is currently a worldwide shortage of recombinant. "Ministers are now giving this careful consideration."

26 March 2001.Title: Needles, the deadly threat on NHS wards; Scandal of 100,000 accidents a year that could be avoided
26 March 2001.Author: BEEZY MARSH
26 March 2001.chunks: DOCTORS and nurses are being put at risk of life-threatening illnesses because the NHS does not have enough money to provide safer needles. More than 100,000 needle injuries occur every year on Health Service wards, exposing medical staff to incurable diseases such as HIV and hepatitis C. Nearly every doctor and nurse in Britain can expect to be accidentally jabbed by a needle in any three-year period. Experts say many of these incidents could be avoided by using needles fitted with safety guards, which close around the tip on withdrawal from the patient's arm. Such devices a legal requirement in all hospitals in the United States cost twice as much as regular needles. The most sophisticated kits cost ten times more. Campaigners believe the Department of Health is reluctant to introduce them because using safety needles for taking blood or giving injections would add between Pounds 25million and Pounds 40million a year to health service costs. The full extent of needle injuries in the NHS is due to be revealed at a conference on occupational blood-borne viruses in London later this month. Researchers at the newly- formed Safer Needles for Safer Health Care Network audited accidents at 14 hospitals throughout Britain. Preliminary results show that at least 100,000 injuries are occurring every year, though the true figure could be higher because many staff fail to report the accidents. Consultant anaesthetist Philip Bickford Smith, chairman of the campaign group, said: 'There is a fear among managers that the costs for safer needles could spiral out of control. 'We don't think that is the case, and they have to offset that against the cost of counselling and treating those who have suffered such an injury.' A Department of Health spokesman said few safer needles had been identified that could be supplied under medical devices regulations. MARTIN Alster, above, faced the nightmare prospect of being infected with hepatitis C which can cause total liver failure after injuring himself on a needle. The 37-year-old nurse from King's Lynn, Norfolk, pricked his finger after taking blood from a drug abuser who was carrying the infection. The married father of one underwent an immediate blood test, but faced a three-month wait for the results. A second, quicker test wrongly gave a false positive result because it had been taken too early. He was later given the all-clear. Mr Alster, a mental health specialist, said: 'I went through agony. Some of my patients were infected with hepatitis C and it was very difficult to hear what they were going through knowing it could be me.'

26 March 2001.Title: Lover with HIV guilty of risking woman's life.
26 March 2001.Author: Gillian Harris Scotland Correspondent.
26 March 2001.chunks: A WHIRLWIND romance that began at a party led yesterday to Britain's first court conviction for knowingly infecting a lover with the HIV virus.Stephen Kelly, 33, was found guilty of culpable and reckless conduct by having unprotected sex knowing that he was risking the life of his lover, Anne Craig, 34.Miss Craig, from Manchester, found that she had become HIV positive within three months of first sleeping with him. After the verdict, she said: "I am delighted that justice has been done and hope this will be a deterrent to others. If the verdict saves one life from the misery I have been through then it will all have been worthwhile. "Over the last few years I have fought to get my life back together but it can never be the same. Similarly, the lives of my children, other family and close friends have been damaged. "Sentencing of Kelly was deferred until March 16. During the nine-day trial at Glasgow High Court, the jury was told that the couple met at a Glasgow party in January 1994. Before they slept together for the first time, within hours of meeting, Miss Craig asked him if there was any reason other than pregnancy why they should not have unprotected sex. Kelly replied: "No. "In fact, Kelly, a heroin addict from Provanmill, Glasgow, had contracted HIV after sharing dirty needles with other prisoners while serving a sentence for assault and attempted robbery in Glenochil jail, Clackmannanshire.Kelly, a widower with two children, had received his HIV test results in July 1993. He was tested as part of the prison's voluntary screening programme, prompted by an outbreak of hepatitis. He was advised about the importance of practising safe sex.Anne Thompson, a nurse from Ruchill Hospital in Glasgow, who talked to Kelly about his condition, said that he seemed intelligent and aware of the potentially devastating consequences of unprotected sex. Kelly told Miss Craig that he had been tested negative for HIV.Evidence that Kelly was the likely source of her infection was given by Andrew Leigh-Brown, Professor of Evolutionary Genetics at Edinburgh University, an expert on HIV. He told the court that the strain of the virus uncovered at Glenochil prison was the same one which showed up in Miss Craig's blood sample from March 1994.Kelly later claimed to have caught the virus from a former girlfriend.Donald Findlay, QC, defending Kelly, suggested to Miss Craig that she had been fully aware of Kelly's condition but had unprotected sex with him because of the obsessive nature of their relationship.Miss Craig, a mother of three, denied the claim but admitted that after her diagnosis she continued to see Kelly. She said that her family had disowned her and she was afraid of dying alone. Her solicitor, Cameron Fyfe, said she would now pursue a claim for criminal injuries compensation to help support her children aged 16, 14 and nine.The case was brought under Scottish common law because there is no criminal charge of deliberately infecting a person with the HIV virus in Scotland. In England and Wales, it became a criminal offence in 1997. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2001.

26 March 2001.Title: DNA therapy could be safe cure for haemophilia, say American doctors.
26 March 2001.Author: By Michael Durham Health Correspondent.
26 March 2001.chunks: Haemophilia affects 10,000 people in Britain and, in the most severe cases, can cause internal bleeding in joints, vital organs and soft tissue. Many victims lose so much blood they need regular injections of the blood clotting agent factor VIII. The new technique, developed by doctors in Boston, uses genetic engineering to replace missing sequences of DNA that control the manufacture of factor VIII. It is much safer than existing treatments because there is no risk of contamination from blood products. In the 1980s, thousands of haemophiliacs in Britain became infected by HIV and hepatitis C after being treated with contaminated blood products. More than 900 have died of Aids because of the contamination. The new technique works by doctors extracting skin cells from patients unable to produce their own clotting agent and then welding them with snippets of synthetic DNA before they are cultivated in a test tube and implanted into tissue near the patient's stomach. Tests on six sufferers showed success in four cases in which the patients became markedly better after the therapy. But the improvement only lasted up to 10 months. Although so few patients have received the treatment, doctors believe it could become a safe and effective alternative to existing therapies, which can cost up to #100,000 a year for each patient. Dr David Roth, director of haemophilia research at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Centre in Boston, who led the research, said: "This is not a cure, but it has opened the door. It is completely safe because it uses patients' own cells, not other products. The patients felt great and were much less ill."  Haemophilia, which is transmitted through the female genes but affects mainly men, is extremely disabling in severe cases. There is no cure, but the disease is usually controlled by regular injections of plasma.

The college issued a statement stressing that no member of the public had been at risk at any time. "Hepatitis C virus infects around 200m carriers worldwide," it said. "This research project intended to produce a new type of hybrid hepatitis C virus which would allow researchers to speed up their search for a vaccine and to replace the use of animals in much of this work."
 But the case was a reminder that in every university town, every teaching hospital, in pharmaceutical laboratories and in big health clinics, researchers are working with the invisible agents of sickness and death. They handle radioactive isotopes, powerful toxins, unstable chemicals and the huge arsenal of infectious microbes that enters hospitals with almost every patient.
 Neither Imperial College, nor the public health laboratory service, nor the Wellcome Trust, which recently pumped pounds 525m into improving Britain's research labs, would be drawn into any discussion of the latest case.
 But John Oxford, a professor in charge of a lab at the Royal London hospital's medical college, admitted the news was worrying. "One is dealing with a few more dangerous organisms now than previously and we are manipulating them. Before, you could say with your hand on your heart 'there is no problem'. Now there is always a degree of doubt, because you are trying to create something new." Herpes, influenza, the common cold, syphilis and HIV are public health hazards. About 20 completely new infections have emerged in the past two decades, and researchers are also altering genes of microbes to try to develop safer vaccines and new treatments.
 Scientists' lives would be easier if the labs in Britain were state of the art and designed for modern research. But after nearly 20 years of neglect many, as the science minister Lord Sainsbury has noted, are "appalling". The buildings are far older than the regulations now governing them and many safety arrangements have been tacked on rather than built in. "That does not make for good working practice in terms of efficiency nor, I believe, safety," said Lord Sainsbury.
 The government and the Wellcome Trust, the world's largest medical charity, announced pounds 1.75bn for research and to restore university "infrastructure". For "infrastructure" read laboratories. "Decades of neglect have left our university research facilities dilapidated," said a Wellcome Trust spokesman. "Long term political and financial commitment is now required to make sure they never get so run down again."
 The world's most lethal microbes - the so-called level four infections such as Ebola virus, Lassa fever and Spanish influenza - are dealt with in special high security institutions at Porton Down, in Wiltshire, the public health laboratory service at Colindale, north London, and the national institute for medical research at Mill Hill, north London.
 But if laboratory researchers sometimes seem casual about the microbes they handle, that is because they know that there is even more infection outside the labs. There could be 10,000 microbes in a cubic metre of air, a billion in a crumb of soil. "There are maybe 100m in your throat, in your nose, in your gastrointestinal tract, in your skin," said Professor Oxford. "They sit there quite happily, unless something upsets the equilibrium."
 Meningitis microbes live in millions of human throats, only rarely migrating to inflame the brain. Tuberculosis is another threat; probably one person in three is a healthy carrier. Last week US researchers confirmed another hazard for us all - an examination of dollar bills in Ohio re vealed that one in 14 was smeared with microbes that could lead to serious illness, with nine in 10 carrying germs including Haemolytic streptococcus, the notorious "flesh eating bug".
 Scientists agree on the need for strict discipline and tightly monitored working practices. But great discoveries have arisen from what is now considered bad practice. In labs today food is not permitted. But a more casual attitude used to prevail: in 1946 a US engineer studying microwaves found they melted the candy in his pocket - that led to the microwave oven.
 While they wait to learn the court sentence, the St Mary's hospital team may recall another story closer to home, beginning with a stack of bacteria laden culture dishes sitting in a sink. "The health and safety executive and everyone else would have had a fit," said Prof Oxford. Fortunately for the human race, the researcher concerned looked at each dish before dropping it into the washing up.
 One of them was not only mouldy but the mould had killed all the infectious bacteria around it. That was Penicillium notatum. The researcher was Sir Alexander Fleming. The discovery was the first antibiotic. And the hospital was St Mary's.

26 March 2001.Title: Patients still face postcode lottery over new drugs.
26 March 2001.Author: By Gaby Hinsliff and Kamal Ahmed.
26 March 2001.chunks: ONE health authority in five is denying patients expensive drugs in defiance of the government body set up to end NHS rationing. Thousands of patients are missing out on new treatments for conditions from diabetes to motor neurone disease even though the drugs have been cleared by the National Institute for Clinical Excellence (Nice), a survey shows. Respondents blamed lack of cash.

26 March 2001.Title: 'Three years in jail isn't enough.. I might not see my boy grow up'.
26 March 2001.Author: By JAMES TAIT.
26 March 2001.chunks: HIV DANGER DENTIST PUT 4,500 PATIENTS AT RISK  A DANGER dentist who exposed up to 5,000 patients to the risk of HIV by using dirty equipment was jailed for three years yesterday. As William Duff, 39, was led away, his former patients hit out. Mum-of-one Ellen Barclay, 35, from Glasgow, faces an agonising wait for the results of an HIV test after Duff carried out unnecessary work on her teeth. The tearful mum said: "I'm absolutely terrified. "Three years isn't good enough - he'll be out in 15 months. I might not see my seven-year-old son grow up." Moanne Russell, 37, suffered 11 years of pain after unnecessary treatment. Duff also left part of a metal tool in her mouth. Moanne, of Summerston, Glasgow, was offered #40,000 compensation but insists it is not enough. She said: "Three years isn't good enough. This man caused me a lot of pain." At Glasgow Sheriff Court yesterday, Duff was sentenced to 21 months for recklessly exposing patients to the risk of infection by repeatedly using unsterilised equipment. He also received 15 months for making fraudulent claims totalling more than #11,800 from his surgery in Maryhill, Glasgow, and his home in Kilbarchan, Renfrewshire. Greater Glasgow Health Board is now trying to trace the 4,500 patients treated by Duff between 1990 and 1994. Those at risk from Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C or HIV will receive a letter in the next two weeks offering tests and counselling. Health board consultant Dr Syed Ahmed said: "We believe the risk of transmission of these blood borne viruses is small. "But it is impossible to estimate the risk accurately and the only way of assessing if a patient has been infected is to have a test for all three viruses. "Patients who wish to have the blood test will be offered counselling prior to the test." Dental records are routinely kept for only two years, which will make the task of tracing patients difficult. But the health board said it would work with the dental practices division of the common services agency to trace the patients. The General Dental Council erased Duff from the Dentists' Register in 1997 after finding him guilty of serious professional misconduct. The GDC's professional conduct committee said erasing his name from the register was necessary "for the protection of members of the public".

26 March 2001.Title: Acambis - Tempus.
26 March 2001.Author: Robert Cole.
26 March 2001.chunks: ACAMBIS, the biotechnology company formerly called Peptide Therapeutics, has made an impressive fightback from the failure of its overambitious vaccine against all allergies.Yesterday the company unveiled positive early trial results for a vaccine against Japanese encephalitis - a mosquito-borne viral disease afflicting up to 100,000 people, mostly in Asia. The data appear to validate both the ChimeraVax technology platform from which the vaccine was developed, and the logic of acquiring the US company OraVax, which owned it.The results were early stage, but showed that the vaccine produced a good antibody response. Moreover, it is possible that vaccines for hepatitis C and other conditions can be developed from the same platform.Acambis has developed a strong intellectual property position in vaccines and the harnessing of the immune system to prevent and treat disease. Both are hot areas of medical research. A strategic alliance last year with Baxter Healthcare, which agreed to invest #28 million, underpins confidence in Acambis. Baxter brings technological and distribution skills and will give invaluable help to Acambis in its quest to bring its products to market. Baxter's presence also creates takeover excitement.The firm already has products enough to commend the stock. But it is also likely to seek acquisitions that will strengthen its position. The share price, however, fails to reflect the company's progress and potential. Buy. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2001.

August 2001.Title: Schering hepatitis drug gets go
August 2001.Author: By ADRIAN MICHAELS.
August 2001.chunks: Schering-Plough announced yesterday that a more convenient and effective version of its successful hepatitis C treatment had been approved by US regulators. The approval by the Food and Drug Administration is a welcome piece of good news for the US pharmaceuticals company which is otherwise in trouble with the FDA over manufacturing quality deficiencies. Many large pharmaceuticals companies have suffered setbacks in drug approvals at the FDA this year. However, Schering said that a sustained-release, once-a-week, version of Intron-A - called Peg-Intron - had been approved in combination with another drug, Rebetol. The combination has been more effective in the treatment of hepatitis C than previous formulations and also involves fewer injections. Intron-A and related drugs are Schering's second-biggest sellers after Claritin, its allergy blockbuster. They are also used in the treatment of some cancers and last year earned revenues of $1.4bn. "Ten years ago, there were no approved therapies for hepatitis C. Today ... physicians have an improved treatment regimen that is more convenient for patients," said Richard Zahn, president of Schering Laboratories. Roche, the Swiss pharmaceuticals company, has seen its competitor to Peg-Intron, called Pegasys, held up by the FDA. It was approved in Switzerland this week. Schering's FDA problems have caused large disruption to production, resulting in profit warnings and stifled growth. The manufacturing issues have also held up approval for the successor drug to Claritin, its allergy blockbuster.

August 2001.Title: SHORTS - Drug boost for Schering.
August 2001.Author: No author in byline
August 2001.chunks: Schering-Plough, US pharmaceuticals company, has had approval from regulators of a more convenient and effective version of its hepatitis C treatment. Page 27.

August 2001.Title: Roche acquires  Hepatitis C  drug rights from ICN.
August 2001.Author: By DAVID FIRN IN LONDON.
August 2001.chunks: In a move to beef up its product pipeline, Roche, the Swiss healthcare group, has acquired the rights to levovirin, an experimental treatment for hepatitis C, from ICN Pharmaceuticals of the US. The decision to license levovirin, a follow on product to ribavarin, ICN's leading antiviral treatment, is the first sign that Roche is serious about its recently-announced strategy of acquiring products to fill the gaps left after a number of its own medicines failed. Levovirin is a "cleaned-up" version of ribavirin with fewer toxic side effects. The acquisition is also a coup in Roche's battle with Schering-Plough, the US group, over dominance of the hepatitis market. Schering-Plough had the right to license levovirin from ICN, but did not take it up. Roche and Schering-Plough are both poised to launch new hepatitis treatments based on interferon. Roche's candidate, Pagasys, seems to have the edge over Schering-Plough's PEG-Intron in clinical trials. However, the launch of Pegasys has been held up by closer than expected scrutiny from US regulators, giving Schering-Plough a head start in the market. Roche faces a lean year following a fall in pharmaceutical sales in 2000. Pegasys is one of the few major product launches planned for this year. Analysts expect it to have peak sales of $900m. Mark Booty of Commerzbank said levovirin could give Roche the edge it needed to catch up with PEG-Inton. "Combining Pegasys with a cleaned up version of ribavirin has the hallmarks of turning it into a very serious competitor to Schering Plough," he said. Roche will pay ICN a one-time licensing fee, as well as milestone payments, and a royalty on sales. Roche will also give ICN a compound at a similar stage of development. Separately Roche has signed a five year agreement with deCode, the Icelandic genomics company, to develop tests for genetic diseases. It follows an earlier agreement to hunt for the genes that cause conditions such as cardiovascular disease and schizophrenia. The new deal could be worth up to $300m in research payments and royalties to deCode.

August 2001.Title: COMPANIES &FINANCE EUROPE - Roche drug delay takes edge off growing sales.
August 2001.Author: DAVID FIRN and WILLIAM HALL.
August 2001.chunks: Roche, the Swiss pharma-ceutical company, said it expected full-year operating profit to equal last year's SFr4.3bn ( $2.6bn), after reporting a 7 per cent rise in sales for the first nine months yesterday.However, delays to the launch of Pegasys, its hepatitis C treatment, overshadowed accelerating pharmaceutical sales.Franz Humer, chairman and chief executive, said the core pharmaceuticals operation outgrew the market for the second quarter in a row. "In the last six months the world pharma market was growing at 10 per cent and we were growing at 12 per cent," he said.However, growth is expected to slow in the fourth quarter, and Mr Humer refused to say whether Roche would outpace competitors in 2002.Roche is under pressure to launch new medicines because the US patent on its number-three drug, acne treatment Roaccutan, expires in February.However, the launch of Pegasys has been put back to the second half of next year, following modifications to the production process, giving a head start to Peg-Intron, the Schering-Plough treatment.Mr Humer played down the problem saying Roche would also launch a new type of HIV treatment, T-20, next year.Sales for the nine months to September 30 were SFr21.6bn up from SFr20.2bn a year ago. Diagnostics sales climbed 12 per cent - outpacing the market by a considerable margin. Sales of vitamins and fine chemicals, seen as a possible divesment, were up just 4 per cent, missing analysts' forecasts.Mr Humer said the pharmaceutical figures showed that plans to shed 3,000 jobs - the biggest cutbacks in Roche's 105-year history - were having an effect. "We are focusing our resources on the key products in terms of promotion, advertising and marketing," he said.However, Denise Anderson, analyst at Julius Baer in Zurich, said growth in pharmaceuticals would remain below average for the foreseeable future. Margins were low and the pipeline weak, she said.Last year the pharmaceuticals division had an operating margin of 18 per cent compared with 30.7 per cent at Novartis, its arch rival.Roche also said that it did not expect any contribution from financial operations in the second half.Last year financial income, which has underpinned growth for several years, was SFr1.7bn. Financial income was SFr1.5bn in the first half of 2001.

August 2001.Title: USFDA panel split on Lilly sepsis drug.
August 2001.Author: By ADRIAN MICHAELS IN NEW YORK AND VICTORIA GRIFFITH IN BOSTON.
August 2001.chunks: Eli Lilly on Tuesday suffered a setback in efforts to have its breakthrough treatment for sepsis, or septic shock, approved by regulators. An advisory panel to the US Food and Drug Administration was split over whether to recommend approval of the drug, originally known as Zovant and now called Xigris. The FDA, which normally follows panel advice, could be prompted to delay approval after 10 of 20 panel members voted against. Xigris has already been held up by the FDA once this year over manufacturing quality concerns. In addition, Tuesday's panel hearing had been delayed by the September 11 terrorist attacks. The drug was hailed by some analysts as the most exciting expected approval this year. Sepsis is an often fatal condition that affects 1.5m people worldwide. Tuesday's split decision surprised analysts, who had expected Xigris to be recommended. Some panel members urged more clinical studies, unconvinced that the drug had demonstrated a clear benefit. Lilly says it saves the lives of a significant number of patients. The FDA could decide to limit severely the number of situations for which the drug's administration is approved. Such limitations, stated on the drug's label, could mean that as few as 25 per cent of sepsis patients would be prescribed the drug, so cutting into Xigris sales. "Restrictive labelling often does not have the desired effect, but in the case of Xigris it may, because of stringent enforcement by hospitals due to its high expected cost," said Barbara Ryan, analyst at Deutsche Banc Alex Brown. Lilly had been hoping for more positive news from the panel and its shares may come under further pressure on Wednesday. The company has already suffered at the hands of investors this month. It scaled back earnings forecasts in response to competition from generic equivalents to Prozac, the anti-depressant drug. Roche, the Swiss pharmaceutical company, said it expected full-year operating profit to equal last year's SFr4.3bn ($2.6bn), after reporting a 7 per cent rise in sales for the first nine months on Tuesday. However, delays to the launch of Pegasys, its hepatitis C treatment, overshadowed accelerating pharmaceutical sales.

August 2001.Title: Roche.
August 2001.Author: No author in byline
August 2001.chunks: Roche seems to be responding to treatment better than expected. The 5 per cent growth in first-half pharmaceutical sales - 11 per cent in the second quarter - and jump in operating margin to 19 per cent all beat forecasts. But Kytril, a drug acquired from GlaxoSmithKline, contributed half the sales increase - and last year's second quarter was particularly weak. While an improving product mix helped the margin, cost-cutting was the biggest factor. The success of the restructuring at least suggests Roche can achieve its planned SFr600m annual savings by 2003 - and get its operating margin into the 20-25 per cent range. But it remains difficult to see how Roche can meet its other target: matching industry sales growth. It has only one big drugs launch planned - Pegasys, a hepatitis C drug that will come up against Schering-Plough's PegIntron. A merger or acquisition looks the only way to resuscitate the top line. Speculation over a Bayer tie-up has intensified since the latter's withdrawal of Baycol. This might be a good cultural and therapeutic fit. But it would not solve Roche's sales growth and late-stage pipeline problems. Novartis, with 20 per cent of voting shares, could also hardly be expected to sit back and watch Roche get together with Bayer. And a cross-Basle merger still looks the best option. It would have huge cost-cutting potential, and put Roche back among the drugs industry giants. Unless its family shareholders show they are open to such a move, Roche's shares, on 23 times 2002 earnings, look unlikely to narrow their discount to the sector.

August 2001.Title: Older haemophiliacs hit by rationing of safest drugs.
August 2001.Author: By Jennifer Trueland.
August 2001.chunks: HUNDREDS of older haemophiliacs in Scotland are being denied risk-free treatment because limited supplies of the safest drugs are being diverted for use among children. A worldwide shortage of Recombinant Factor 8 - a genetically modified agent that thickens the blood - means that supplies will be rationed for the rest of this year. Although Scotland was ahead of England in making sure everyone received the safest treatment, Scots over 30 have been told to go back to using a riskier form of Factor 8. Haemophiliacs fear it could leave them vulnerable to bloodborne infections. In the past patients have been infected with HIV and hepatitis C from blood products. The development comes just days after it was revealed that 206 non-haemophiliacs in Scotland developed hepatitis C from infected blood transfusions. The victims are currently involved in a dispute with Susan Deacon, the health minister, over compensation. More than 300 haemophiliacs also contracted hepatitis C from blood products. Sufferers were told about the switch in their drug treatment in a letter sent by doctors at haemophilia centres across Scotland. The letter warned that younger Scots may also have to give up the treatment as the shortage takes hold later in the year. Recombinant Factor 8 replaced a less safe, non heat-treated variety of the drug which was derived from human plasma about a decade ago. The new form is manufactured from genetic material so does not carry the same risks as products made from human plasma. Philip Dolan, a haemophiliac from Glasgow who has already contracted hepatitis C, said sufferers were wary of going back to the older form. "I have enough recombinant at home to take when I go to the dentist for a filling to prevent excessive bleeding. After that, I really don't know what to do," said Dolan. Although haemophiliacs have been told the older, plasma-based Factor 8 is safe, they are unconvinced. "We know the Factor 8 which is made in Scotland goes through one viral inactivation process, but it is not heat-treated and we believe this is potentially unsafe," said Dolan. Members of the Haemophilia Society recently told the health and community care committee of the Scottish parliament that they had not been informed of the risks of developing hepatitis C before products were made safer in the late 1980s. Karin Pappenheim, the chief executive of the Haemophilia Society, said the UK health departments were doing all they could to ensure that children and babies continued to get Factor 8. "It's almost like war-time rationing - they're really having to eke it out," she said. The shortage came about because one of the three manufacturers of the product, Bayer, has had production difficulties in America. The other two suppliers, Baxter and Wyeth, are unable to keep up with demand. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2001.

June 2002.Title: Haemophiliacs demand pounds 522m payout
June 2002.Author: No author found

The Guardian (London)

June 19, 2002

Haemophiliacs demand pounds 522m payout

BYLINE: James Meikle Health correspondent

SECTION: Guardian Home Pages, Pg. 4

LENGTH: 227 words

 
 The government yesterday faced demands for a pounds 522m 10 year compensation package for more than 2,800 people with haemophilia who were infected with hepatitis C through contaminated blood products before 1990.
 Many are suffering the consequences of acquiring the virus which can cause liver conditions, including cancer. Some have died from the infection which can take many years to manifest itself.
 The Haemophilia Society is trying to overturn ministerial opposition to financial assistance. The Department of Health has argued that the dangers of the infection spreading through the use of clotting factors made up from contaminated blood donations were unknown at the time. But six countries have implemented payments to infected haemophiliacs.
 The scheme for an English equivalent would involve payments depending on the severity of the condition caused by hepatitis C and include com pensation for loss of earnings and financial assistance for relatives of those who have died.
 The scheme, worked out for the society by legal, financial and medical experts, would give an average of pounds 144,000 per person.
 The patients are most likely to have been infected between 1969 and 1985 - before heat treatment of blood donations was introduced.

June 2002.Author: Richie Taylor
June 2002.chunks: Joy over new moveA NEW compensation deal worth more than 100million has been agreed for haemophiliacs infected by blood products.The deal was reached between the Irish Haemophilia Society and Health Minister Micheal Martin.In the arrangement the state will overturn a "full and final" financial settlement from 11 years ago.The move opens the way for further compensation.Minister Martin said he believed the settlement would be a "fair and equitable one. June 2002.Title: A safer solution - Letter.
June 2002.Author: No author in byline
June 2002.chunks: IT IS welcome news that the government is finally waking up to the theoretical risk of the transfer of vCJD through contaminated blood products (Blood ban to curb CJD, News, March 31). However, it needs to consider carefully whether a ban on anyone who has had surgery being a blood donor is really the best way to address this problem.For people with haemophilia - 95% of whom contracted either hepatitis C or HIV or both through contaminated blood products during the 1970s and 1980s - the solution to this problem is very clear. In Scotland and Wales, all people with haemophilia receive a treatment called recombinant, which is genetically engineered and eliminates the possibility of infection from contaminated blood. Adult patients in England and Northern Ireland, however, do not receive recombinant, opening themselves up to the risk of contracting vCJD or other blood-borne infections.Everybody with haemophilia should have the choice of the safest form of treatment possible - recombinant. With the government now considering how to prevent the spread of vCJD through contaminated blood products, it is time for them to end the existing anomaly and prevent a repeat of the tragedy which devastated our patient community.Chris HodgsonThe Haemophilia Society(c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2002.

June 2002.Title: BLOOD BOARD 'SORRY' FOR HEP C MUM AGONY.
June 2002.Author: By NIALL MOONAN.
June 2002.chunks: THE Blood Board yesterday apologised in court to a woman who cried for a year after contracting Hepatitis C.  Devastated Eleanor Healy, 51, said the infection she received from tainted Anti-D plasma was just like getting AIDS. Her son also contracted the infection. In Dublin's High Court yesterday, the Blood Transfusion Service Board said sorry for her nightmare. The BTSB's senior counsel Paul Gallagher said he was instructed to apologise unreservedly for the injury she had suffered. He said the board was anxious to minimise the worry and stress for Mrs Healy. Mr Gallagher said the BTSB did not dispute Mrs Healy's claim for loss of earnings. They would, however, dispute a claim that Mrs Healy had been infected by a second batch of anti-D and they would challenge her claim to be entitled to aggravated or exemplary damages. Mrs Healy was given anti-D at the birth of a daughter in 1977 from a batch of blood product manufactured by the BTSB, which tested positive for Hepatitis C. She claimed she was also infected from another batch in 1993 at the birth of a son. Mrs Healy, of North Dublin, is suing the BTSB, the Minister for Health and the State.

June 2002.Title: Make those responsible for blood fiasco face justice.
June 2002.Author: No author in byline
June 2002.chunks: OUR revelation today that health officials ignored repeated warnings that blood products used in the UK were potentially lethal beggars belief. The figures are quite staggering: up to 2,000 people died as a direct result of being infected with contaminated blood or blood products and a further 4,000 are currently infected and, in some cases, dying. This tragedy was entirely avoidable: as early as 1975, US hepatitis expert Dr Garrott Allen warned the UK Government Blood Products Laboratory that US blood was "extraordinarily hazardous". And this, mark you, before HIV and Aids had been properly identified. What more would anyone have to say to highlight the risks? As it happens, more was said: throughout the Eighties warnings continued to come through - and continued to be ignored. And so thousands of patients were injected with contaminated blood; most notably haemophiliacs, who were repeatedly injected and, as a result, became infected with HIV and hepatitis C. When, a couple of years ago, similar cases came to light in France, the reaction on this side of the Channel was one of horror. It seemed inconceivable that officials charged with looking after public health should have knowingly allowed the sick and the vulnerable to be infected with a potentially fatal disease. It couldn't happen here, we were assured. June 2002.chunks: FORMER Tory and Labour ministers could face criminal charges over the use of contaminated blood in the NHS which infected thousands with HIV and hepatitis C. Terence Grange, chairman of ACPO's personal crime division, has written to the Crown Prosecution Service to see if there is enough evidence for a criminal prosecution. Thousands of people received contaminated blood or blood products from the Seventies until the early Nineties. The scandal has been described as the worst medical treatment disaster in the NHS's history. So far up to 2,000 have died and another 4,000 are infected or dying. Pregnant women and individuals undergoing operations were among those given infected blood. But most at risk were haemophiliacs who were repeatedly injected with unsafe imported blood-clotting products. One victim was Colette Wintle, 43, from Tunbridge Wells, Kent, who was infected with hepatitis B and C in 1982 from blood products used to treat her haemophilia. The former nurse said: "I am in constant pain and often exhausted. I am terrified about my future. I have the most lethal and difficultto-treat type of hepatitis C." Mr Grange's move follows the convictions of former health ministers in Italy, France and Japan. Last night he said: "This could well be a scandal. If the allegations in the documents are true we may have to involve criminal law." The new legal move comes as the Government orders hospitals to import US blood supplies to ensure children under six are not infected with CJD, the human form of mad cow disease. Furious health campaigners say American blood has an appalling contamination record and point to recent evidence of US safety violations. Mr Grange will examine Government memos, internal blood company documents and secret reports from the Government's Public Health Service Laboratory which reveal UK health officials have long ignored warnings that blood products were dangerous. Some of these documents have been seen by the Sunday Express. One, dated May 1983, from the PHSL to the Health Department, advised immediate withdrawal of all US blood products because they had caused three HIV infections in haemophiliacs. They never were. ANOTHER is a letter from an American hepatitis expert to the Government Blood Products Laboratory, dated July 1975. It warned US blood was taken from high-risk groups such as prisoners and "skid-row derelicts" and was "extraordinarily hazardous".  Hepatitis runs wild

BYLINE: Dr Thomas Stuttaford

SECTION: Features

LENGTH: 818 words

 
 Pictures of the body of Rachel Whitear, who died from a heroin overdose, lying on the floor of her flat, outraged many people. But her mother defended their use, saying that she hoped it would prove a powerful deterrent to other adolescents who were tempted to use intravenous drugs.
 Mrs Whitear is backing the latest campaign, run by the charity DrugScope, to cut the number of drug-related deaths in the UK. At present, 39 per cent of drug deaths in Western Europe happen in Britain. 
 In her broadcasts, Mrs Whitear has focused on sudden deaths following an overdose. She has not publicised the dangers of hepatitis C, another hazard of injected drugs, which may affect the occasional "recreational" user as well as the addict. Unless the disease is diagnosed and treated early, the epidemic of hepatitis C may, over 20 or 30 years, kill more than those who at present die from overdoses. Hepatitis C may not echo the terrible biblical threat of afflicting descendants to the third and fourth generation, but it can be transmitted to partners, and 5 per cent of women with hepatitis C will infect their unborn babies. One of the speakers at a recent conference on liver diseases in Madrid described the increasing frequency with which young people in their early twenties are now awaiting liver transplants as a result of hepatitis C caught from their mothers in utero.
 Doctors who attended the Madrid meeting, the annual conference of the European Association of the Study of the Liver, were given statistics relating to hepatitis C which suggested that it was destined to become one of the major public health problems of the 21st century. Approximately 170 million people are already infected. In the United States there are four million sufferers, five million in Western Europe, and two million in Japan. The incidence is highest in African countries: in Egypt, for instance, nearly 20 per cent of the population has been infected.
 In one case in five, a patient with hepatitis C will show signs and symptoms recognisable as acute hepatitis soon after infection. In the other cases, the disease proceeds without notice to the chronic stage of hepatitis C. They will much later complain of such vague symptoms as tiredness, nausea, and occasionally flu-like troubles, but within 20 years 10 per cent will have developed cirrhosis, and within 30 years 20 per cent will have done so.
 In the UK it is estimated that there are between 200,000 and 400,000 people who carry the disease, but the prevalence varies between different sub-groups of the population.
 Fifty per cent of patients attending drug centres are positive for hepatitis C; the Madrid conference was told that 70 to 80 per cent of those who have mainlined drugs have been infected. Conversely, 1 per cent of those attending genito urinary clinics test positive, but only 0.04 per cent of the general population. In one of the major medical disasters of the past century, the overwhelming majority of people with haemophilia in the UK were infected by the use of blood products contaminated with the virus.
 Hepatitis C has presented a challenge that has been met by scientists, and research shows an amazing success story. In the 12 years since treatment for the disease was first introduced, an apparent cure rate has increased from an average of 6 per cent to 56 per cent.
 There are at least six major strains (genotypes) of hepatitis C. The ease with which successful treatment is achieved depends on the strain. Genotype 1 is, unfortunately, the most common in the UK, and the most difficult to treat; genotypes 2 and 3 the easiest; success rates with genotype 4 tend to be similar to genotype 1; and little is known about genotypes 5 and 6, which are comparatively rare.
 Initially, hepatitis C was treated with standard interferon monotherapy; later, ribavirin was added to the mixture and treatment efficacy increased to 40 per cent. Recently standard interferon has been superseded by pegylated interferon, in which the interferon molecule is modified; this has increased the cure rate to more than 50 per cent of all those treated.
 During the conference in Madrid, the results of the latest trial were announced. This assessed the efficacy of using Pegasys, the pegylated interferon manufactured by Roche, in combination with ribavirin.
 The analysis showed that more than 50 per cent of patients, including those with genotype 1, were cured by this combination. Furthermore, the trial demonstrated that three in four patients with genotypes 2 and 3 could be cured with a much shorter course (24 rather than 48 weeks) of treatment and with doses only half the standard size.
 The trial also demonstrated that patients with genotype 1 will continue to require the full 48 weeks of combined therapy. Cure was also achieved in 50 per cent of patients with cirrhosis-complicating hepatitis C.

 What are the implications of testing patients and staff for the HIV virus?
 THE routine testing of surgical patients for HIV is simply a bad idea. If patients are tested and found to have HIV then treating them differently exposes the healthcare worker to more risk because he or she will not have as much experience with new precautions as they have of normal procedures.
 In any case, HIV is not the only risk that a healthcare worker is exposed to. Hepatitis C, for example, can be equally serious. Above all, testing patients raises the awkward problem of consent. 
 Every patient should be treated with the maximum care and every precaution should always be taken to avoid transmission from a patient to a health worker.
 Steven McClure, medical student, University of Dundee
 Nurses vulnerable
 A PATIENT undergoing a surgical procedure is operated on and looked after by a small team of doctors and nurses. To contract HIV from this group a patient would have to be directly infected by their blood. So far, a case of this happening has not been recorded in the UK. For a medical patient, the risk would be infinitesimal.
 For doctors and nurses the risk of being infected by a patient's blood is much greater because of the nature of operations and surgical aftercare. Also the sheer number of patients that health-care professionals deal with every day of their working lives has to increase this likelihood.
 To protect the more vulnerable of these two groups, perhaps all patients should be screened before medical care, especially surgery, is offered. However, that leaves the problem of what happens to patients who are found to be HIV- positive. Will doctors and nurses be willing to risk their health and jobs by treating such patients?
 P. Clarke, Ilford, Essex
 Foreign folly
 AS USUAL, the Government has got its priorities wrong: a matter of much greater urgency than testing NHS surgeons for HIV is the introduction of measures to prevent the recruitment of HIV-positive nurses and doctors from overseas in the first place.
 While the presence of HIV-positive foreign health service workers may not greatly increase the risk of transmission in hospital, it must add disproportionately to the number of HIV/Aids patients in this country, and burden the already overstretched NHS with a minimun cost of Pounds 10,000 per patient per year for medication alone. Moreover, those overseas health workers will undoubtedly transmit HIV/Aids to their sexual partners in this country, further adding to the already alarming incidence of the disease and its cost to the British taxpayer.
 It is folly to accept applications from doctors or nurses from South Africa, Botswana, Zimbabwe or other countries with endemic Aids without prior testing and certification from appropriate authorities in their home country that they are HIV-free.
 Dr S. R. Duff, Amersham, Buckinghamshire
 Human rights
 I ADDRESSED this issue in 1984 by having a medical student count the number of times surgeons doing serious abdominal surgery at the Univeristy of Michigan got a hole in their gloves and blood over their fingers or hands. It was an astonishingly high proportion, something like 70 per cent of cases, as I recall.
 When I approached the hospital infection control committee with the data, it informed me that it did not matter unless I had a cut in my hand. Since I always get small splits in my fingers in the winter, this was not very reassuring. I tried wearing two gloves but found an unacceptable loss of tactile sensation.
 Testing all patients was declared a violation of human rights because it would deprive HIV-positive patients of as high a standard of care as that provided to HIV-negative patients. So the losers were the majority of patients who were HIV-negative and whose human rights are deemed less important than those of the minority who are HIV-positive.
 Richard G. Fiddian-Green, London W1

The Times (London)

March 14, 2002, Thursday

 When hepatitis strikes

BYLINE: Dr Thomas Stuttaford

SECTION: Features

LENGTH: 724 words

 
 In those far-off unreformed days when doctors made rude and pejorative remarks about patients on their medical notes, the shorthand TATT was so widely known that it became unusable. These patients, dreaded by every doctor, were tatties, whose complaint was that they were tired all the time (TATT).
 Nobody doubts that these patients are abnormally tired, and less well endowed with vitality than most people of their age, but the question their complaint always raises is whether the tiredness is psychosomatic or there is a physical cause.
 Extreme tiredness without any other obvious signs or symptoms can signal a host of troubles, including cancer of the stomach, caecum or other parts of the colon, Parkinson's disease, congestive heart failure or coronary heart disease. 
 The nagging worry they implant in the doctor is that even if the patient could be shown to have been perfectly fit the last time they came to discuss their lethargy, how can anyone be certain that by now they have not developed some specific disease?
 A recent Woman's Hour programme emphasised that doctors now have another possible explanation, which needs to be excluded when a patient complains of constant tiredness. They might have hepatitis C, in which case they will need treatment.
 People who were young and caught up in the revolutionary years of the Sixties, Seventies and Eighties may have experimented with intravenous drugs and in all probability indulged in a sex life that would have surprised an earlier generation.
 The student drugtaker in the Seventies may since have graduated, become a respected chartered accountant -or doctor -and may have no idea why they are suffering headaches, falling asleep over their spread sheets, and once home cannot stay awake to watch the news or summon up the energy to make love. It is too easy to ascribe their symptoms to mid-life crisis or the female, or male, menopause. If hepatitis C is not eliminated from the body, patients may develop cirrhosis, which can lead to chronic liver failure and, in a proportion of patients, cancer of the liver.
 Fifty per cent of UK patients infected with hepatitis C are, or have been, intravenous drug users, while another cause is having sex with an infected partner. Transmission seems to occur more readily with homosexuals than heterosexuals; in the UK the rate of prevalence in homosexual men is 2.2 per cent, as opposed to 0.4 per cent in heterosexuals, although there is a higher incidence among prostitutes.
 Contaminated blood transfusions had been a frequent cause of hepatitis C and was responsible for infecting 76 per cent of patients with haemophilia with the virus. Since all blood and blood products used for transfusion are now screened, transfusions have been virtually eradicated as a cause of infection in this country, but the risk is greater overseas. A survey showed that nearly 20 per cent of blood donors in Egypt had been infected with hepatitis C.
 In a sizable proportion of patients, the source of the infection is never discovered, and for this reason no one should assume that finding a positive hepatitis C blood test can be equated with uncovering a former drug-taker or Don Juan. The good news is that the treatment for hepatitis C, although not universally successful, is improving by leaps and bounds. A great advance is the introduction of treatments which are more efficient at not only clearing the virus from the blood for a time but permanently eliminating it.
 Duo therapy using a combination of Pegasys (peginterferon alfa-2A) with Ribavirin (tribavirin) eradicates the hepatitis C virus in 55 per cent of patients and is more efficacious than monotherapy. When there is resistance, it seems to be related to the genotype of the virus. Monotherapy using Pegasys alone has advantages in some patients as it is more free of side-effects than when used in combination with Ribavirin. Results of a trial published in the journal Hepatology showed that patients taking Pegasys as a monotherapy had fewer adverse reactions, such as headache, fatigue, bodily pain and general malaise. than those taking a combination.
 Their quality of life during treatment was so improved that those who were unable to tolerate the combined drugs would persevere with their potentially lifesaving treatment.

June 2002.Title: Free drug injection kits to halt spread of hepatitis.
June 2002.Author:
Gaby Hinsliff Chief Political Correspondent.

June 2002.chunks: DRUG addicts are to be handed free sterile injecting kits by the state under controversial plans to combat a threatened epidemic of potentially fatal diseases. An explosion of the hepatitis C virus is likely to claim thousands of lives over the next decade if nothing is done, experts have warned. It is so easily transmitted that even snorting cocaine through a shared straw could cause infection. Home Office Ministers are now considering changing the law to allow the distribution of the kits to try to prevent the virus spreading through shared equipment. They could include tourniquets to help isolate veins and clean vessels for 'cooking' heroin prior to injection. Critics fear the scheme will encourage drug use by undermining the message that it is dangerous. Experts argue that the spectre of serious hepatitis C outbreaks among heroin and crack cocaine users outweighs such concerns. More than half of all inject ing drug users are now infected with the virus, which can cause liver failure. It is expected to claim more lives than drug overdoses in the next two decades. The Government's Advisory Council on Misuse of Drugs has recommended lifting the ban on supplying 'drug paraphernalia', including citric acid to be mixed with heroin and 'cooking' spoons. The recommendation is still being studied by Ministers but Home Office sources said they were expected to regard it favourably. 'We will certainly be looking at this very, very closely,' said one. The hepatitis C threat will be discussed at a Home Office summit on crack cocaine to be held later this month. Although clean needles are regularly given out to prevent infection, it remains illegal to distribute other drug-taking equipment. This, the experts say, hampers the battle against hepatitis C. It is tougher than the HIV virus, and can survive for weeks on spoons or shared water containers. Occasional dabblers, who think themselves least at risk, are most likely to share equipment. Norman Brennan of the Victims of Crime Trust attacked the plan: 'This is the Home Office saying that we accept that people will be shooting Class A drugs into their veins. I would like to see a lot more emphasis on prevention.' However a spokeswoman for the National Treatment Agency, a joint Home Office and NHS body which treats addicts, said agencies must be free to reduce the harm of drugs 'safely and appropriately.' 'This is worth looking at, but we need to strike the balance between potentially encouraging injecting and genuine harm reduction.' The Lifeline drugs treatment agency in Manchester is preparing to hand out its own kits from next month. Users who see a nurse will get: disposable heroin 'cookers', citric acid, sterile water, matches, clean syringes, a night light and instructions. The agency is asking the Home Office whether it faces prosecution, and will then decide whether it is prepared to break the law. 'The drug paraphernalia law is a nonsense,' said a spokesman for Lifeline. 'Until somebody can demonstrate that cooking up in the most unhygienic situation is not a health risk, then I think giving out cookers is a sensible thing to do.' The advisory council's recommendations were backed by a recent Home Affairs Select Committee report. A Home Office spokesman said no final decision had been taken. 'We are studying the report and will publish a full response in due course.' Hepatitis C was identified in 1989. Reported cases have soared from 241 in 1992 to 5,108 in 2000, piling pressure on liver transplant services. The British Liver Trust says Britain is dangerously ill-prepared for a looming crisis, with up to 400,000 Britons already infected - most of them without realising it. June 2002.chunks: Hundreds of thousands of people are to be encouraged to have their blood tested for hepatitis C, a potential killer that can take decades to show itself. People who have had a blood transfusion before 1991, kidney dialysis, surgery or dental treatment in countries with high infection rates, or experimented with injecting drugs earlier in life are among those to be targeted under a strategy for tackling the disease in England recommended by a government advisory group yesterday. Ministers will establish clinics where people who might unknowingly carry the disease can be screened, and step up testing in drug treatment centres and prisons. The virus, identified in the 1980s, is diagnosed in more English people than HIV, but infection is curable, with up to half those given medication being cleared. Lifestyle changes, such as cutting alcohol consumption, also help people live with the infection. So far 26,500 people in England have been diagnosed, but only an estimated one in 10 of those carrying the virus is identified, so the government might be facing a public health timebomb, with untold misery for patients and a financial crisis for the NHS. Already 100 people a year are dying from hepatitis C infection and the virus is often a factor in cirrhosis of the liver and liver cancers which kill 5,000 people a year. Some health campaigners want an advertising campaign like that which accompanied the Aids outbreak in the 1980s. Others think a "non-alarmist" public education campaign through GP surgeries, schools and other less official channels might be enough to help identify up to 200,000 people who do not know they are infected. Just over 1m has been set aside for publicity. Blood services have screened for hepatitis C since 1991 and told donors why their blood is being rejected. Thousands of haemophiliacs were infected before anti-viral treatments were introduced in 1984. But many people in risk categories might be reluctant to go to clinics treating drug addiction or sexually transmitted diseases. The most common way of catching the virus is injecting drugs with contaminated equipment, although it can be sexually transmitted, passed from mother to baby and spread through shared toothbrushes or shavers. The infection cannot be spread through normal everyday contact. For every 100 people infected, 20 will clear the virus from their body naturally within six months. Of the 80 left, a quarter will never show liver damage or physical symptoms. The remaining 60, however, may experience weight loss, muscle aches, depression, nausea or liver disease. Of those, 16 will develop cirrhosis over 20 years, and one or two of them will then contract liver cancer. Peo ple over 40 when first infected develop disease more quickly. Pat Troop, the deputy chief medical officer, said: "It is essential we intensify our efforts to prevent new cases and to diagnose and treat those who are already infected." * The government is to offer thousands of women testing for chlamydia, a sexually transmitted disease which often has no symptoms but which can lead to inflammation of the pelvis and infertility.
