June 2002.Title: INSIDE TRACK - NHS management change will not help tackle virus - VIEWPOINT NIGEL HUGHES - Deaths in the ...
June 2002.Author: NIGEL HUGHES.
June 2002.chunks: INSIDE TRACK - NHS management change will not help tackle virus - VIEWPOINT NIGEL HUGHES - Deaths in the UK from hepatitis C could overtake those from HIV, but the health service lacks a strategy to cope.There is a potentially fatal viral infection that is eight times more common than HIV. It poses the largest public health threat since HIV and both the medical community and the government have known about it for 12 years.But unlike the government's response to the HIV crisis in 1983, there is no national policy for dealing with this new virus and changes to the National Health Service management structure are likely to make matters worse.The virus is hepatitis C and until last month, when the actress Pamela Anderson admitted she had contracted the disease from a tattooing needle shared with her ex-husband, most people had probably never even heard of it.About 300,000 people in the UK are infected with hepatitis C, according to conservative estimates from the Department of Health. Only 35,000 have been diagnosed; the others are unaware of their condition. Some may have had the disease for as long as 20 years but attribute their symptoms - tiredness or aches - to flu or exhaustion, rather than to a viral infection that could lead to cirrhosis, liver cancer or even liver failure.The average hepatitis C patient receiving medical attention is a male in his early forties. He may have caught the infection by experimenting with drugs once or twice in his youth - or he may have no idea how he caught the virus.People who inject drugs have one of the highest infection rates for hepatitis C but, as the virus is spread through blood-to-blood contact, there are other routes of transmission. Cases of infection have been reported through tattoos or body piercing, shared razors and toothbrushes and shared "straws" for cocaine snorting. Some people who received a blood transfusion before 1991, when screening for the virus was introduced, also became infected.Treatments are available and can be highly effective. In its 2000 review of hepatitis C treatments, the National Institute of Clinical Effectiveness suggested 7,000 patients should be treated in three years. But few regions implemented this guidance. In the UK only about 0.4 per cent of the infected population (1,300 cases) has received treatment.Most of the blame for this poor rate of diagnosis and treatment stems from a lack of will in the UK to recognise the issue. In the rest of the European Union, in North America and in Australia, treatment guidelines and national policies are in place or under development.A year ago, Yvette Cooper, the health minister, announced the formation of an expert steering committee to develop a consultation document for setting a hepatitis C strategy in England. There is still no sign of this document. Other areas of the UK have made progress but the country as whole is still a long way from a coherent policy for diagnosing and treating hepatitis C.The new NHS management system, which was introduced this month, is likely to worsen the diagnosis and care of hepatitis C.Under the new system, 75 per cent of the NHS budget and the responsibility for how it is spent now rest with the primary care trusts (PCTs) - groups of local general practitioners' surgeries. Their priorities have been set by the prescriptive targets put in place over the past eight years.The management structure that previously planned the hospital service and all conditions treated at this level - the regional and local health authorities - has been replaced by 38 strategic health authorities. These are purely advisory and have no powers to put service contracts and budgets in place or to monitor provision of care. Equally, PCTs have received little support in setting treatment policies and have been given no guidance on how to plan.What is needed is a national strategy for hepatitis C now, not tomorrow, and an overseeing authority to ensure the recommendations are put in place. This was the response to the HIV crisis. Money was made available and ring-fenced for Aids treatment. Measures were put in place to screen for HIV and to carry out public awareness campaigns.If predictions are right, without action now we will face a 500 per cent rise in the need for liver transplants in the next five years, with the number of hepatitis C deaths overtaking those from HIV. The cost to the NHS is difficult to calculate. But liver transplants alone, which cost 4.4m a year in the five years to 2000, could rise to 22m a year.With a virus that poses a far greater risk than HIV in terms of the number of people involved - and the length of time that a person can be unaware they have an infectious, potentially fatal disease - no action now will mean huge costs to lives and healthcare budgets later.The writer is chief executive of the British Liver Trust, a registered charityLondon Edition 1.

June 2002.Title: Police want Aids test on attackers.
June 2002.Author: Lucy Adams.
June 2002.chunks: POLICE who are stabbed, bitten, scratched and spat on while on duty are demanding legislation to force their attackers to undergo blood tests.More than 150 officers risk being infected by HIV and hepatitis C every year after being attacked or stabbed with needles and other weapons.However, under the current law their attackers cannot be forced to submit to a blood test to establish if they are carrying an infectious disease.As a result police say they are forced to go through debilitating medical treatment, often waiting months for the return of test results.Last week the Scottish Police Federation (SPF) petitioned the Scottish parliament for a new law which would force the growing number of attackers to be tested.The federation, which represents 98% of Scottish police officers, wants the legislation to state that refusal to submit to such a test constitutes an offence and holds an appropriate penalty.They are also calling for an amendment to the Data Protection Act 1998 to allow the results to be retained on a central computer system.When officers are attacked by people thought to be a risk, vaccination and a cocktail of drugs known as post-exposure prophylaxis are provided, but this treatment has unpleasant side effects, including vomiting which can last for months.Officers are also disadvantaged by having to admit to tests for HIV and hepatitis when applying for insurance, mortgages and loans.They claim that if their attackers were tested they would not have to take the treatment or wait for their own results.Douglas Keil, general secretary of the federation SPF, said: "Some officers have been so badly affected by the stress involved that they had to be medically retired from the force. "Roseanna Cunningham, SNP spokesperson for justice, supports the principles of the petition. "This is an issue for officers which should be taken seriously," she said. "I think they have a reasonable point but we need to check what the ramifications might be. "(c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2002.

June 2002.Title: CJD FEAR SPARKS CRISIS IN BLOOD SUPPLIES.
June 2002.Author:
KATE FOSTER.
 Daily Mail
June 2002.chunks: SCOTTISH hospitals are to import foreign blood supplies because of fears local stocks are contaminated by the human form of mad cow disease. The drastic step is being planned after health experts warned that there was an 'uncertain risk' of the deadly variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (vCJD) being present in donated blood. Leading scientists have already predicted that Britain is on the verge of a potentially disastrous vCJD epidemic - and people living in Scotland are thought to be twice as likely to contract the disease as those in the South of England. Last night, the Scottish Blood Transfusion Service said only babies and children under five would receive blood from overseas because of a worldwide shortage. But they added that, in an ideal world, all patients would be offered the 'lower risk' foreign blood. The move will bring to an end Scotland's Boys are 20-year tradition of self-sufficiency in the supply of blood. But such is the lack of confidence in Scottish blood that the transfusion service is now looking to countries which have recorded very few cases of vCJD, or none at all, for supplies. The decision was welcomed by the families of young vCJD victims, but patients' groups warned there could be other deadly viruses lurking in foreign blood banks. Marc Turner, the clinical director of the transfusion service, said he was looking at importing stocks from other European countries, such as Germany, which were free of vCJD. He said: 'There's quite a lot of concern that vCJD may be transmissible through blood transfusions. 'It poses an uncertain threat and, relatively speaking, blood from unpaid donors in Europe is perceived as being of lower risk than that from British donors. 'It is clear we could not possibly source all our blood components from abroad because we require up to 300,000 units of red blood cells every year. However, it is possible that some blood could be sourced from other European countries. 'It's going to be very difficult to source blood so we are going to have to look after the most vulnerable and, in general, babies and children require a high pro- portion of donated blood. Most people would accept that if we are going to have a limited resource of a safer product the group that should have it is the youngest generation. 'The virus may lie dormant in the body for many years so it would make sense to protect babies and children up to the age of five. 'This is something we are looking at very seriously and in principle it is something we would probably want to go through with in Scotland.' Experts are now convinced there is a link between the virus and eating meat infected with BSE. But scientists are uncertain if present screening measures are enough to rule out any risk of transmission through blood donations. Potentially fatal infections, including HIV and hepatitis C, have already been passed on to patients during routine NHS treatment and Scotland's doctors are anxious to reduce the risk from vCJD as far as possible. Last year, Professor James Ironside, from the Government' s national surveillance unit for vCJD at Edinburgh's Western General Hospital, said people in Scotland and the North of England were twice as likely to contract the disease as those in the South of England, due to their high consumption of cheap meats in pies and burgers. The latest official figures show there have been 122 confirmed cases of vCJD in the UK, six in France, one in the Republic of Ireland, one in Italy and one in the U.S. Thirteen people are known to have died of vCJD in Scotland. Earlier this month, scientists at the national vCJD surveillance unit warned that Britain faced a potentially devastating epidemic of the virus. The team, who studied the first 100 cases, found the youngest victim was 12 and the average age was just 25. Estimates for the final death toll have ranged from hundreds to hundreds of thousands. Tricia Lowther, whose 19-year-old daughter Victoria was one of Britain's first vCJD victims, backed the move to import blood. She said: 'The Blood Transfusion Service is being ultra-cautious and I think that is a very good idea.' Victoria was about to embark on a hotel management course in 1996 when she fell ill. At first doctors thought she had depression, but as her condition rapidly deteriorated they realised she was suffering from vCJD. It is believed she caught it from eating infected meat. Mrs Lowther, from Carlisle, added: 'This is a horrendous disease that robs its victims of their personality before they die. It was harrowing to watch Victoria slip away, losing her ability to talk and walk. 'I very much fear there will be an epidemic in the coming years. I hope I am wrong, but we must do everything to minimise the risk.' But Margaret Davidson, chief executive of the Scotland Patients' Association, urged caution over importing foreign blood. She said: 'How are they going to prove blood from abroad is less risky than blood from Scotland? I think they are not taking into consideration that foreign blood may carry viruses just as dangerous as vCJD.' kate.foster@dailymail.co.uk.

June 2002.Title: Police assault may mean compulsory blood test.
June 2002.Author: Angus Macleod Scottish Political Correspondent.
June 2002.chunks: A NEW law may be introduced in Scotland to force people who assault police officers to undergo compulsory blood tests.The Scottish Executive indicated its support for the proposal yesterday after police officers warned MSPs on the Petitions Committee that they faced an increasing risk of infection from criminals and drug addicts infected with HIV and hepatitis C.Constable Raymond Pratt, 41, an officer with Strathclyde Police for 23 years, told the committee that his wife had lost her baby because of stress while he waited three months for test results after a heroin addict spat in his mouth while he was being arrested for breach of the peace. He said that the man had also tried to spray him with blood from a cut to his eye.Constable Pratt said that he had been advised it was easier for him to have a test and wait for three months than it was for the suspect to be tested. A suspect has the right to deny information about the result of a test to the police.Constable Pratt told the committee: "It seemed to me a ludicrous situation because it led to my wife losing her baby. It was a thing my wife didn't understand as well; how someone could do this and deliberately not undergo a test. "The Scottish Police Federation, which brought the petition before the committee, said that compulsory testing would allow officers to know much sooner whether they were at risk.The federation, which represents 98 per cent of police officers, said that in Scotland each year more than 150 were exposed to infection by being bitten or spat at.Douglas Keil, the general secretary of the federation, said that the police had to protect the public regardless of the circumstances, but that the police looked to the public, through the Scottish Parliament, to protect them. "Although exposure to risk cannot be prevented, the measures we are seeking could prevent officers undergoing unnecessary and unpleasant treatment and prevent unnecessary anxiety to officers on the front line", Mr Keil said.John McAllion, the Labour MSP for Dundee East and convener of the committee, said that he would write to the Scottish Executive asking what action it planned to take to address the problem.Mr McAllionsaid that he would highlight the use of breath testing as a precedent for a change in the law.He said he also wanted to know whether compulsory blood-testing could be extended to cover other frontline staff, such as health care workers.A spokesman said that the Scottish Executive was sympathetic to the proposals the Police Federation had made but that there were human rights issues to consider.

June 2002.Title: Hepatitis C fear for patients of crooked dentist.
June 2002.Author:
KATE FOSTER.
 Daily Mail
June 2002.chunks: FIFTEEN dental patients treated by a fraudster who failed to sterilise his equipment have been diagnosed with a potentially lethal blood infection. Dentist William Duff was jailed for three years last year for carrying out unnecessary work on his patients and endangering them by using unsterilised equipment. Now health officials have discovered that cases of hepatitis C among 1,000 of his former patients are double that of the general population. They have appealed for 3,000 more treated by Duff to come forward for testing. Duff made about 1million during a three-year period at his surgery in Maryhill, Glasgow, extracting teeth and fitting crowns and fillings when no work was required. Although he became one of the highest-paid dentists in Scotland, he ignored vital safety procedures, leaving thousands of patients at risk of potentially fatal diseases. Health officials yesterday said 15 of his patients had been infected with hepatitis C, which can cause liver cancer and liver failure, and they are 'unable to rule out' the possibility that they may have caught it from Duff 's dirty equipment. Last night patients left in agony following botched treatment by Duff said they were appalled at the latest revelations. Mairi Patrick, 44, from Glasgow, had 16 crowns fitted unnecessarily by Duff which has left her with abscesses and bone loss. She said: 'I am disgusted. Not only did he botch treatment, he may have exposed many people to hepatitis C.' Greater Glasgow Health Board appealed to thousands of Duff's former patients after fears were raised they were at risk of a range of deadly diseases, including HIV, which can be transmitted through unsterilised medical instruments, contaminated needles and exposure to infected blood. Of 1,000 people who came forward for testing, none had HIV but 15 were found to have been infected with hepatitis C. Jeff Frew, spokesman for Capital C, a campaign group for hepatitis C sufferers, said: 'The proportion of Duff's patients with hepatitis C is higher than that of the general population, at 1.5 per cent compared to between 0.5 per cent and 1 per cent. This indicates they may well have caught the virus from his dirty equipment. 'There is something wrong here which gives us immediate cause for concern. 'There could be many more people out there who have caught hepatitis C from Duff or any other dentist who is not scrupulous about the sterilisation of equipment.' David McCall, Greater Glasgow NHS Board's Consultant in Dental Public Health, said: 'Despite this unfortunate and isolated episode, I would like to reassure the public that high standards of hygiene and care are provided by our dentists.' k.foster@dailymail.co.uk.

June 2002.Title: Consumers lose a battle, but are winning the war - City Law.
June 2002.Author: Andrew Austin.
June 2002.chunks: EU product liability law is a mess. But the ECJ is imposing some order, says Andrew AustinWhen Senora Gonzalez Sanchez found she had contracted hepatitis C, she sued the owners of the medical centre in Oviedo, Spain, where she had received a blood transfusion. So far, so like the hundreds of other contaminated blood cases that have been heard by the European courts over the past few years. What she probably did not expect was that her case would end up being ruled on by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) in a judgment that has repercussions for both consumers and manufacturers across the EU.Sanchez's lawyers based her case on old Spanish consumer law, rather than newer EU rights. They used a 1984 Spanish statute that confers wider rights on consumers than the law passed ten years later to implement 1985's European Product Liability Directive (85/ 374/EEC). Both laws make manufacturers liable for damage caused to a consumer by a defective product (in her case, a blood product), but claimants under the earlier regime enjoy a lesser burden of proof and a wider variety of persons to proceed against than under the directive and its implementing legislation.Sanchez, with support of the French, Greek and Austrian Governments, argued in the ECJ that it would be contrary to the consumer protection objectives of the directive to interpret the regime it instituted as being capable of narrowing consumers' rights. The ECJ's judgment, handed down on April 25, disagreed.The essence of the ECJ's verdict in Sanchez is that EU governments, when drafting their implementing legislation, had no discretion to depart from the strict terms of the Product Liability Directive, the aim of which was "the complete harmonisation of the legislative, regulatory and administrative rules of the member states" in this sphere.The directive did contain a limited carve-out allowing member states to maintain certain contractual, fault-based or sector-specific liability systems after implementation, which is why a UK consumer can still sue the retailer or manufacturer of a defective product in contract or negligence, as well as proceeding under our own implementing statute, the Consumer Protection Act 1987. But the directive did not allow rival strict liability regimes to coexist and, the Court ruled, hinder the establishment and functioning of the common market. Which is why Sanchez presumably faces a struggle in pursuing her claim for compensation.In separate (but joined) judgments, the Governments of France and Greece were found to have fallen behind this drive towards "complete harmonisation" of consumer protection law. Greece, in the legislation which it introduced to implement the directive, had done away with the parent text's 500 minimum threshold in respect of damage caused to a person's property by a defective product, making it easier for consumers to sue. France had done likewise, and - contrary to the wording, if not the spirit, of the directive - had further imposed primary liability to pay compensation on distributors as well as manufacturers and restricted producers' ability to rely on certain defences. The ECJ found that both countries were in breach of their Community obligations and ordered them to conform the wording of their national legislation to that of the directive. Other member states can now be obliged, as a matter of EU law, to follow suit.Business has every reason to feel happy with these three judgments. Product liability law at a Community level has long been a legal jungle, with each national government choosing to implement the Product Liability Directive with varying degrees of fidelity to the original text. Good for the lawyers, less so for a company defending a multi-jurisdictional product liability claim of the sort that is becoming common in the European legal marketplace.Consumers can, however, take some consolation. The past few years have seen a concerted drive towards greater consumer protection, often in the name of harmonisation. The Commission's recent initiatives include conducting a wide-ranging consultation into reform of the product liability regime, producing proposals for a consolidated EU law on food safety and common rules on legal aid in cross-border cases and winning approval for a new General Product Safety Directive. Meanwhile, English courts - ruling in our own blood products litigation - have made the UK strict liability regime stricter still and narrowed the defences available to defendants under the Consumer Protection Act. All of which is likely to increase litigation risk and regulatory compliance costs for business, but make lawsuits and prosecutions that bit more common. Sanchez and her supporters in the French and Greek Governments may have lost the battle, but consumers are definitely winning the war.The author is an associate in Freshfields Bruckhaus Deringer's product risk and liability group. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2002.

June 2002.Title:
Health service recruits may have to take HIV test - Plan for health
service HIV test.
June 2002.Author:
Nicholas Pyke.
 The Guardian
June 2002.chunks: New doctors and nurses may be required to take a test for HIV infection under plans being considered by the government as concern grows at the number of infected recruits already working in the NHS. Last night a spokeswoman for the Department of Health confirmed that it is looking at proposals for a screening system. "An ad hoc expert group was set up on the request of ministers in August 2001," she said. "It reviewed the policy options for offering or requiring HIV testing for all new NHS healthcare workers and the department is currently considering their recommendations. Ministers have yet to make a decision on this." The review was triggered in January last year when Wolverhampton health authority discovered that 10 of its nurses were HIV positive. At the time health ministers said there was no risk to the public. In February, more than 500 patients were offered HIV tests after an unidentified healthcare worker in the south-east was found to have the virus associated with Aids. In May, another 500 patients were offered tests after a healthcare worker in east Yorkshire was found to be HIV positive. There are estimated to be 33,000 people aged between 15 and 59 living with HIV in Britain. A third of them are unaware of their condition. The Department of Health does not keep figures on the number of infected doctors and nurses in the system. However, the chronic shortage of nurses in the NHS has resulted more staff being recruited from abroad, including sub-Saharan Africa, an area ravaged by the virus. One report claimed that - based on infection rates abroad - more than 700 infected nursing staff may have been recruited last year, mainly from Africa. Liam Fox, shadow health secretary, told the Times: "The government's policy of trawling the world's poorest countries is not just morally suspect in itself but it is increasing the risk of recruiting HIV-positive staff to the NHS. If the government believes testing is required in the interests of safety, why have they waited so long to do it?" However, the proposals are likely to meet substantial opposition from doctors. Dr Sandy Macara, former chairman of the British Medical Association and current chair of its public health medicine consultative committee, described them as discriminatory and wrong in principle. "My first question would be why HIV and not hepatitis C? "Any compulsion on individuals to commit themselves to discriminatory tests which have grave professional consequences is wrong in principle. "The answer is not compulsion. The answer is to ensure that any health care professional who knows that they have HIV or has good reason to believe they may be infected takes a test voluntarily and in confidence. I'm confident that my colleagues in the BMA would be opposed to any form of compulsion." Healthcare workers who are found to be HIV positive are restricted in the type of work they can do within the health service. The Department of Health until recently routinely ordered a retrospective check on patients on advice from a specialist panel, but now checks are made on a case by case basis. More than 20 such checks for thousands of patients of HIV positive healthcare workers in Britain have failed to find one case where a patient is known to have the virus, although instances have been reported in France and the United States.

January 30, 2003, Thursday

 Hepatitis row set for Privy Council

BYLINE: Angus Macleod

SECTION: Home news; Scotland; 13

LENGTH: 263 words

 
 THE Privy Council could be asked to adjudicate in a looming row between the Scottish Executive and the UK Government over about Pounds 15 million compensation due to be paid to 568 hepatitis C victims who contracted the illness through contaminated NHS blood.
 It emerged yesterday that the Executive has agreed to pay people at least Pounds 20,000, rising for some up to Pounds 45,000. If the Privy Council is called in, it would be the first time since devolution in 1999.
 The Scotland Act, setting up the Scottish Parliament. makes provision for conflicts between the Parliaments to be resolved by the Judicial Committee of the Council, made up of judges from both sides of the border.
 The Department of Work and Pensions has said that any form of state health benefit would come under social security payments, which are reserved to Westminster. It has said, too, that the payments might be clawed back through social security benefits.
 No compensation payments have been made to hepatitis C sufferers in England.
 Malcolm Chisholm, the Executive's Health Minister, said yesterday that everyone living in Scotland who developed the liver disease from NHS blood products before 1988 would get an initial payment of Pounds 20,000. Those who developed chronic conditions would get more.
 Nicola Sturgeon, the Scottish National Party shadow health minister said: "If it's the will not just of the Scottish Parliament but also the Executive to make payments, it really would not be acceptable for this to be prevented by Westminster intransigence."

20 January 2003.Title: MSPs demand £90m for hepatitis victims.
20 January 2003.Author:
KATE FOSTER.
 Daily Mail
20 January 2003.chunks: MSPs are preparing to push for a 90million compensation package for hepatitis C victims which has been rejected by the Health Minister. Malcolm Chisholm said he could not afford the money recommended by an expert group for 4,000 patients who caught the deadly virus from infected blood. Instead, he suggested a 30million deal for the worst affected. But yesterday members of the health committee warned that if he did not agree to compensate all victims of the NHS blood scandal they would press their case in parliament. Thousands of haemophiliacs and other patients caught hepatitis C during routine treatment in the 1970s and 1980s. Both the health committee and expert group agreed unanimously there was a 'moral obligation' to pay. But Mr Chisholm refused to endorse their findings, amid accusations that Westminster officials are attempting to halt the plan. Committee convener Margaret Smith said: 'We will doggedly pursue an equitable solution for all sufferers for as long as it takes. We want to see a solution before parliament dissolves next March. We will be inviting the minister to appear before us again in January to tell us what the Executive has done towards achieving this.' She added: 'We will be pursuing other avenues and may take it to parliament ourselves.' Mr Chisholm's refusal to help all victims prompted the accusation from Labour MSP and committee member John McAllion that he had 'a cash limit on compassion'. Philip Dolan of the Haemophilia Society, a member of the expert group, said: 'The 30million figure is an insult. Why did he bother to set up an expert committee? He's wasted a lot of people's time.' The group recommended that victims who contracted the virus but are now clear should receive 10,000 for stress and anxiety and those who developed chronic hepatitis C should be given an additional 40,000. Patients who have suffered 'serious deterioration' such as liver cancer should receive ongoing financial support from the Executive. Committee chairman Lord Ross said: 'The first step to righting this wrong is to give everybody a lump sum.' Mr Chisholm said Westminster may wish to claw back social security payments to anyone who received compensation. Ministers south of the Border have already rejected compensation calls.

20 January 2003.Title:
Hepatitis patients to get £15m but only if Westminster agrees -
Chisholm admits Scottish parliament ...
20 January 2003.Author:
KATE FOSTER.
 Daily Mail
20 January 2003.chunks: Hepatitis patients to get 15m but only if Westminster agrees - Chisholm admits Scottish parliament could be overruled. PATIENTS in Scotland who contracted hepatitis C during NHS treatment could share a 15million compensation package, Health Minister Malcolm Chisholm said yesterday. But the move can only go ahead if the Westminster Government agrees the Scottish parliament has the power to implement the deal. Mr Chisholm yesterday unveiled his proposals for a long-awaited compensation scheme for around 570 patients who caught the deadly liver virus through blood transfusions or other treatment during the 1970s and 1980s. He said all patients who caught hepatitis C from infected blood should receive 20,000 and those who went on to develop life-threatening complications would be awarded an extra 25,000. However, Mr Chisholm admitted that while the Scottish Executive is in favour, it is uncertain if constitutional legislation will allow the payments. Similar moves for the rest of Britain have already been ruled out by Westminster. Last night campaigners welcomed the promise of money but were furious at the setback. They also said the proposal fell short of an 89million deal recommended by Mr Chisholm's own hepatitis experts. Bill Wright, a member of the Scottish Haemophilia Groups Forum, said: 'This makes a mockery of devolution. Health is devolved to Scotland. I think we have been sold short again.' Patients, including hundreds of haemophiliacs, have relentlessly campaigned for compensation for the bad blood scandal, which affected Britain's blood supply until screening for hepatitis was introduced in 1989. Yesterday Mr Chisholm told the parliament's health committee: 'I am keen to give financial assistance. 'I would like to give 20,000 to everyone who has the virus and a further 25,000 to those who have cirrhosis.' What is unclear, however, is whether the Scottish parliament can make individual pay-outs for health issues under the terms of the Scotland Act, because they could be seen as social security payments - a reserved matter. 20 January 2003.chunks: HEALTH Minister Malcolm Chisholm is refusing to honour a 90million compensation package for 4,000 patients infected with hepatitis C through NHS blunders. An expert group, set up by the Scottish Executive, yesterday recommended the huge pay-out, but Mr Chisholm said he cannot afford to meet the bill. He said he was prepared to go ahead with a payment for the most seriously ill victims but the overall package was far too expensive. His refusal sparked a furious reaction from campaigners, with one describing his decision as a 'fudge'. Thousands of Scots, including 500 haemophiliacs, caught the deadly virus from tainted blood during transfusions and routine treatment in the 1970s and 1980s, before screening for hepatitis C was introduced. Many went on to develop cirrhosis of the liver and liver cancer and only 1,165 are still alive. The Executive set up a group of experts to examine the issue of compensation after pressure from campaigners. But yesterday the Health Minister rejected its key recommendation that all sufferers should be compensated. Philip Dolan, chairman of the Scottish Haemophilia Groups Forum (SHGF) and a member of the expert group said: 'How can the minister welcome this report yet reject its main recommendations. ' The SHGF is extremely disappointed. This issue has been one of the greatest tragedies in the NHS. We find this astonishing.' Experts are also alarmed by the Executive's admission that 4,000 people contracted the virus through routine NHS treatment - around 3,500 by blood transfusions. Last year the Executive said around 500 patients were known to have received contaminated blood during the 1970s and 1980s but yesterday Mr Chisholm said the latest calculation was at least eight times that figure. Mr Dolan said: 'The expert group was not aware of this new figure and I would like to know why the Executive is only admitting this now. Why have they kept it under wraps? We do not know if it is going to rise and whether even more people will be found to have been infected.' The interim findings of the expert group call for financial and other practical support for victims. They recommended initial lump sum payments of 10,000 then a further 40,000 to those who develop chronic hepatitis. They also call for payments to be made to the families of victims who have died. However, Mr Chisholm said the NHS could only afford to pay the sickest patients and any final settlement would be 'nowhere near' that recommended. The chair of the expert group, the Rt Hon Lord Ross, the former Lord Justice Clerk, said that although the cost of the package was high, payments were 'necessary to avoid injustice to patients'. But Mr Chisholm, who as a backbench MP in 1995 called for compensation, yesterday said he wanted to set up a monthly payment scheme for the sickest sufferers in conjunction with the Department of Social Security. The Executive would look at setting up a scheme providing financial support to those suffering 'serious long-term harm and who are experiencing hardship. He said: 'However, there are complex medical, legal and financial considerations. What we need to do now is think carefully about who needs help, what is the best way to structure payments while taking account of the cost in the light of other health priorities.' He was unable to confirm an exact date for the scheme. The Executive has until now refused financial assistance to those infected by blood products or transfusions before 1988. Around 20 Scots with hepatitis C are entitled to compensation under the Consumer Protection Act of 1988 but the majority were infected before the Act came into force. The Executive has argued that an effective method of screening blood was not available before 1991. Compensation packages have been agreed in several countries, including the Republic of Ireland. SNP health spokesman Nicola Sturgeon said: 'The Executive now has to act quickly to alleviate the suffering of these patients.' We're innocent victims ... and deserve better ANDY GUNN, a haemophiliac, was infected with HIV and hepatitis C through blood treatment he received as a child. The 27-year-old from Edinburgh suffers from chronic fatigue, memory loss and a painful burning sensation in his liver - the first signs of cirrhosis. Mr Gunn says he is furious about what has happened and believes the NHS should fund a compensation package for him and fellow hepatitis C sufferers. He believes the Health Minister should back the findings of the expert group on financial support for victims and authorise a trust to be set up to pay out up to 90million for the 1,165 living Scots who contracted hepatitis C from the NHS. He said: 'British hospitals used blood from the U.S. despite warnings from experts that it may be contaminated. 'The blood came from prisoners and paid donors, many of whom were drug addicts. Understandably, I am very angry. 'Someone, somewhere decided to use blood from junkies, prisoners and down-and-outs. A mistake would have been a bitter pill to swallow but this was no mistake. 'I see it as mass murder.We have got to get a decent compensation package because many of us cannot work.We deserve a decent settlement.

20 January 2003.chunks: Haemophiliacs in England and Wales infected with the liver-damaging hepatitis C virus through tainted blood transfusions had no case for NHS compensation, the government said yesterday, after it appeared that those in Scotland would get payments. Yesterday the Scottish executive's health minister, Mal colm Chisholm, welcomed a report recommending that a fund be set up immediately for those with hepatitis C who could prove they had been given infected blood or blood products by the health service. The executive "would very much like to do something to help them", he said, undertaking to consider how to set up a compensation scheme. The Department of Health in London reiterated the government's long-held position that the infections took place at a time when the NHS did not know that the blood was tainted. "We deeply regret that so many people were infected," it said in a statement, adding: "However this government and its predecessor have held that compensation is only paid to patients when the NHS has been at fault, and that an exception to this rule is not justified in the case of people infected with hepatitis C." Of 5,000 people with haemophilia in Britain, 2,800 live with hepatitis C after tainted blood transfusions - 320 in Scotland but the vast majority in England and Wales. The virus causes chronic liver damage in 80% of those infected, cirrhosis in a quarter, and liver cancer in 1% to 5%. Some 1,200 were also infected with HIV. 20 January 2003.Title: Pledge to force minister 'to the brink' in blood scandal inquiry.
20 January 2003.Author: EXCLUSIVE
20 January 2003.chunks: EMBATTLED Malcolm Chisholm will be forced "to the brink" when grilled over a blood scandal which may also have left hundreds of Scots with CJD. The Health Minister is expected to be publicly mauled when he appears before MSPs this week to answer questions over the recent Hepatitis C scare. Last month, nearly 300 Scots haemophiliacs with the blood infection were warned they may also be contaminated with CJD, the human form of Mad Cow Disease. While the health department found out at least a year ago, they only told those who could be infected in November. Mr Chisholm will face the sternest test of his career when he goes before the Scottish Parliament health committee on Wednesday. Victims and medical experts will give evidence before the committee, which is expected to also hear demands for a full public inquiry. Mr Chisholm, who supported their plight while serving as a Westminster MP, has so far refused to allow compensation for those infected with hepatitis C during botched blood transfusions dating back almost 20 years. Government officials in Ireland have already held a public inquiry into their hepatitis C scandal and have paid compensation of up to 2.5million to each victim. Payments in Scotland could open the floodgates for similar actions in England and Wales. Health Committee member, MSP DorothyGrace Elder, yesterday said she expected the minister would face the toughest test of his career. She said: "I can promise he will receive some pretty tough questions. It is likely he will be pushed to the brink. "There is huge public anger over this affair and we as MSPs are reflecting this anger. Many of the victims of this tragedy are unable to get mortgages or hold down jobs, so 50,000 is a small amount. The state must take responsibility. "Victims of HIV and thalidomide have been compensated so there is no reason why haemophiliacs should be treated any differently." She added: "These victims are not simply after money, but recognition for the suffering they have endured. They have a terrible sense of injustice." More than 400 haemophiliacs, who contracted the disease through infected blood supplies as far back as the Seventies, have been waging a vociferous campaign for compensation. However, their pleas have been continually ignored by the Scottish Executive and Mr Chisholm. Initially, Mr Chisholm rejected calls for a public inquiry, but after coming under pressure from the committee, which includes four members of his own Labour Party, he asked an independent expert group to investigate the issue of compensation. The group, headed by former judge Lord Ross, found that the victims should be awarded a total of 50,000: 10,000 up front and an extra 40,000 as their health deteriorated. Lord Ross will make his formal recommendations in a presentation during Wednesday's meeting. Victim Andrew Gunn, 27, who was infected as a baby has been staging a protest outside the Scottish Parliament. A constituent of Mr Chisholm, he met the minister yesterday to demand answers to why his plight has been ignored. He said: "I asked why he backed us at Westminster but has taken a different position in Holyrood. All he could say was 'it seemed a good idea at the time'. "This has been a murderous cover up." Mr Chisholm will be joined in front of the committee by Lord Ross and Phil Dolan, chairman of the Scottish Haemophiliacs Group Forum. Mr Dolan said: "The Executive has ignored us for so long. "It is quite likely many of us will be dead before any action is taken."

The Times (London)

January 16, 2003, Thursday

 All children may be given hepatitis B vaccination

BYLINE: Anthony Browne

SECTION: Home news; 1

LENGTH: 479 words

 
 Every child in Britain could be vaccinated against hepatitis B after a twentyfold increase in the number of people infected with the liver disease in recent years.
 Leading liver doctors have told the Government that a nationwide vaccination scheme is needed and the Health Department has set up a committee to consider a scheme to inoculate all teenagers.
 Hepatitis B is incurable, and can lead to liver cancer or cirrhosis, killing about a million people a year around the world. The vaccine prevents infection, but has been linked to side-effects including multiple sclerosis and paralysis. 
 Most European countries have a national vaccination programme, but with about 300 cases a year, Britain regarded that as unnecessary and too expensive. Now, however, the position is being reviewed after a Public Health Laboratory Service study suggested that 6,300 infected people had entered Britain in each of the past four years, raising fears that the disease could spread more widely.
 Hepatitis B spreads in a similar way to HIV: through sex, injecting drugs or mother-to-baby transfer. About a third of infected people do not display symptoms of the virus, which include jaundice, fatigue and abdominal pain. Up to a quarter of those with the chronic form will develop fatal diseases, but this can be prevented by drugs.
 At present, only babies of infected mothers and some drug users are vaccinated in Britain, but a sub-committee of the Government's Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation is considering extending that either to all children, or to children in cities with large immigrant populations. It is expected to report in the second half of this year. Professor Roger Williams, director of the Institute of Hepatology at University College London, said: "There's a pool of unrecognised hepatitis B infection that has been greatly swollen over the past three or four years. This is a concern because it will spread to others. The only way to protect people is by universal vaccination -and pretty well every liver doctor in the country agrees."
 The Government wants 150,000 immigrants to settle in Britain every year, and plans to issue 175,000 work permits this year, as well as giving visas to 300,000 students. It has resisted calls for pre-immigration health tests, but is now reviewing the policy.
 Hepatitis is the generic term for inflammation of the liver and there are five strains: A: can affect anyone, does not cause chronic infection, transmitted through faeces; B: can cause lifelong infection, cirrhosis and cancer. transmitted through bodily fluids; C: found in the blood of those with the disease and spread by contact with the blood of an infected person; D: also found in blood, but needs hepatitis B virus to exist, transmitted through blood; E:virus that is least common form, transmitted through faeces.

The Guardian - Final Edition

October 29, 2003

Families 'excluded from hepatitis payouts'

BYLINE: James Meikle: Health correspondent

SECTION: Guardian Home Pages, Pg. 9

LENGTH: 385 words

 
 Widows and children of haemophiliacs who died from hepatitis infection caused by contaminated blood products could be excluded from a government aid package for infected patients, campaigners warned last night.
 The Haemophilia Society fears that ex gratia payments promised to infected patients in England and Wales will go no further than a package outlined for Scotland, where the executive has proposed pounds 20,000 payments, with an extra pounds 25,000 to those with an advanced condition.
 The society believes more generous payments should be made, the final size depending on the number of dependants. 
 More than 210 of around 5,000 Britons infected with hepatitis C in the 70s and 80s after being given contaminated blood-clotting concentrates have died from liver cancer and other liver diseases.
 Haemophilia is a condition that affects men, although women can carry the gene responsible. The government package is expected to include related, less common conditions, which can affect women.
 Dependants, and many patients who have been successfully treated for the virus after years of suffering, are unlikely to benefit from the "compassionate" payments.
 It is also unclear whether the 500 people co-infected with HIV and hepatitis C, or surviving close relatives, would get the award. In all, 1,240 patients infected with HIV have received payments totalling pounds 33.5m since 1988 but only 400 of these are still alive.
 Patients given payments for HIV infection had to sign a waiver promising not to pursue compensation for hepatitis, but campaigners argue that such a waiver was unfair.
 Society representatives are meeting the health minister Melanie Johnson today to press for a better settlement.
 The organisation's chief executive, Karin Pappenheim, said: "Surely those who have died from this terrible virus have suffered the most serious consequences of the contaminated blood disaster. It seems inconceivable that the government could even consider excluding their dependants from this scheme, yet we fear this is what is being considered."
 The government has never accepted responsibility for the infections, but John Reid, the health secretary, is keen to end the embarrassing row with the haemophiliac community.

29 August 2003.Title: Blood risk for haemophiliacs 'covered up'
29 August 2003.Author: Sue Leonard
29 August 2003.chunks: THE danger of using infected blood products on haemophiliacs was known to government officials more than 20 years ago, newly uncovered documents reveal.Papers seen by The Sunday Times show doctors had linked cases of hepatitis C to specific brands of blood-clotting agents during a monitoring project in the 1970s.The study, funded by what was then the Department of Health and Social Security (DHSS), found that 197 cases of hepatitis C were reported by haemophilia centre directors between 1974 and 1979.Thousands of haemophiliacs in Britain contracted hepatitis C from contaminated blood-clotting products used in their treatment in the 1970s and 1980s. The condition attacks the liver and can cause cirrhosis, liver failure and cancer.The government has always insisted it could not have known that people were being infected because the heat treatment to deal with the contamination was not available until the mid-1980s, and a test for hepatitis C was only introduced in 1991.The documents were uncovered by the Haemophilia Action UK group. Scottish campaigners for compensation for haemophilia sufferers now say they will use the new evidence in private court cases and will renew calls for a public inquiry.They will also use the evidence to put pressure on the Scottish executive to make higher pay-outs to sufferers. Scottish ministers announced last week they would go ahead with ex-gratia payments of up to Pounds 45,000 to those who contracted hepatitis C as a result of their NHS treatment.Financial assistance is also being provided to people in England by the Department of Health at Westminster.The unearthed documents include a report from the haemophilia centre directors' hepatitis working party for the year 1980-81. It says of the number of hepatitis cases: "Current investigations are attempting to relate the results in different groups of patients to their transfusion history, and there is strong evidence that different types of non-A, non-B hepatitis (now known as hepatitis C) are related to different products. "In 1982, Dr John Craske, of the Public Health Laboratory Service, recommended that the surveillance should continue. "He thought it might be necessary to again ask for details of all patients who had received treatment with a particular 'suspect batch'," the report said.Phil Dolan, chairman of the Scottish Haemophilia Forum, said the documents provided compelling evidence that information had been kept quiet. "I think it may push the government into reviewing its position because obviously that information has been around. It has been hidden. It is further evidence that we need a public inquiry. "Dolan plans to raise the issues with the Scottish health minister, Malcolm Chisholm.Carol Grayson, co-ordinator of Haemophilia Action UK, who uncovered the documents, said: "We were told nothing. They knew there was another type of hepatitis that was attacking the liver whether there was a test or not. "Haemophiliac Andy Gunn, who is pursuing legal action in America against plasma manufacturers over alleged contamination, said he would ensure his lawyers were aware of the documents.Chisholm will be put under new pressure this week by members of the Scottish parliament's health committee, who will question why the payments are much lower than the amount recommended by the executive's own expert group, led by Lord Ross.Sufferers in the republic of Ireland are believed to have received an average of about Pounds 300,000.Christine Grahame, convenor of the Scottish parliament's health committee, said she did not think the amount being offered was enough. "I want to know why Scotland is being so shabby compared with Ireland," she said. Frank Maguire, solicitor advocate with Thompsons Scotland, who was on the expert group, said he was preparing a number of cases against the NHS in Scotland which, if successful, could cost the executive millions.The executive said: "We are not currently aware of these documents and would not therefore wish to comment on them. The test used to detect hepatitis C was introduced in the UK in September 1991. The development and introduction of this test marked a major advance in microbiological technology and could not have been implemented before this time. "(C) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2003

29 August 2003.Title: News - Doctors defuse hepatitis C timebomb.
29 August 2003.Author:
Roger Highfield.
 The Daily Telegraph
29 August 2003.chunks: Science Editor DOCTORS have found a way to help defuse the "timebomb" of hepatitis C, a disease that may affect as many as 400,000 people in Britain. Only a small proportion are diagnosed because people can live with the hepatitis C virus (HCV) for more than 20 years before serious health concerns make them aware they are infected. The drug Pegasys - pegylated interferon alfa-2a, where pegylated refers to the use of the antifreeze chemical, polyethylene glycol - can get to the liver, the primary site of infection, more easily than conventional interferon. As a result, it can cut the virus to undetectable levels in 61 per cent of all patients and a study reported yesterday that more than 99 per cent will remain virus-free up to four years later. The results were announced by Dr Mark Swain, associate professor of medicine, University of Calgary, at the annual meeting of the European Association for Study of the Liver in Geneva. Dr Graham Foster, consultant hepatologist, Royal London Hospital, said: "These results are very encouraging. This suggests that patients who eliminate the virus when therapy is stopped may be totally cured. "It is estimated that 200,000 to 400,000 in Britain are living with hepatitis C, although 90 per cent are unaware they are affected. This is a critical message for patients - whether they are newly diagnosed or in the midst of therapy - the end result may be lifesaving." Hepatitis C affects the liver and is caught through blood-to-blood contact. Many Britons were infected through blood transfusions before screening began in 1992. However an even larger number may have contracted the virus through intravenous drug use, sharing cocaine equipment, body piercing, tattooing or possibly even sharing an infected person's razor or toothbrush.

29 August 2003.chunks: PATIENTS infected with deadly viruses from contaminated NHS blood products have missed out on the chance of compensation because hospitals have lost or destroyed their medical records, it has been claimed.More than 200 British haemophiliacs are involved in a class action in the United States which is about to be lodged against four large pharmaceutical companies who allegedly supplied blood plasma from high-risk donors, including prisoners, to the NHS in the late 1970s and early 1980s.British haemophiliacs who subsequently received the US blood products, namely a clotting agent called Factor 8, went on to develop hepatitis C and HIV.The class action is being co-ordinated by a firm of solicitors in San Francisco and evidence from affected British patients was meant to be submitted by tomorrow.But scores of patients, particularly those in Scotland, have had difficulty accessing their complete medical records - vital to prove that their infection was caused by imported American blood plasma.Some patients have been told by hospitals that their records have been lost, or destroyed, while others have received documents with huge gaps in data, invariably involving the years 1980-85 when the mass contamination of 3,000 haemophiliacs (568 in Scotland) is thought to have taken place.The blunder over archiving of records has proved remarkably consistent across Scotland, raising suspicions among haemophiliacs that it may be more than coincidence.It came to light after American lawyers visited Scotland last November to talk to haemophiliacs about the class action and patients began requesting their medical records. Even so, "the short-term data are extraordinary", he says.

Features - Health & Wellbeing - I caught hepatitis C first - but Guy
died Sandra Waters had no idea that ...
29 August 2003.Author:
CHRISTINE DOYLE.
 The Daily Telegraph
29 August 2003.chunks: Features - Health & Wellbeing - I caught hepatitis C first - but Guy died Sandra Waters had no idea that a blood transfusion had given her a killer disease until tragedy hit her family. Christine Doyle reports. Fifteen years ago, Sandra Waters had a successful operation to remove a ruptured spleen. During the surgery, doctors transfused eight pints of donated blood and one pint of plasma. The blood saved her life but, many years later, it was to have tragic consequences for her family. Not only did Waters develop severe liver disease, which was likely to have been caused by a virus carried in the donated blood, but the operation also led indirectly to the death of her boyfriend of 21 years, Guy Norman. Norman developed cirrhosis of the liver five years ago and, within two months, had deteriorated so quickly that a transplant was out of the question. When Norman was acutely ill in intensive care, Sandra, 41, discovered, from reading his notes, that he was infected with hepatitis C, a deadly liver virus known to be passed through donated blood and blood products. "At the time of my operation, virtually nothing was known about hepatitis C. I had always been relatively fit and healthy, knew very little about hepatitis C and never imagined that I might have been infected or that I might pass on a deadly virus. "Guy's death was a huge shock, and I felt, for the sake of our son, William, who was then only 11, that I should find out more about the virus. I could not take any risk that William might be left an orphan. So I asked to be tested." Two initial tests proved positive. "I was shaking and my heart was pounding when I got the result - just as I felt when Guy died." Two months later, a biopsy showed that her liver was moderately inflamed with fibrosis. Luckily, cirrhosis had not yet developed. But it took six months of gruelling treatment to clear the virus from her body, and she is still having check-ups. In Norman's memory, Waters, who works with community health councils, is speaking out to support the first annual National Hepatitis C Awareness Day, which is today. The aim is to highlight the widespread lack of knowledge about hepatitis C. "We know that at least 200,000 people could be infected with the virus and that only about one in 10 has been diagnosed. Up to a third of these could be at risk of potentially fatal disease," says Nigel Hughes, of Mainliners National Hepatitis C Resource Centre, which, with the Hepatitis C Trust, has launched the campaign. One major issue is the virus's legacy, says Hughes. "Donated blood has been screened since 1991, but the virus has a long latency period and the effect on the liver might become obvious only years later." Another is that many people are unaware of how the virus is transmitted or how they might have picked it up years ago, says Charles Gore, director of the Hepatitis C Trust, which is launching a new website. "Many people are still not aware of the possible risk of medical treatment or emergency dental treatment in countries where sterility standards are lax." Alan James, 50, who is in arts management, was horrified when he tested positive for hepatitis C three years ago. "I had been run down and lacking my usual energy for some time," he says. "The only explanation is my wild youth. I injected smack - heroin - intravenously and, crucially, shared needles. It was more a weekend than a serious habit, but enough to pick up hepatitis C. The infection probably lay dormant for years. No one knew about the risk at the time, and I would say to anyone now, avoid any possible risk and never share needles." So far, Alan has opted not to have the "toxic treatment" necessary to clear the virus. "I am waiting for something gentler to come along, and am trying to minimise symptoms by being kind to my liver with a very low fat diet." By contrast, having seen how swiftly Norman's liver succumbed, Waters was determined to rid her body of the virus as quickly as possible. "I had a very potent cocktail of alpha interferon and a drug called ribavirin," she explains. "It has a similar affect to chemotherapy for cancer. Half my hair fell out, I lost weight and had to take three months off work. But, wonderfully, the virus has gone. Alternative treatments, such as acupuncture, evening primrose oils and some Chinese herbal remedies, have helped." Britain has not yet woken up to the hidden risks of undetected hepatitis C, says Professor Roger Williams, director of the Foundation for Liver Research in London. "The virus is more common than many people realise. It is becoming the commonest reason for liver transplants, and will be for the next 13 to 14 years, as people who were infected in the past come forward. Treatment is effective, if given early." There are several different viral genotypes and treatment success varies from 50 to 80 per cent. Williams and Mainliners are highly critical of government inaction. "The issue has largely been pushed to one side," says Hughes. "The Government produced a hepatitis C strategy. Although the document, which was published a year ago and late, contained a promise for an action plan, nothing has yet appeared." Compared with many other EU countries, we treat less than one tenth of the proportion of infected patients, says Hughes. Williams points to a potential hepatitis C epidemic among immigrants. "Leaving aside asylum seekers, each year for the past four years an estimated 6,000 to 7,000 infected immigrants have moved to Britain," he explains. "These figures are based on the prevalence rates in the countries of origin. I believe we must carry out checks for the virus, preferably in the country of origin." This includes southern Europe, Africa, south-east Asia and countries in the former Soviet Union. "In most similar EU countries, there are already procedures in place," says Hughes. "We don't want any discrimination, but, if immigrants' health needs are catered for, it is better for them and helps to prevent the virus spreading."

29 August 2003.Title: Features - Health & Wellbeing - Who's at risk and what does it do?
29 August 2003.Author: No author in byline
29 August 2003.chunks: How does hepatitis C damage the health? The virus replicates in the liver, which becomes inflamed as the immune system fights to quell it. This leads to scarring and fibrosis and, if not detected, life-threatening cirrhosis and possibly cancer. The virus has a long incubation, possibly of more than 15 years. Liver damage often develops slowly with no obvious symptoms until disease is advanced. In some, the virus never causes problems but can be transmitted. How is the virus transmitted? Hepatitis C is carried in the blood, and those infected pass it on if their blood gets under the skin, or is mixed with the blood, of someone else. Sexual transmission is low. The virus is thought to be 10 times more infectious than HIV and can be passed through sharing a razor or toothbrush. Waters believes that that is how Norman became infected. Who is most at risk? Those who received blood transfusions before 1991. Drug users who inject and share needles. The problems caused by one-off needle-sharing in the Seventies are still emerging. A surgeon or health worker can pass blood to a patient's wound: there have been several hospital scares in this country. Patients can also infect health workers. Those who have an injection, transfusion, dental treatment or tattoo in a country with a high rate of hepatitis C and poor health standards. There is a five to seven per cent chance of transmission from a pregnant mother to her baby. What are the symptoms? At first, there may be vague feelings of malaise and lethargy, aching muscles, nausea and loss of appetite. In retrospect, Waters says she had all these and a feeling that her memory and concentration were fading. "I thought it must be a sign of age," she says. Other symptoms include joint pains and signs of jaundice. How is the virus tested? A blood sample is taken to check for antibodies to the virus. This indicates that an infection occurred at some time, though at least one person in five gets rid of the virus within a few months. If this result is positive, a second test checks for the presence of the actual virus. Blood tests will also be done to check liver function. What are the other hepatitis viruses? Hepatitis A is usually transmitted by contaminated food or water, although it can be transmitted in blood. It is infectious only for a short incubation period, and is not passed on by carriers. Hepatitis B can take much longer, possibly months, to incubate, and is transmitted through unsterile hypodermic needles, exchange of blood and sexual intercourse. Mainliners National Hepatitis C Resource Centre, helpline: 020 7582 5226. Hepatitis C Trust, www.hepcuk.info.

 Health tourists who use bogus business trips to get thousands of pounds worth of free health service treatment are to be banned under a government crackdown.
 Ministers intend to stop foreign businessmen and their families from receiving free treatment unless they can prove that they work full time in the country, The Times has learnt.
 At present, foreign citizens can run up huge healthcare bills by getting a business visa to visit the UK and applying for treatment for themselves and their families. No official figures are available, but the total cost is thought to run into millions of pounds a year.

 The wife of a businessman working temporarily in the UK flew into the country days before she was due to give birth and presented herself at a London hospital, which had to admit her. She flew home shortly after the birth.
 The Government intends to ban relatives of foreigners working full time in the UK from receiving treatment unless they can prove that they are also full-time residents.
 At present, anecdotal evidence from doctors suggests that many relatives fly to Britain when they get ill. The sister of a businessman who arrived in Britain for a wedding was diagnosed with Aids within days of arrival. Patients have turned up at hospitals with advanced hepatitis B and C when they had come to Britain "on holiday" to see a family member. At present all must be treated on the NHS.
 At present any foreign citizen and dependants in Britain are entitled to treatment if they are "engaging in employment as an employed or self-employed person".
 That will be changed to include only people working full-time for a UK company.
 Relatives will only be covered if they live in Britain full time. At the same time, the Government will publish guidance on how to spot abuses.
 Some doctors, particularly in London, have complained that they have to treat many patients who should not be entitled to use the health service.
 Professor Roger Williams, the haematologist at University College London who supervised George Best's liver transplant, said that he saw many patients who were in Britain only for its healthcare service.

29 August 2003.chunks: GBH charge after cops raid homesTWO top doctors from the blood transfusion service appeared in court yesterday after being dramatically arrested over the 1970s contamination scandal.Former chief medical consultant Terry Walsh and ex-senior biochemist Cecily Cunningham were charged with causing grievous bodily harm to patients.They appeared at Dublin District Court after cops called at their homes at 8am and took them away for questioning yesterday.The arrests came five years after gardai launched a probe into how patients, including haemophiliacs, were given blood infected with hepatitis C.The case against the doctors involved pregnant women given a blood product called anti-D immunoglobulin, which prevents their newborns developing blue baby syndrome.It emerged in the mid-Nineties that 1,200 women given anti-D were infected with the Hepatitis C virus. which can cause fatal liver cancer.NoxiousYesterday it was alleged in court that the doctors "unlawfully and maliciously caused a noxious thing, namely infected anti-D immunoglobulin, which caused grievous bodily harm to seven women" between 1977 and 1992.Dr Walsh's solicitor Padraig Dwyer asked why 26 years had elapsed before the case had been brought before the court.Mr Dwyer also demanded to know why his client had not been kept up to date with developments in the case more than four years after making a statement to cops.Both Dr Walsh, from Dublin's exclusive Foxrock neighbourhood, and Dr Cunningham, from Clontarf, Dublin, were smartly dressed in suits.They were remanded on their own bail to appear before the district court on September 24.Hepatitis C support group Positive Action said it welcomed the first prosecutions in the controversy. (C) The Sun, 2003

29 August 2003.Title: LIFELINE FOR SICK PAMMY.
29 August 2003.Author: STUART WINTER.
29 August 2003.chunks: BATTLING Pamela Anderson has received a double boost in her fight against the disease that she fears will kill her in five years. A revolutionary medicine has been invented that could save her from the "silent killer" hepatitis C.  And at the same time Pammy has made up with ex-husband Tommy Lee. She was pictured yesterday kissing the former Motley Crue drummer at their children's football training session in Malibu, California. Brave Pam said last week that she may have as little as five years left to live after contracting the liver disease. She is reported to be quitting the limelight to spend more time with her family. But as the former Baywatch actress, wearing a tight white top and trousers, spent the weekend with Lee and her children, doctors revealed they had made a major breakthrough in the fight against hepatitis C.  The drug blocks an enzyme that is needed by the hepatitis C virus to reproduce. It is the first of its kind to be tested by patients - and the results were dramatic. Eight people infected with hepatitis C drank four liquid doses of the drug, codenamed BILN 2061, over 48 hours. Two days later, their virus levels had dropped by 100 to 1,000-fold. In most patients, the virus could no longer be detected by standard tests and no side effects were reported. An estimated 170 million people worldwide have the disease. In most cases, there are no symptoms until it is at an advanced stage, which is why it is called the "silent killer". The virus is transmitted in the same way as HIV - through sexual intercourse and in the blood. MAKING UP: A kiss for her ex husband Tommy.

29 August 2003.Title: Four killed by Aids-infected needles
29 August 2003.Author: No author in byline
29 August 2003.chunks: THREE nurses and a health worker who took blood samples have died from Aids following accidents with HIVinfected needles, it has emerged. A further 13 NHS staff who were working on wards are believed to have become infected, and 437 more feared they might have been. The figures were released by the Health Protection Agency to the MPs' Public Accounts Committee after the Department of Health initially denied the fatalities. Campaigners say many of these accidents could have been avoided if the NHS were forced to use safer needles which automatically retract after injections. HIV is a blood-borne virus, so pricking your finger with a needle that has been in contact with the blood of an infected person can be enough to pass it on. The accidents took place between 1997 and last year. One of the 13 victims still alive is known to have contracted the virus on the ward. However, because the other 12 came from high-risk areas such as Africa, they could have had the virus before they started work in the NHS. Almost half the HIV incidents involved nurses, and a third involved doctors. The other workers affected were porters, cleaners and laboratory workers. Three NHS staff a dentist, a surgeon and a junior doctor working on AE also contracted the potentially fatal hepatitis C virus from patients, but all are still alive. A report by the Public Accounts Committee has called for the NHS to take steps to reduce the risk of needlestick injuries.

29 August 2003.Title: Tattoo dangers - Letter.
29 August 2003.Author: No author in byline
29 August 2003.chunks: From Professor Norman NoahSir, Mr Charles Gore (letter, June 24) need hope no more for the "the beginning of (the) end (of tattooing) as a health hazard".The beginning of its end as a health hazard was in 1980 when, together with the British Tattoo Artists' Federation (now the Tattoo Club of Great Britain), I produced guidelines for hygienic tattooing. These guidelines were taken up, enthusiastically for the most part, by the tattooists of Great Britain even before the law requiring that they register with the local authority came into being in 1982.I expanded the guidelines in 1982 to cover acupuncture, ear-piercing and hair electrolysis, and these were distributed widely through the Public Health Laboratory Service. They were formulated to prevent transmission of hepatitis B virus, and proved to be more than adequate for hepatitis C and HIV when these two blood-borne viruses came on the scene. There have been frequent updates since then. I am confident that no major incidents of infection have occurred since 1980 from any practitioner following these guidelines.Body piercing was fairly widely practised but not well-known in the 1980s and the law did not cover it. However, most body piercers registered voluntarily and follow my own or other suitable guidelines.In this country, people can be assured that they remain protected from hepatitis B, C and HIV when having a professional tattoo, acupuncture, ear or body piercing or beauty therapy, provided they visit a registered premises, or one belonging to a recognised professional association. The great majority of street premises fulfil these criteria.Yours faithfully,NORMAN NOAH(Professor of Public Health),London School of Hygiene andTropical Medicine(University of London),Department of Infectious andTropical Diseases,Keppel Street, WC1E 7HT.norman.noah@lshtm.ac.ukJune 24.

29 August 2003.Title: Hepatitis virus could be passed on by kissing.
29 August 2003.Author: Maxine Frith Social Affairs Correspondent.
29 August 2003.chunks: THE POTENTIALLY fatal hepatitis C virus can be passed on more easily than doctors have thought, a study shows. Researchers have found traces of the virus in the saliva of people infected with hepatitis C, meaning it could be contracted from simple acts such as kissing or sharing a toothbrush. Millions of people who suffer from gum disease could be particularly at risk, the scientists said. Around 400,000 people in Britain have hepatitis C, although 90 per cent are unaware they are infected because they have no symptoms. Around one in five sufferers manages to get rid of the virus without experiencing any problems, and 40 per cent of the rest can be cured with combination drug therapy. For some patients, however, the virus remains in the body and can cause fatal liver damage. The virus is carried in the blood and can also be caught through sexual contact. Researchers at the Interscience Conference on Antimicrobial Agents in Chicago say that infected people carry the virus in their saliva. Scientists from the University of Washington in Seattle tested the saliva of 12 people who were infected with hepatitis C every day for 21 consecutive days. Of the 248 samples taken, 52 or one in five tested positive for the virus. Traces were found in the saliva of seven of the volunteers. Those most likely to have traces of the virus in their saliva had relatively high levels of the virus in their body. They were also more likely to detect the virus in saliva if the volunteer had gum disease. The scientists said this may occur when the gums bleed after brushing, leaving tiny drops of blood in the saliva. "This study suggests that the saliva of individuals infected with hepatitis C may be infectious," they said. "Microscopic amounts of blood in the saliva due to gum disease may be responsible. "People with HCV (hepatitis C virus) are cautioned not to share toothbrushes with other people in the household." The findings suggest the virus could also be spread from kissing. Basil Williams, chief executive of the UK's National Hepatitis C Resource Centre, said more research is needed to determine if it is possible to catch the virus from kissing. He said: "It is technically possible to catch hepatitis C from kissing, but the risk appears to be very small."
