January 2004.Title: Hepatitis C sufferers to receive Pounds 15m payout
January 2004.Author: KATE FOSTER
January 2004.chunks: SCOTTISH patients who caught hepatitis C during NHS treatment will share Pounds 15million in compensation, the Executive confirmed yesterday. About 600 Scots who contracted the potentially deadly blood virus will receive up to Pounds 45,000 each. They include haemophiliacs and patients who received transfusions during the 1980s, before screening measures were introduced. But last night, sufferers said the deal announced by Health Secretary Dr John Reid was inadequate. Bruce Norval, chairman of the Manor House Group, which represents Scottish haemophiliacs, said: 'Haemophiliacs are unique because we have been exposed to so many different viruses through blood treatment. We should be compensated individually and we should be getting six-figure sums.' An expert group set up by Scottish Health Minister Malcolm Chisholm recommended a Pounds 90million package in November 2002, but he rejected this as too expensive. Mr Chisholm said yesterday: 'I believe that these are fair and reasonable payments.'

January 2004.Title: NHS hepatitis victims to get up to Pounds 45,000
January 2004.Author: Sam Lister
January 2004.chunks: PATIENTS infected with hepatitis C after being given blood by the NHS will receive payments of up to Pounds 45,000 each, the Government said yesterday. The scheme, outlined by John Reid, the Health Secretary, will also include patients cleared of the virus through treatment and others who caught the virus from someone infected by NHS blood or blood products. But the Department of Health, which plans to start the scheme in April, was accused last night of a gross oversight for excluding widows of haemophiliacs who had died from the disease as a result. Lord Morris of Manchester, the Labour peer and president of the Haemophilia Society, said that the omission was symptomatic of a scheme that fell far short of the benefits offered by other governments around the world. Dr Reid announced his intention to award ex-gratia payments to British hepatitis C victims last August. Announcing details of the scheme yesterday, he reiterated his belief that patients should receive payments on compassionate grounds. "I believe that these are fair and reasonable payments and I hope that they will help to alleviate some of the problems," Dr Reid said. Under the deal, every person in Britain who was alive on August 29, 2003, and whose hepatitis C was caused by NHS treatment with blood products before September 1991 will be eligible for an initial lump sum of Pounds 20,000. Patients with more advanced stages of the illness will get a further Pounds 25,000. The total payout is expected to be Pounds 100 million. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2004

January 2004.Author: No author found

The Guardian (London) - Final Edition

January 28, 2004

Go ahead for hepatitis C drug

BYLINE: James Meikle, Health correspondent

SECTION: Guardian Home Pages, Pg. 6

LENGTH: 296 words

 
 Thousands of patients who developed chronic liver disease after being infected with hepatitis C will be switched to more effective and expensive treatments. The decision was announced as the government steps up its battle against hepatitis C, a potential killer which has shown alarming increases over the last decade. 
 Official endorsement for the drug pegylated interferon, usually taken in combination with another anti-viral drug, could significantly increase the drugs bill for fighting one of Britain's most serious public health threats.
 But the drug's success in treating many patients has meant that the National Institute for Clinical Excellence (Nice), the government's good-practice watchdog in England and Wales, has backed its far greater use.
 Only about 2,000 patients are thought at present to use either pegylated interferon or the more standard interferon alpha, but that number is expected to grow rapidly, using regimes which could be £3,200 more expensive for each patient. Even conservative estimates put the extra cost at around £11m a year.
 People infected with hepatitis C often carry it unknowingly for years. Between 50,000 and 500,000 people may have the virus. If the higher figure is accurate, far fewer than one in 10 people with the disease is diagnosed.
 Around one in five known to have been exposed to the virus will eventually develop acute hepatitis, which can take more than 20 years to become evident.
 Graham Foster, consultant hepatologist with Barts and the Royal London NHS trust, said: "This is the first positive step which will allow patients in the UK to receive the same treatment choice which has been available to patients in other parts of the world for many years."

March 1, 2004

National roundup: Health: Hepatitis case to go to Europe

BYLINE: James Meikle

SECTION: Guardian Home Pages, Pg. 9

LENGTH: 160 words

 
 People with haemophilia hope to take the British government to the European court of justice to win better payments for their infection with hepatitis C through treatments with blood-clotting products.
 The health departments in the four parts of the United Kingdom are offering up to £45,000 under a no-fault scheme to thousands of people made ill through contaminated blood or blood products. 
 These are said by haemophilia campaigners to be barely a 10th of awards made in Ireland. About 200 Britons have died from liver cancer or other diseases as a result of infection, with many more suffering serious chronic illness.
 Members of a pressure group, Haemophilia Action UK, are planning to complain to the European Union's arbiter on equal rights, although the Department of Health in England says Ireland sets no precedent because public inquiries and criminal charges affected the scheme in that country.

January 2004.Title: Fury at 'abysmal' level of payouts in blood scandal
January 2004.Author: James Meikle Health correspondent
January 2004.chunks: Haemophiliacs and others infected with hepatitis C through contaminated blood products expressed outrage last night at the level of government ex gratia payments and the exclusion of widows and families from help. Payments of up to pounds 45,000 were said to be barely a tenth of some awards in Ireland. Well over 200 Britons have already died from liver cancer or other illnesses caused by the hepatitis infection. About 7,000 people may benefit from payouts later this year - many of them haemophiliacs infected by clotting factors before a satisfactory test for detecting the virus was introduced in 1991. The government accepts no responsibility for the infections and wants to settle the long-running dispute on compassionate grounds. Many clotting factors were imported fromAmerica, but some people were infected from transfusions carried out in this country before 1991. Others who can prove they contracted hepatitis C through close contact - such as sharing toothbrushes or having sex - with a person infected in this way will also receive payments, which in many cases will not exceed pounds 20,000. But widows and dependants will not receive any aid otherwise. One widow, Harriet Bullock, said: "This is unbelievable. If I was a farmer and my husband was a sheep, I would have been compensated. I am so angry." Ken Bullock died five years ago, leaving three children and three grandchildren. He had continued to work as a civil engineer despite failing health. "The disease left him exhausted almost all the time," said his widow. "He couldn't play with the children or go for walks at the weekend." Other campaigners pointed out that some carers had given up jobs or could not start them because they were caring for sick patients. Haemophilia is a condition that affects only men. Those with families did get higher awards in the early 1990s when a similar scheme was announced for those accidentally infected with HIV. About 500 people are co-infected with the two diseases. Carol Grayson, a spokeswoman for Haemophilia Action UK whose husband Peter is one of these, said: "This is abysmal. It is a terrible illness and those women who gave up a career to care for their husbands are being treated in a disgusting manner." Karin Pappenheim, the Haemophilia Society's chief executive, said the exclusion of bereaved families was "a bitter blow to those who surely have suffered the worst harm from this tragic treatment disaster". The payments, announced by John Reid, the health secretary, amount to pounds 20,000 per person plus pounds 25,000 for those living with advanced stages of the disease. This falls short of the pounds 50,000 recommended by a Scottish inquiry and is far less than the average pounds 140,000 suggested by the society, based on a scheme in Canada. SocietyGuardian.co.uk/health

October 29, 2003

Families 'excluded from hepatitis payouts'

BYLINE: James Meikle: Health correspondent

SECTION: Guardian Home Pages, Pg. 9

LENGTH: 385 words

 
 Widows and children of haemophiliacs who died from hepatitis infection caused by contaminated blood products could be excluded from a government aid package for infected patients, campaigners warned last night.
 The Haemophilia Society fears that ex gratia payments promised to infected patients in England and Wales will go no further than a package outlined for Scotland, where the executive has proposed pounds 20,000 payments, with an extra pounds 25,000 to those with an advanced condition.
 The society believes more generous payments should be made, the final size depending on the number of dependants. 
 More than 210 of around 5,000 Britons infected with hepatitis C in the 70s and 80s after being given contaminated blood-clotting concentrates have died from liver cancer and other liver diseases.
 Haemophilia is a condition that affects men, although women can carry the gene responsible. The government package is expected to include related, less common conditions, which can affect women.
 Dependants, and many patients who have been successfully treated for the virus after years of suffering, are unlikely to benefit from the "compassionate" payments.
 It is also unclear whether the 500 people co-infected with HIV and hepatitis C, or surviving close relatives, would get the award. In all, 1,240 patients infected with HIV have received payments totalling pounds 33.5m since 1988 but only 400 of these are still alive.
 Patients given payments for HIV infection had to sign a waiver promising not to pursue compensation for hepatitis, but campaigners argue that such a waiver was unfair.
 Society representatives are meeting the health minister Melanie Johnson today to press for a better settlement.
 The organisation's chief executive, Karin Pappenheim, said: "Surely those who have died from this terrible virus have suffered the most serious consequences of the contaminated blood disaster. It seems inconceivable that the government could even consider excluding their dependants from this scheme, yet we fear this is what is being considered."
 The government has never accepted responsibility for the infections, but John Reid, the health secretary, is keen to end the embarrassing row with the haemophiliac community.

January 2004.chunks: A new drug may help those with hepatitis C. The molecule, called BILN 2061, slams the brakes on virus replication, and has performed well in a preliminary trial. Some 170 million people worldwide are infected with the hepatitis C virus, which can cause cirrhosis and liver cancer. The new treatment could help those who carry strains that are resistant to current drugs - around half of all sufferers. In the trial, eight patients took doses of the new drug for two days. More than 210 of around 5,000 Britons infected with hepatitis C in the 70s and 80s after being given contaminated blood-clotting concentrates have died from liver cancer and other liver diseases. Haemophilia is a condition that affects men, although women can carry the gene responsible. The government package is expected to include related, less common conditions, which can affect women. Dependants, and many patients who have been successfully treated for the virus after years of suffering, are unlikely to benefit from the "compassionate" payments. It is also unclear whether the 500 people co-infected with HIV and hepatitis C, or surviving close relatives, would get the award. In all, 1,240 patients infected with HIV have received payments totalling 33.5m since 1988 but only 400 of these are still alive. Patients given payments for HIV infection had to sign a waiver promising not to pursue compensation for hepatitis, but campaigners argue that such a waiver was unfair. Society representatives are meeting the health minister Melanie Johnson today to press for a better settlement. The organisation's chief executive, Karin Pappenheim, said: "Surely those who have died from this terrible virus have suffered the most serious consequences of the contaminated blood disaster. It seems inconceivable that the government could even consider excluding their dependants from this scheme, yet we fear this is what is being considered." The government has never accepted responsibility for the infections, but John Reid, the health secretary, is keen to end the embarrassing row with the haemophiliac community. guardian.co.uk/medicine.

January 2004.Title: Plea for guidance on vCJD risk with bleeding
January 2004.Author: James Meikle Health correspondent
January 2004.chunks: Haemophiliacs who fear their families might be at risk of accidental infection with the human form of BSE are demanding guidance on how to deal with blood spills in their homes. The wife of one patient said they had been advised by hospital staff to incinerate clothing and bedding and to put compensation claims to their local primary care trust. The risk that variant CJD has been given to haemophiliacs from contaminated clotting factors is, according to most experts, probably small, but patients are worried by the announcement that a person might have contracted the disease through blood transfusion. They fear their families might be endangered if rogue prion proteins said to be involved in vCJD were present in blood spills. There is official safety guidance to hospitals, professional health staff and families of known vCJD patients, but nothing specifically for haemophiliacs, who are said to remain only at theoretical risk. Some have been told they may have been exposed to vCJD risk in 1996 and 1997, because donations from people who later suffered from vCJD were included in the manufacture of clotting factors. The clotting factor is now imported from the US and the government has promised synthetic alternatives within three years. But some haemophiliacs have gone on "treatment strike" until then. Peter Longstaff, in Jesmond, Newcastle, already infected with HIV and hepatitis C, is one of those. When he burst a vein, the bloodied carpet was removed by men in biohazard suits. His wife, Carol Grayson, said hospital staff had advised her that clothing and bedding should be incinerated. "If we have to have bloody clothes and bedding incinerated we need guidelines and reimbursement of cost." The Newcastle primary care trust said: "We would need to take legal advice on any claim." guardian.co.uk/bse

January 2004.Title: The Sex Doctor - THE SILENT KILLER.
January 2004.Author: DR Catherine Hood.
January 2004.chunks: ISSUE OF THE WEEK: HEPATITIS C HEPATITIS C BAYWATCH beauty Pamela Anderson says she got Hepatitis C from sharing a tattoo needle with ex-husband Tommy Lee. But it isn't just a disease of the rich and famous - the silent viral killer is predicted to claim more victims in the West than AIDS. WHAT IS IT? HEPATITIS C is a lethal virus carried in the blood which affects the liver. It's estimated that 200,000 people in the UK might be infected. WHAT DOES IT DO? THE virus causes inflammation of the liver. Twenty per cent of sufferers will recover quickly but one in five will develop liver cirrhosis or even cancer. WHAT ARE THE SYMPTOMS? THE infection can be silent or cause mild tiredness, loss of appetite, flu-like symptoms, nausea and anxiety. HOW IS IT SPREAD? THE virus is mainly spread by blood-to-blood contact. It is believed that the majority of drug abusers who inject drugs and share needles are infected. Hep C can also be passed by sharing toothbrushes, razors or, as in Pamela Anderson's case, tattoo needles. Transmission through sex is possible but not common. CAN I GET TESTED? ANTIBODIES to the Hepatitis C virus can be detected by a blood test that is freely available on the NHS. CAN IT BE TREATED? A COCKTAIL of antiviral drugs can help prevent liver damage in around 60 per cent of cases. HOW CAN I PROTECT MYSELF? STICK to your own toothbrush and razor, and always practise safe sex. - FOR information visit www.britishlivertrust.org.uk.

January 2004.Title: Hepatitis C, The silent killer;Health
January 2004.Author: No author in byline
January 2004.chunks: NINE out of ten people with the hepatitis C virus in the United Kingdom are unaware that they have this tiny ticking time bomb coursing through their veins and infecting their livers. Hepatitis C is a virus that takes time to make its presence felt: its initial symptoms are so trivial as to go unnoticed, and the patient may not realise that the incident which caused the trouble could give rise to a potentially fatal liver condition 20 or 30 years later. The first symptoms are often tiredness, listlessness and lethargy, a more literary way of describing the diagnostic term TATTY: doctors' shorthand for patients who complain that they are tired all the time. There is an increasing demand for patients who could have been at risk of catching hepatitis C to be tested if they have these symptoms. It is shaming that whereas in France doctors have diagnosed the disease in half the estimated number of patients -and they have a government plan to identify the rest within the next two years -in the UK 90 per cent remain undetected. Only by uncovering the presence of hepatitis C while it is still asymptomatic will many thousands of patients avoid a premature death following a lengthy and expensive illness. Any occupation or habits that might bring people into contact with someone else's blood or body fluids increases the chance of catching hepatitis C. Although blood is the most important vector, and in the past cases were spread by blood transfusion and blood products, these sources are now eliminated (although not all those who were infected before blood screening will yet have been uncovered). Fifty per cent of regular intravenous drug-users become infected, and others may become positive through contact with other body fluids. One new development is that the National Institute for Clinical Excellence (Nice) approves of the use of pegylated interferons and decrees that these should be made available as they are clinically effective and highly cost-effective. And today the results of an international trial were announced: when patients with hepatitis C who also have HIV took a treatment that combined Pegasys peginterferon alfa 2a 40kDa with Copegus ribavirin, it was found that the chances of ridding the body of hepatitis C were trebled, or even quadrupled, when the most resistant forms of hepatitis C were involved. One in three of the HIV-positive people in the UK also suffers from hepatitis C. Complications of the liver are their most common cause of death. January 2004.Title: Virus sufferer is forced to wait three years for treatment.
January 2004.Author: Jeremy Laurance Health Editor.
January 2004.chunks: HEPATITIS C One of the 200,000 people caught in a silent epidemic  IN THE three years since Brenda Binge was diagnosed with hepatitis C, she has seen a doctor once, a nurse twice and had an ultrasound test but she is still waiting for treatment. The 57-year-old former hotelier has been married for 30 years, never dabbled in drugs, and suspects she became infected through a blood transfusion in the early 1980s. She is angry at the lack of urgency shown by the NHS to people in her predicament. "It is very distressing because I feel I have a death sentence hanging over me," she says. "Although there are drugs that can treat hepatitis C I am denied them. You can have cirrhosis, liver cancer and liver failure and no one is doing anything." After being diagnosed in 2000, Mrs Binge moved from Bath to Sussex where she was referred to a liver specialist only after "constant pestering". Her appointment has been cancelled twice and she has not yet seen him. A week before Christmas she received a letter telling her that the kind of hepatitis C she had - genotype 1B - was one of the hardest to treat. "To say I am upset is to put it mildly," she says. "I was going to call my MP. The Government is burying its head in the sand. A lot of people don't know they have got it and because no one makes a fuss no one is doing anything. It's a shocking neglect of the nation's health.This is a very nasty illness." Mrs Binge, who serves as a councillor on Mid-Sussex District Council and once stood as a Tory parliamentary candidate, has been told that after treatment starts with a cocktail of drugs she will need an injection once a week and pills each day for a year. The cost of the drugs is about 7,000. "What are they waiting for?" she asks. "Perhaps if I die they can save money and won't have to treat me." Although her marital status was known to the NHS, she had never been given any advice about how to prevent her husband, Rod, 59, a financial adviser, becoming infected. "We never had any advice about protective sex even though the virus can be passed on that way," she adds. "I am anxious now to do anything I can to get this issue more widely known." More information on hepatitis C can be found at  www.hepcuk.info.

January 2004.chunks: ABOUT 100 women were given cervical smear tests with unsterilised equipment over an 18-month period, health chiefs said yesterday. Lothian NHS Board apologised to patients at the Newland Medical Practice in Bathgate, West Lothian, and has begun an investigation. Unsterilised equipment could expose women to HIV, hepatitis and sexually transmitted diseases. But in an attempt to reassure patients the board yesterday described the risk of infection as low. It is understood a GP raised the alarm last week after realising she had been mixing sterilised and unsterilised stainless steel speculae -the metal instrument used to take vaginal swabs. They were then used by the GP and her colleagues to carry out gynaecological examinations between March 25, 2002, and November 3 this year. The women affected are being identified from practice records and will be contacted individually by letter over the next few days. Patients will be offered counselling, advice and screening. A special telephone helpline has also been set up on 01506 422 816.

January 2004.Title: Cash: Pounds & Sense : Money Coach: 'And I still want to live a full life': Health problems have made Mandy look again at investments
January 2004.Author: Margaret Dibben
January 2004.chunks: MANDY , 41, writes: ' I have not felt ill but have just discovered through a routine test that - to my horror and surprise - I have hepatitis C. I am having treatment which may or may not work. If it doesn't, my long-term prognosis is unclear as I will have had the virus for up to 22 years, so it may have done significant damage. This has made me want to review my finances. I earn pounds 25,000 a year. I have no other income and a large wage increase is unlikely, owing to my health problems. When I have paid all my domestic bills, I am left with virtually nothing for savings, let alone luxuries. Yet I would be foolish to move to better-paid work as I need the security of sick pay and annual leave. The charity I work for gives us six months on full pay and six months on half pay. Whether it could be extended depends on the goodwill of the organisation - or they might offer me reduced hours. With hepatitis C you are not necessarily ill all the time but you can be sometimes. I have a pounds 210,000 flat on a leasehold and am currently trying to buy the freehold. I am just changing my mortgage into an Abbey tracker of pounds 70,000. I do not have mortgage protection insurance. I pay pounds 100 a month net into a Standard Life pension and my employer contributes pounds 130.75 a month. I had payment protection insurance built in with my Standard Life pension, but I recently had to declare the diagnosis on a new medical form and they said from that point on I would not be covered. I have two previous pensions on hold. One is with Merchant Investors, worth about pounds 8,000, and the other with Equitable Life, worth perhaps pounds 5,000 at most. I have two Fidelity Peps with a value of pounds 9,000 each, and a Clerical Medical with-profits bond worth pounds 14,000. I have a Halifax Isa with pounds 2,000 for emergencies that I am dipping into more and more. I recently took out a loan to buy a new car at pounds 82 a month for the next three years. I paid the pounds 2,500 deposit with my credit card, which was interest-free until a couple of weeks ago. I am looking for another zero-rate interest card, although I am wondering whether to use some of my savings to get the bill right down. I want to ensure that, if I live to retirement age, I will have a decent income. On the other hand, I want to be able to live a full life with regular holidays but without money worries now. I would like to provide as much as possible for my partner, sister and nephew in the event of my death and not burden them too much with debts.

January 2004.Title: Martin studies tainted blood lawsuit
January 2004.Author: Richard Oakley
January 2004.chunks: THE government is considering hiring an American law firm to take a multi million- dollar case against US-based drug companies implicated in infecting Irish haemophiliacs with HIV and hepatitis C.Micheal Martin, the health minister, has sought advice from the the attorney-general on filing a lawsuit in America. A decision on whether to proceed is expected within weeks.Haemophiliacs and their families from Britain, Italy and Germany have already filed claims in America. Martin has been approached by Lieff Cabraser Heimann and Bernstein, a California law firm that began a case for 15 people last summer. If the minister proceeds, the contract will go out to tender The firm, which has won damages for Holocaust victims, cigarette smokers and businesses affected by the Exxon Valdez oil tanker wreck, is alleging that the drug companies sold blood products that they knew, or should have known, were infected with HIV and hepatitis C agents.The blood products of some of the drug companies cited in the claim are implicated in the cases of Irish victims. The fact that the law firm is taking cases for non-Americans prompted the department to consider pursuing a case there too.Martin's officials became aware of the case after it was brought to their attention by legal representatives of the Irish Haemophilia Society.The department has been examining ways of holding an inquiry into the role played by US drug companies in the contamination of blood products ever since the Lindsay report was published in 2002. It considered setting up a tribunal of inquiry, but received legal advice that there was no guarantee the American authorities would provide judicial assistance.Since then Martin has contemplated sending a team to America to see what information could be obtained from those willing to volunteer it, and from material publicly available. Last week in the Dail, however, he said his department was considering a "potential alternative route".The American companies named in Lieff Cabraser's lawsuit include Baxter Healthcare Corporation, Armour Pharmaceutical Company and Alpha Therapeutic Corporation.The lawsuit alleges that the defendants manufactured and sold blood factor products as beneficial "medicines" when they were contaminated with HIV and resulted in the mass infection or deaths of thousands of people with haemophilia.The defendants are also accused of using or purchasing blood plasma knowingly obtained from the highest-risk populations, including prisoners and intravenous drug users. The companies contest the claims.A number of Irish haemophiliacs have already taken private cases against drug companies, including Baxter and Armour. In 2001, five drug firms settled a E5.3m case taken by 60 haemophiliacs infected with HIV from contaminated products. (C) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2004

January 2004.Title: Drug injectors still sharing equipment
January 2004.Author: James Meikle Health correspondent
January 2004.chunks: A third of those who inject drugs are still sharing equipment, posing a health hazard to themselves and others, the government's Health Protection Agency said in a report yesterday. Two in five injectors have been exposed to hepatitis C and are at risk of becoming chronically ill and developing cirrhosis and liver cancer. Many of them do not know they have been infected, even though testing and effective treatments are available, the report, Shooting Up, says. Most of the 50,000 laboratory-confirmed cases of hepatitis C last year are thought to have been drug users. Hepatitis B, a condition for which there is a vaccine, con tinues to be transmitted: more than one in five injectors display antibodies produced in response to the infection. There is an increasing number of patients with hepatitis A. The danger of HIV infection continues: more than 100 cases were diagnosed as being acquired though drug use last year, although in most instances this seems to have happened abroad. There have also been worrying outbreaks of wound botulism and tetanus. The agency suggests that there are not enough needle and syringe exchanges. It wants health services to take advantage of a recent change in the law, which allows other equipment - such as sterile water, swabs, spoons, bowls, cups and dishes - to be provided.

January 2004.Title: Life Health - The silent epidemic.
January 2004.Author: MAXINE FRITH.
January 2004.chunks: Almost half a million Britons have an incurable form of hepatitis that was unknown 15 years ago. MAXINE FRITH hears how easy it is to catch,  For almost as long as she can remember, Jane Wynn Parry has felt unwell, plagued by bouts of extreme fatigue and debilitating pain which leave her unable to work and confined to bed. Over 20 years she went to numerous doctors and specialists who either dismissed her problems as "all in the mind" or said they could find no explanation for the exhaustion and sickness she suffered. Then, six years ago, she was given a devastating diagnosis: she had hepatitis C, a potentially fatal liver disease which is caught from infected blood. "I was just totally shocked," says Jane, 44, who is from south London. "It has taken me a long time to come to terms with the fact that I have a chronic, infectious disease which dominates my life and could kill me. It affects everything - my work, social life, relationships with men. It is very difficult to live with." Hepatitis C has been dubbed "the silent epidemic" by doctors, who are warning that rates of the disease in Britain are soaring while most people remain unaware they are infected. More than 400,000 people in the UK have the disease, and 100 new infections are occurring every week. It is already the main reason for liver transplants, and experts say that by 2020 it will be killing more people than Aids. Hepatitis C causes inflammation of the liver, and in severe cases can cause jaundice, cancer and liver failure. Early symptoms include weight loss, vomiting, flu-like feelings and fatigue. Yet because many people do not suffer any symptoms, and those that do are often misdiagnosed, only 20 per cent of victims actually know they have the disease. Less than one per cent are receiving treatment, even though 60 per cent could benefit from the drugs available. The virus is spread via blood, but was only identified in 1989. A screening test was introduced in 1991, but before then, many thousands of people were contaminated by blood transfusions during operations. Jane Wynn Parry believes she was infected from a blood transfusion she was given at birth. "All through my teens, I just felt generally unwell," she says. "I would just have bouts of extreme fatigue when I would just have to go to bed for days at a time. I had pain around my liver area, but no-one even knew about hepatitis C then. It was very depressing, especially as there were times when there was an inference from doctors that it was all in my mind, or there was nothing really wrong." The exhaustion and pain meant it was difficult to work, and an endless round of GP visits, hospital appointments and specialist referrals still failed to find a cause for Jane's problems. Then, in 1998, a doctor said she had gall bladder problems and ordered a series of tests. "I was in his room expecting to hear about the gall bladder, when he just said, almost by-the-by, `Oh, you have hepatitis C'. They had done a hepatitis C test without telling me. I went into shock, but in a way I was relieved because I finally knew what was wrong with me." However, Jane discovered there was very little support for people with the disease - and still very little awareness among doctors and the world at large about it. She suffered a further blow when tests showed that the type of virus she had meant the drug treatments available would not work for her. "I felt very alone," she says. "Basically I was told there was nothing they could to help me and there were no support groups because so few people are even aware they have the disease. I would have periods of feeling better, then times when I would be laid completely low by the symptoms, as well as depression because of how I felt. "I couldn't go out, couldn't meet friends or family, and it is obviously difficult to form relationships when you have to tell someone that you have this disease. I have been out with one man since I was diagnosed, but he was a friend who already knew so I didn't have to broach the subject." Hepatitis C can be passed through sexual contact, and there is a small risk of infection from toothbrushes, razors and other objects which may have blood on them. It is ten times more infectious via blood-to-blood contact than HIV, although less infectious than the virus via sexual contact. Alarmed by the soaring number of cases, the Government published a strategy on hepatitis C 18 months ago, and promised an action plan to tackle the epidemic. However, no plan has emerged and doctors have become frustrated by the lack of progress. Graham Foster, professor of hepatology at the Royal London Hospital said: "There is much disappointment in the lack of an action plan. Absolutely nothing is happening." He added: "The figures are horrifying. Over the next 10 to 15 years liver disease and cancer rates will soar. The Government is talking the talk but it is doing nothing else." Last week, a new drug for people with a chronic form of hepatitis C was approved by the National Institute for Clinical Excellence, the body which approves medicines and therapies for use on the NHS. The drug, peginterferon alfa, is more effective than current treatments, and has been welcomed by patients and doctors. And after years of prevaricating, the Government has finally announced a compensation package for people infected with hepatitis C through blood transfusions. They will receive 20,000 each, and those with the advanced form of the disease will get a further 25,000. More than 1,000 people who contracted hepatitis C from contaminated blood have already died and thousands more are infected. The total payout is expected to be 100 million. While blood is now screened and heat treatment can kill off the virus, the disease is still being spread, partly because many people are unaware they are infected and therefore take no precautions with their partners. The former Baywatch star Pamela Anderson has hepatitis C, which she believes was contracted by sharing a tattoo needle with her ex-husband Tommy Lee. She has spoken openly about having the disease, which has helped to bring it into the open. But charities are still pushing for a national awareness campaign in order to get more people tested and treated. One reason for the lack of action and commitment is that hepatitis C has previously been regarded as a "low-life" disease mainly affecting drug users who share needles. Charles Gore, of the Hepatitis C Trust, said: "We are going to have to face the consequences of this disease and it is better to do it sooner rather than later. There are hundreds of thousands of people out there with hepatitis C who at the moment are undiagnosed and are a risk to themselves because they are not getting treatment, and a risk to others because they could infect them. There is also a wider problem of the huge burden this is going to put on the NHS." The Government is set to launch a publicity campaign this year. Meanwhile, Jane Wynn Parry has found ways of living with the fact that she has an incurable and infectious disease. "I have found that alternative therapies like acupuncture and Chinese medicine have helped me a lot," she says. "Spiritual exercises have helped me to focus on the positive things and to come to terms with the disease. I don't dwell on what could happen in the future, I just try to stay focused on feeling well in the present." The Hepatitis C Trust is at  www.hepcuk.info.

January 2004.Title: Four killed by Aids-infected needles
January 2004.Author: No author in byline
January 2004.chunks: THREE nurses and a health worker who took blood samples have died from Aids following accidents with HIVinfected needles, it has emerged. A further 13 NHS staff who were working on wards are believed to have become infected, and 437 more feared they might have been. The figures were released by the Health Protection Agency to the MPs' Public Accounts Committee after the Department of Health initially denied the fatalities. Campaigners say many of these accidents could have been avoided if the NHS were forced to use safer needles which automatically retract after injections. HIV is a blood-borne virus, so pricking your finger with a needle that has been in contact with the blood of an infected person can be enough to pass it on. The accidents took place between 1997 and last year. One of the 13 victims still alive is known to have contracted the virus on the ward. However, because the other 12 came from high-risk areas such as Africa, they could have had the virus before they started work in the NHS. Almost half the HIV incidents involved nurses, and a third involved doctors. The other workers affected were porters, cleaners and laboratory workers. Three NHS staff a dentist, a surgeon and a junior doctor working on AE also contracted the potentially fatal hepatitis C virus from patients, but all are still alive. A report by the Public Accounts Committee has called for the NHS to take steps to reduce the risk of needlestick injuries.

January 2004.Title: LIFELINE FOR SICK PAMMY.
January 2004.Author: STUART WINTER.
January 2004.chunks: BATTLING Pamela Anderson has received a double boost in her fight against the disease that she fears will kill her in five years. A revolutionary medicine has been invented that could save her from the "silent killer" hepatitis C.  And at the same time Pammy has made up with ex-husband Tommy Lee. She was pictured yesterday kissing the former Motley Crue drummer at their children's football training session in Malibu, California. Brave Pam said last week that she may have as little as five years left to live after contracting the liver disease. She is reported to be quitting the limelight to spend more time with her family. But as the former Baywatch actress, wearing a tight white top and trousers, spent the weekend with Lee and her children, doctors revealed they had made a major breakthrough in the fight against hepatitis C.  The drug blocks an enzyme that is needed by the hepatitis C virus to reproduce. It is the first of its kind to be tested by patients - and the results were dramatic. Eight people infected with hepatitis C drank four liquid doses of the drug, codenamed BILN 2061, over 48 hours. Two days later, their virus levels had dropped by 100 to 1,000-fold. In most patients, the virus could no longer be detected by standard tests and no side effects were reported. An estimated 170 million people worldwide have the disease. In most cases, there are no symptoms until it is at an advanced stage, which is why it is called the "silent killer". The virus is transmitted in the same way as HIV - through sexual intercourse and in the blood. MAKING UP: A kiss for her ex husband Tommy.

January 2004.Title: CJD plan for personal blood banks
January 2004.Author: Jonathon Carr-Brown and Jonathan Leake
January 2004.chunks: PATIENTS may soon be encouraged to provide their own mini-blood bank before undergoing surgery to counter the danger of contracting variant Creutzfeldt Jakob disease (vCJD).The move reflects growing concern about the safety of blood supplies after the Department of Health announced last week that a man had died after being given blood by a person incubating vCJD. It was the first time that blood had been shown to be capable of transmitting the disease between humans.The proposal to create personal blood banks before operations is one of several ideas being considered by the health department.The ideal solution would be for every patient to have their own permanent blood bank, but this has been dismissed as impracticable.Other ideas being considered include the development of "blood salvaging" equipment that would recycle blood back into a patient during surgery.It is even possible, one senior source confirmed, that transfusion patients may be banned from giving blood. But the source added: "It would be an extreme measure which would have serious repercussions on the supply of blood. "The National Blood Service conservatively estimates that a ban on transfusion donors would reduce its blood supply by between 3% and 14%. However, one study suggested donations could drop by 50%.Blood is recognised as one of the most infectious materials and since 1986 most supplies have been treated with heat and chemicals to eliminate viruses. But the process is not perfect and a small number of people are still infected each year.Haemophiliacs are particularly at risk. The Haemophilia Society has already contacted 300 sufferers who may have received blood from vCJD victims and there are fears of thousands more possible cases.Haemophilia is a blood condition in which an essential clotting factor is either partly or completely missing. People with the condition can be given clotting factors extracted from donated blood.One haemophiliac, Haydn Lewis, 46, a carpenter from Cardiff, has been warned by doctors that he was given blood products infected with vCJD. Lewis, who has already caught HIV and hepatitis C from other batches of infected blood, said the health department's announcement had shocked him. "When HIV first appeared the doctors dismissed the risk to haemophiliacs. Then they said the same about hepatitis C, and they were wrong again. When I heard about variant CJD I made a point of asking about it. Again they said there were minimal risks -and once again they misled us," he said.Since 1996, haemophiliacs have been exposed to the risk of vCJD because several of the 143 victims of the disease gave blood before they had been diagnosed. Until now health ministers have refused to introduce clean artificial clotting factors, made with genetically engineered bacteria.However, it is understood that next month John Reid, the health secretary, will announce that this programme is to be accelerated with a national recall of all human blood products from haemophiliacs and their replacement with the safer variety. (C) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2003

January 2004.Author: No author found

The Guardian (London) - Final Edition

February 21, 2004

Hepatitis link to pigs may hit transplant hopes

BYLINE: James Meikle: Health correspondent

SECTION: Guardian Home Pages, Pg. 7

LENGTH: 448 words

 
 Britons might be catching hepatitis from pigs, a hypothesis that could undermine hopes of eventually using pigs' organs to cut waiting lists for human transplants, it emerged yesterday.
 Vets investigating the prevalence of the hepatitis E virus in British herds found its signature looked like a strain identified in a human.The disease is rare in Britain, most of the 30 to 40 cases a year being people who have travelled to developing countries where hygiene is poorer. It is often endemic in pig herds in such countries. 
 It is usually mild compared with hepatitis B and C, which can lead to chronic disease, but it can cause severe liver failure in pregnant women.
 Researchers from the government's Veterinary Laboratories Agency, writing in the Veterinary Record, have warned that the disease, which seems to have been well established in pigs for a decade, might on rare occasions leap from animals to humans. Pigs appear to carry the virus without symptoms and many humans may be carriers too, so hepatitis E might be more widespread than clinical cases suggest.
 Xenotransplantation, using animal organs in humans, is still some years away but experiments between animal species have been attempted for some time. Pig cells may help cure diabetes, if experi ments using monkeys are any guide, while scientists have tried to transplant piglets' hearts to baboons.
 But there have long been fears that diseases harmless to pigs might turn into killer viruses when transferred to humans, undermining hopes that humans could soon have life-saving heart, liver or kidney transplants from specially bred GM pigs. No near-human trials are even near development in Britain.
 The virus found in young pigs from farms in Bedfordshire and Suffolk was very like that found in a patient from Cornwall who had not travelled outside Britain for more than four years, according to yesterday's report. "Further work is needed to establish more precisely the extent and impact, if any, of infection in pigs and people in the UK and other countries," it said.
 But "limited data" so far suggested transmission between species could not be ruled out. The presence of such potential animal-to-human viruses "also has implications in the field of xenotransplantation."
 * Tests for a bat form of rabies suggest it may occur more often than previously thought. In parts of Scotland one in 12 may have been exposed to the disease, while across Britain one in 50 bats may carry antibodies, though not necessarily infecting animals or people. A conservation volunteer died from bat rabies in 2002, one of only four confirmed human deaths in Europe in more than 25 years.

January 2004.Title: BLOOD DONOR BAN ON COKE SNORTERS.
January 2004.Author: JUNO McENROE.
January 2004.chunks: Health chiefs warn of HIV infection risk HEALTH chiefs have banned potential blood donors who have snorted cocaine because they may have contracted HIV. The Irish Blood Transfusion Service and the Dublin Aids Alliance have this week warned of the risk from sharing snorting tools. And it has emerged that a nurse at a blood donation clinic in Cork told a student she may have contracted HIV by sharing snorting equipment. But when college welfare officials were contacted they were unaware of this danger and admitted no warning had ever been given to students about swapping drug snorting tools. On the screening application form for potential blood donors, question 43 asks: "In the last year, have you snorted cocaine or any other drug?". The IBTS say this question was added last year and concerns potential donors who have shared snorting tools who may have contracted Hepatitis C. Donors must wait 12 months, as certain viruses do not show up in blood tests until after that period. But this month, one student was so shocked at being told she might also have HIV, she went straight to an STD clinic for tests. The Irish Blood Transfusion Service chief Dr William Murphy said: "Our question about snorting cocaine was originally brought in because of Hepatitis C concerns. "With Hepatitis C transmission we know that it has gone from person to person through straws. It is the microscopic bleeding on to the straw, which arises from haemorrhaging in the nasal passage." When asked could drug users pick up HIV by using another person's snorting equipment, he said: "I'm unaware of any report that says it but it is certainly possible. "We give a complete answer as we can when people ask questions donating blood. I apologise if the students were misled, but the question is originally for Hepatitis C." The female student in her 20s went to a clinic for a HIV screen test after being told of the risk. She said: "I never knew you could get HIV from snorting cocaine. The nurse said not to get scared though because everyone is disputing it. But I thought, 'Oh, my God, that note that I used could have had HIV on it'." The Dublin Aids Alliance has also admitted that swapping "tooters" runs the risk of spreading HIV. Education coordinator Derek McDonnell said: "It is possible, but it depends on the snorting instrument. "And it's not the quantity of the infected blood fluids that would pass to another person, it's the quality. It could be microscopic, but it is possible."

The Times (London)

December 12, 2003, Friday

 Pinpointing the problem

BYLINE: Anne Woodham

SECTION: Features; Times2; 9

LENGTH: 669 words

 
 An NHS clinic offering Chinese medicine and acupuncture has the royal seal of approval. Anne Woodham reports
 It's wall-to-wall needles in the Gateway Clinic at Lambeth Hospital, London. At least a dozen patients lie side by side on couches in the treatment room: young, old, men, women, needles poking out of their arms, legs, backs and even stomachs.
 The manager even surrendered his office to squeeze in another patient. This is acupuncture on the NHS, and everybody wants it. 
 Patricia Forde, 34, is fresh from 30 minutes of acupuncture for her back problems.
 "It's extremely effective in easing pain," says the charity helpline worker from Lewisham. She was also prescribed Chinese herbal medicine for digestive problems.
 "It worked," she says, though with less enthusiasm -boiling up raw herbs produced a not entirely pleasant smell.
 The Gateway is the only specialised Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) centre in the NHS, offering free body and ear acupuncture, dietary advice, t'ai chi and qi gong exercise and meditation classes and Chinese herbal medicine to about 400 patients a week.
 The physiotherapist and acupuncturist John Tindall persuaded Lambeth, Southwark and Lewisham Health Authority to open the clinic 13 years ago, when it dealt mainly with cases of HIV, hepatitis C and addiction. More than 110 of the 180 GP surgeries in the three districts now refer patients to the Gateway for conditions such as back pain, migraine, irritable bowel syndrome, depression, PMS, asthma and chronic fatigue syndrome.
 Yesterday the Prince of Wales presented the clinic with the 2003 Award for Good Practice in Integrated Healthcare, which is given for innovation in combining complementary and orthodox medicine.
 Acupuncture is available in about 86 per cent of NHS pain clinics and through some GP practices after endorsement by the British Medical Association in 2000. But there is less enthusiasm for other forms of TCM, especially herbal medicine, under a cloud after reports of contamination with steroids and toxic herbs.
 According to TCM, our wellbeing depends on the smooth flow of "vital energy" ("chi") through our bodies along invisible channels under the skin called "meridians". This is dependent on a balance between complementary qualities known as "yin" and "yang". If the balance is disturbed -by factors such as stress, poor nutrition, even the weather -and "chi" disrupted, illness can result. Rather than dealing with a specific disease, TCM aims to restore the flow of "chi" and encourage natural healing processes.
 The clinic manager and TCM practitioner Dominique Joire is meticulous about sourcing herbs from reputable suppliers and insists that, when properly prescribed, Chinese herbal medicine is not a risk.
 A recent clinical trial at King's College Hospital's liver unit found that Chinese herbal medicine improved symptoms of hepatitis C. "That was interesting because everyone is scared that Chinese herbal formulas are dangerous to the liver," says Joire. Gateway acupuncturists are treating hepatitis C patients at the liver unit for side-effects of interferon treatment. Dr Paolo Rizzi, an associate liver specialist, describes the therapy as fantastic, but is firm about its limitations.
 "Acupuncture is excellent at relieving symptoms, but we cure the disease," he says.
 Local GP response in 2001 was so overwhelming that the waiting list was temporarily closed when the waiting list rose from two to six months. The 800 new patients a year now wait an average of four months for ten free treatments, and there is a fast track for those in acute pain, for those with HIV or for pregnant women -acupuncture has been found to be effective in relieving morning sickness and turning breech presentations.
 For others who can't wait, a "drop-in" clinic provides instant ear acupuncture to help induce relaxation, ease sleep problems and overcome smoking and drug addiction, and "detox" herbal tea is on tap all day long.

January 2004.Title: The HIV timebomb in Ireland's jails
January 2004.Author: Petrina Vousden
January 2004.chunks: WATCHDOGS blasted the Government last night over "epidemic levels" of HIV and hepatitis C in Irish jails.They claim the HIV rate is TEN times higher among inmates than on the outside.And there are now A HUNDRED hepatitis C sufferers inside for every one in the general population, says the Irish Penal Reform Trust.Trust boss Rick Lines urged the Justice Department to bring disease prevention in Irish jails up to international standards. He said: "Rates of HIV and hepatitis C have reached epidemic levels among syringe-sharing prisoners in many parts of the world. "Here in Ireland we also face the challenges of preventing disease transmission among drug-using prisoners. "But Ireland is one of the only countries in the EU that does not make condoms available in prisons. Mr Lines said that had to change. Sterile syringes, bleach and disinfectant should also be provided urgently.A study of 108 prisoners in Mountjoy jail in 1997 found nine per cent were HIV positive.Another study of 1,200 men and woman in prison four years ago found an overall HIV rate of two per cent. The hepatitis C rate among the same 1,200 was 37 per cent.And the rate of HIV and hepatitis C among females was HIGHER than for men.Last night the Irish Prison Service claimed it was providing appropriate health care for drug-using prisoners.But a spokesman admitted they did not issue needles and had no plans to hand out condoms or disinfectant. (C) The Sun, 2003

January 2004.Title: 260 women traced over surgery scare

January 2004.chunks: HEALTH officials are contacting 260 women who could have been exposed to serious diseases when unsterilised instruments were used for internal examinations.The patients, who attended their doctor's surgery for cervical screening between April 2000 and November 2003, will be offered advice and tests for diseases including HIV, chlamydia and syphilis.It is believed the problem arose at the Clarkston Medical Practice in Airdrie, Lanarkshire, because a metal speculum was used to perform smear tests on different women without being properly sterilised.It is the second time in four months that the practice, run by Dr Tahira Indrees, has been investigated.Last November it was the centre of an inquiry into allegedly out-of-date vaccines being stored at incorrect temperatures.A spokesman for NHS Lanarkshire said that all the women affected were being traced and stressed that there had never been a recorded case of any disease being transmitted to patients through unsterilised instruments used in vaginal examination. January 2004.Author: CHRISTOPHER BOWE IN NEW YORK.
January 2004.chunks: Schering-Plough on Tuesday asked investors again for more patience in its restructuring project, but said it has five potential blockbuster drugs, each with peak sales of more than $1bn per year.But Fred Hassan, its chief executive who took over in April, said 2004 would be a "bridge" year until the struggling company could start reaping benefits from its new products. Its Hepatitis C drug franchise will continue to see falling sales next year, from new and existing competition, which have hurt sales this year.Along with trying to stabilise hepatitis drug sales, Mr Hassan said the combination of investment into new products and fixes to its organisational and manufacturing processes will make 2004 earnings a bottom point.He took over a company beset with regulatory problems in manufacturing, declining sales in its biggest drugs and plunging profits. Third-quarter operational earnings were 6 cents per share, and are expected to be even lower in the fourth quarter. In his first company meeting with Wall Street, Mr Hassan said he could fix Schering-Plough, and build new products to make it a growing company again in 2005. "We have turned from the hunted to the hunter," he said.Mr Hassan estimated an earnings growth of 15 per cent or more after 2005. The next decade would see limited patent expiry exposure, he added.Schering-Plough expects cholesterol treatment Zetia and Zetia/Zocor combination - both co-developed with Merck - to each become $1bn-per-year drugs. Zetia/Zocor is expected to be launched next year. It also sees similar sales potential in arthritis drug Remicade, and allergy drugs led by Clarinex and Nasonex.

BYLINE: James Meikle

SECTION: Guardian Home Pages, Pg. 9

LENGTH: 160 words

 
 People with haemophilia hope to take the British government to the European court of justice to win better payments for their infection with hepatitis C through treatments with blood-clotting products.
 The health departments in the four parts of the United Kingdom are offering up to £45,000 under a no-fault scheme to thousands of people made ill through contaminated blood or blood products.

July 2006.Title: Copies of lost 'blood row' papers found: Families' delight as vital documents thought to have been destroyed turn up in solicitors' offices
July 2006.Author: No author in byline
July 2006.chunks: CRITICAL DOCUMENTS about Britain's contaminated blood scandal, which the government said had been accidentally shredded, are still available, The Observer has learned. The files provide vital evidence about what has been described as one of the worst medical disasters in the history of the NHS. Earlier this year, the Department of Health said that around 600 sensitive files had been 'inadvertently destroyed' by an inexperienced civil servant. However, in a striking new development it has emerged that several solicitors have copies of the documents, which detail meetings between the blood transfusion service, health boards, government officials and consultants. Some of the files were returned to the department of health last Tuesday. During the late Seventies and early Eighties, thousands of people, including nearly every haemophiliac in the country, were infected with deadly viruses such as Hepatitis C and HIV through infected blood. At least 800 have already died from Aids-related illnesses and hundreds more from chronic liver disease caused by hepatitis. Despite public health concerns over the contaminated blood, successive governments have refused to hold an inquiry into the tragedy. Investigations into tainted blood scandals in other countries have revealed evidence of wrongdoing on the part of government and pharmaceutical companies. Campaigners in the UK have accused authorities of an extensive cover-up. It is understood that other solicitors have been contacted and urged to return any files they have about the case. Senior legal figures who have seen the documents told The Observer they contain evidence of 'significant knowledge of risk and fault'. In particular, they claim that officials knew of the risks of contracting deadly diseases such as HIV and hepatitis from contaminated blood products years before they alerted patients. The latest development comes as a complaint was lodged with the parliamentary ombudsman seeking an investigation into the destruction of the original documents, which should have been stored for at least 25 years. Campaigners said they were delighted that copies of the paperwork still existed. 'We have waited more than 20 years to find out what happened,' said Carol Grayson, whose husband died after receiving contaminated blood imported to the UK from high-risk prisoners in America. 'We cannot turn the clock back but at last we have some hope in our search to find out the truth.' However, she expressed concerns that they had been returned to the department which had appears to have accidentally destroyed the original files. 'We would have preferred these copies to have been held by some independent or neutral body,' she said. Her solicitor has written to the DoH asking them to provide an undertaking to preserve the documents. A spokeswoman for the DoH confirmed that documents relating to the contaminated blood case had been received last week. 'The department will consider these papers in light of the Freedom of Information Act,' she added. < THE NUMBER of young people in Scotland languishing on 'hidden' waiting lists for NHS treatment has increased dramatically, according to new figures, which also show a significant cut in hospital beds available to treat sick children. More than 1,000 children are on deferred waiting lists, meaning they do not qualify for treatment within the current 'guarantee' of six months. At the same time the number of paediatric beds across the country has fallen by almost 15 per cent.

THE Scottish Executive will be urged today to adopt an action plan to diagnose and treat thousands of hepatitis C sufferers.  
The call comes as two reports reveal a "worrying postcode lottery of care" in England and Wales.
The All-Party Parliamentary Hepatology Group found that 92 per cent of 191 primary care trusts had failed fully to implement a 2004 Department of Health action plan to tackle the disease. Its report said that hepatitis C care "depends on where you live".
The Executive is now being urged to learn from those mistakes; there is no action plan north of the border. The Executive said that it provides £ 8.6 million of annual funding to help to prevent the disease.

19 February 2007.Title: Contaminated NHS blood inquiry begins
19 February 2007.Author: No author in byline
19 February 2007.chunks: An independent public inquiry opened today into how the NHS gave thousands of haemophiliacs blood contaminated with HIV and hepatitis C.  The inquiry, led by the Labour peer Lord Archer of Sandwell, will hear evidence from patients who are now terminally ill as a result of what has been described as "the worst treatment disaster in the history of the NHS". More than 4,800 haemophiliacs in Britain were infected with hepatitis C, and 1,200 of those also contracted HIV after being given contaminated blood products in the 1980s and early 1990s, and many more are terminally ill.  More than 1,700 patients have since died, although around 380 haemophiliacs and 20 other patients given contaminated transfusions during surgery are still alive. The inquiry's remit is to investigate the circumstances surrounding the supply of contaminated blood products, examine its impact on haemophilia patients, and to recommend steps to help those affected and relatives of those who have already died. But Lord Archer, a former solicitor general, said the inquiry was not expected to examine the treatment of individual patients or examine the role played by particular doctors or hospitals. The first full hearing of the inquiry today comes after the BBC's Newsnight programme reported that the Department of Health ignored warnings about using haemophiliacs to test new blood products. Haemophilia is a blood condition in which an essential clotting factor is either partly or completely missing, which can lead to serious internal bleeding. Newsnight reported that many haemophiliacs became infected from supplies of the clotting agent Factor 8 from abroad and, unknown to them at the time, much of the plasma came from donors such as prison inmates in the US who were allowed to sell their blood even though there were questions about their health. The programme said many official documents had "mysteriously disappeared", although the government claimed some were shredded and others had not been released on grounds of commercial confidentiality. One of the "most shocking" documents was a letter from the head of Britain's public health surveillance centre warning the Department of Health that some Factor 8 supplies could be contaminated with HIV. Despite this, Factor 8 imports continued to be used. Some haemophiliacs also told the programme that they were convinced they were used as medical guinea pigs without their knowledge or consent. In some cases, even when those tests showed they were HIV positive, the patients themselves were not told for several years. Lord Morris of Manchester, a former minister for the disabled who has campaigned for years on behalf of the victims of this "tragedy" and their families, said the opening of the inquiry was a "historic" day for the haemophilia community. Previous governments had all, he claimed, "resolutely resisted" calls for a public inquiry. Lord Morris, who is also president of the Haemophilia Society, said: "For the first time the voices of the victims which have so far gone unheard, will be heard. "All previous inquiries have been held behind closed doors at the Department of Health. Now, the people who know most about this tragedy, the victims, will be able to speak out." About 6,000 people have haemophilia in the UK.

19 February 2007.Title: 2,000 DEATHS AFTER DOCTORS 'IGNORED HIV BLOOD ALERTS'
19 February 2007.Author: DANIEL MARTIN HEALTH REPORTER
19 February 2007.chunks: DOCTORS ignored warnings about contaminated blood that may have led to the deaths of more than 2,000 patients, it was claimed yesterday. From the early Seventies to the mid Eighties, 4,500 haemophiliacs in Britain were exposed to lethal viruses through blood products. More than 2,000 have since died from Aids or the liver disease Hepatitis C.  Haemophilia is a condition where the blood does not clot. Sufferers have to inject themselves with Factor 8 a clotting agent taken from blood donors. Letters seen by the BBC's Newsnight programme show that imports of Factor 8 from America were not suspended even though senior scientists were warning the Government as early as 1983 that many of the products were infected. Much of the plasma used to make Factor 8 came from donors like prison inmates in the U.S.. They were allowed to sell their blood even though there were questions about their health. Officials have always claimed they did not know enough about the dangers of Factor 8 to stop using them in time. But Tainted Blood, a campaign group made up of relatives of those who died, managed to get hold of letters which showed that officials knew more than they have let on. A letter from the head of Britain's public health surveillance centre warned the Health Department about the risk of Aids from Factor 8 after the UK's first case in Cardiff. It recommended all U.S. imports be banned. It said: 'I have reviewed the literature and come to the conclusion that all blood products made from blood donated in the U.S.A after 1978 should be withdrawn from use until the risk of Aids transmission by these products has been clarified.' But despite this warning, Factor 8 imports continued to be used. And even when safer heat-treated versions came along in 1985, it was left to local doctors whether to use them. Many decided to use up non-heat treated versions first. Some haemophiliacs say they were not told for several years after tests had shown they were HIV positive. One, Robert Mackie, had mild haemophlia and did not need to be on Factor 8. He said he would not have taken it had he known the risk. He said: 'They are saying they didn't know about the Aids virus. I'm sorry by June 1983 when the European Commissioners put out a warning that all haemophiliacs in Europe, including the UK, were to be informed of the risk of Aids. Why weren't we warned of the risks?' Mr Mackie believes he was part of a secret study to understand the spread of the Aids virus. In April 1983 - before he was infected - specialists wrote in the Lancet about how valuable it would be to locate a group of haemophilia patients in a country not yet affected by Aids. Mr Mackie checked his records and discovered that although he was infected in 1984, he was not told until 1987. And the words 'Aids study' were clearly written in his medical notes before he was infected. Newsnight approached Mr Mackie's doctor but he said he had a duty of confidentiality to his patients. Liberal Democrat MP Jenny Willott, who has been campaigning for an inquiry into the affair, said: 'These revelations are shocking. The evidence suggests successive governments have been involved in a cold-hearted cover-up of how around 6,000 haemophiliacs were infected with either HIV or Hepatitis C from NHS blood products.' The Health Department said it had been open and transparent on the issue and that it was reviewing all documents on Hepatitis C from 1970 to 1985.

19 February 2007.Title: SEX DOCTOR: Am I just like Anita?
19 February 2007.Author: Dr Catherine Hood
19 February 2007.chunks: I'M 46 and have just heard that an ex-boyfriend I was with 12 years ago has hepatitis C. Now I'm worried I may have caught it just like the Body Shop's Anita Roddick. HEPATITIS C is a virus transmitted in blood. You can become infected from an infected blood transfusion, like Anita Roddick did, or from injecting drugs and sharing needles. The virus is in semen so it's possible to catch it through sex. There are thousands of people in the UK who are infected with the virus but don't know it, as they may not get symptoms for years.
