19 February 2007.Title: HIV chef who recklessly infected his lover is jailed for nine years
19 February 2007.Author: Michael Horsnell
19 February 2007.chunks: * He was 'chillingly callous' to his victim* Aids campaigners criticise prosecutionAn Italian chef who gave his lover a "death sentence" when he recklessly infected her with HIV and hepatitis C was jailed for nine years yesterday.The sentence was criticised by the National Aids Trust, which said that the case could undermine efforts to stop the spread of HIV.Giovanni Mola, 38, who claimed to have had 200 lovers, refused to wear condoms after starting a relationship with the woman in Edinburgh in 2003. He had been found to have the viruses three years earlier but did not tell his new partner, who said that she was a virgin.Judge Lord Hodge told Mola at the High Court in Glasgow: "What you did to Miss X was chillingly callous and showed utter indifference to her welfare. "His victim, who cannot be identified, said that when she had the viruses diagnosed: "I just thought I'd been given a death sentence there and then. "Lord Hodge said: "She will have to take drugs with serious and debilitating side-effects and may face hospitalisation. She may well face an early death. "The relationship between Mola and the woman began after they met in a shop. They had sex nine or ten times between September 2003 and February 2004 but he wore protection only on the first and last occasions.His victim told the trial that he had "aggressively" refused to wear a condom the other times. She broke down after being told that she had tested positive at a clinic in Edinburgh for HIV and hepatitis C in March 2004.Mola was later arrested but fled to Italy. He was extradited last summer.He was convicted of culpably and recklessly failing to tell his partner that he carried the infection and endangering her health and life by having unprotected sex with her.Mola, who has previous convictions for dishonesty, including theft and extortion, has been recommended for deportation at the end of his sentence.Aids charities criticised the prosecution and the nine-year sentence.Deborah Jack, chief executive of the National Aids Trust, said: "The National Aids Trust does not condone Giovanni Mola's actions in recklessly transmitting HIV to Miss X and strongly advises all people living with HIV to protect sexual partners from infection. "However, it is important to understand that prosecuting people for reckless transmission of HIV is actually undermining efforts to stop the spread of HIV. "Stigma and discrimination around HIV is increasing as people living with HIV are cast as criminals, making it even more difficult for them to tell other people. We are particularly concerned at the severity of the sentence. Sending Giovanni Mola to prison is not the way to deal with the HIV epidemic in Scotland and is likely to only make it worse. "(c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2007

19 February 2007.Title: Scientists find way to slash cost of drugs: Indian-backed approach could aid poor nations and cut NHS bills
19 February 2007.Author: Sarah Boseley Health editor
19 February 2007.chunks: Two UK-based academics have devised a way to invent new medicines and get them to market at a fraction of the cost charged by big drug companies, enabling millions in poor countries to be cured of infectious diseases and potentially slashing the NHS drugs bill. Sunil Shaunak, professor of infectious diseases at Imperial College, based at Hammersmith hospital, calls their revolutionary new model "ethical pharmaceuticals". Improvements they devise to the molecular structure of an existing, expensive drug turn it technically into a new medicine which is no longer under a 20-year patent to a multinational drug company and can be made and sold cheaply. The process has the potential to undermine the monopoly of the big drug companies and bring cheaper drugs not only to poor countries but back to the UK. Professor Shaunak and his colleague from the London School of Pharmacy, Steve Brocchini, have linked up with an Indian biotech company which will manufacture the first drug - for hepatitis C - if clinical trials in India, sponsored by the Indian government, are successful. Hepatitis C affects 170 million people worldwide and at least 200,000 in the UK. Multinational drug companies put the cost of the research and development of a new drug at $800m (pounds 408m). Professors Shaunak and Brocchini say the cost of theirs will be only a few million pounds. Imperial College will hold the patent on the hepatitis C drug to prevent anybody attempting to block its development. The college employs top patent lawyers who also work for some of the big pharmaceutical companies. Once the drugs have passed through clinical trials and have been licensed in India, the same data could be used to obtain a European licence so that they could be sold to the NHS as well. Professor Shaunak says it is time that the monopoly on drug invention and production by multinational corporations - which charge high prices because they need to make big profits for their shareholders - was broken. "The pharmaceutical industry has convinced us that we have to spend billions of pounds to invent each drug," he said. "We have spent a few millions. Yes, it will be a threat to the monopoly that there is. "I'm not only an inventor of medicines - I'm an end user. We have become so completely dependent on the big pharmaceutical industry to provide all the medicines we use. "Why should we be completely dependent on them when we do all the creative stuff in the universities? Maybe the time has come to say why can't somebody else do it? What we have been struck by is that once we have started to do it, it is not so difficult." The team's work on the hepatitis C drug has impeccable establishment credentials, supported by a grant from the Wellcome Trust and help and advice from the Department for Trade and Industry and the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. But the professors' ethical pharmaceutical model is unlikely to find much favour with the multinational pharmaceutical companies, which already employ large teams of lawyers to defend the patents which they describe as the lifeblood of the industry. One industry insider envisaged legal challenges if the new drugs were not genuinely innovative. It could become "a huge intellectual property issue", he said. 3 > 4-5 >

19 February 2007.Title: Next stage is cancer..but I plan to be here for a good few years;Interview;Anita Roddick;Health
19 February 2007.Author: No author in byline
19 February 2007.chunks: Body Shop founder reveals her Hepatitis C to warn thousandsBODY Shop founder Dame Anita Roddick admitted yesterday that she is carrying the deadly hepatitis C virus.The Pounds 100million businesswoman caught the disease 35 years ago from a blood transfusion while giving birth to her elder daughter Sam.But in an interview with The Sun the 64-year-old tycoon reveals she had no idea she was ill until a routine blood test two years ago.Now she has decided to go public about her condition after being told that her liver is so badly damaged that she has cirrhosis.When you speak to Anita her youthful looks and boundless energy make it hard to believe she is seriously ill.But she says: "The next stage will be a tumour or cancer. I am being monitored very closely, every three months. "I don't need a liver yet, but it may come to that. There are no guarantees - there are very few livers. "Anita -who nevertheless describes herself as a "pathological optimist" -has genotype one hepatitis, the most aggressive and difficult form to treat. Treatment works in only 50 per cent of cases and there is a small risk of further liver damage.But she says: "I could still have a good few years -even decades -of life left, but it's hard to say. "Anita only discovered she had the virus when she had a medical for an insurance policy.She says: "Over the years I'd had hundreds and hundreds of medical checks but it was only recently, as the insurance got higher, I got older and I was doing so much travelling that they included the hepatitisC test. "They call it the silent killer, it's so anonymous. You don't have any symptoms. "In Britain 60,000 people have been diagnosed with hepatitis C, although health watchdog NICE believes 500,000 are infected. Some experts warn the real figure could be even higher.For a patient, the longer it goes undetected the worse the outlook. Three out of four chronic hepatitis C patients suffer liver damage and it in-creases the risk of liver cancer.For Anita, her husband Gordon and daughters Sam and Justine, her diagnosis has understandably come as a bombshell.Speaking exclusively to The Sun, Sam says: "It has really changed our relationship. You can't feel any more vulnerable in life than when your parent's health is at risk. "It makes you very aware of your own mortality, it makes you reflect on life and the things you love. "Anita, born in Sussex to Italian immigrant parents, launched The Body Shop in 1976 with just 15 products. She developed them in the garage of the family home. Last year she and Gordon sold their stake in the business to L'Oreal for Pounds 117million.Yet workaholic Anita still refuses to curb her hectic schedule. She has just become a patron of the Hepatitis C Trust and as we talk she fires questions at the charity's chief executive Charles Gore -"What about getting all the Cabinet tested?" "Prisons, what's happening in prisons? It must be a huge problem. "Then she tells me: "People have been saying I'm brave for speaking out but I don't get it. I couldn't imagine doing anything else. "I've always been a bit of a whistle-blower and I'm not going to stop now. "I am outraged that the Government has spent Pounds 40million on telling the public about the switchover to digital TV but only Pounds 3million on raising awareness of hepatitis C."The Sun has done a brilliant job getting the message out there but the Government's campaign has been a joke. "They can find Pounds 25billion for a Trident missile, billions to invade Iraq, so why can't they find the money to tackle this condition? "There are hundreds of thousands of people out there with undiagnosed hepatitis C."And what little money is being spent is not working. The latest figures show the Government's FaCe It awareness campaign is a flop.From July to September last year only 1,128 new cases were diagnosed -half the number of the previous quarter.Anita says: "It's the Government that needs to FaCe It -face the fact that people are dying needlessly. "* For more information, call the Hepatitis C Trust helpline on 0870 200 1 200 or visit the website hepctrust.org.uk.Learn more about hepatitis C at thesun.co.uk/news. * Case of Tracy De GietelinkLIKE Dame Anita, Tracy contracted the virus from an infected blood transfusion during pregnancy. She also only found out she was a carrier by chance when she donated blood.Tracy, 46, from Dover, says: "I got a letter from the blood service saying 'We have discovered you carry the hepatitis virus'. It was incredibly blunt. "At the time Tracy was working as a highly-paid PA in London. She says: "I was drinking, eating junk food, working long hours with lots of stress. I was doing all the wrong things but nobody warned me about the risks. "Two courses of treatment failed to clear the bug but Tracy says: "I'm lucky, I know I'm infected and I'm very, very careful. "She even insists her son Zac, nine, uses a separate sink to brush his teeth. * Case of Neil HudsonNEIL was given 164 units of blood after pneumonia led to septicaemia.One was contaminated with hepatitis C -but it was nine years before he knew. He says: "What's really frightening is that hundreds of thousands of people are walking around with it -and they don't know. "Neil, 36, a counsellor from South London, was diagnosed in 1999 when he was being treated for high blood pressure. He began treatment in 2001.He says: "I went clear but within three months the virus came back. After all the side-effects of the treatment, I was still ill."Neil had another year of treatment with pegylated interferon and has now been clear for two years.He says: "I think Anita Roddick is incredibly brave to speak out. "* Case of Kiri NowakKIRI's dad Peter died of a lack of information. He had no idea the blood transfusions that saved his life after a car crash in 1975 were infected. By the time he found out, it was too late.Peter, a designer, was 53 when he went into hospital with a leg infection just over a year ago.Routine tests revealed he had hepatitis C -and three months later he died.Student Kiri, 20, from Camberley in Surrey, says: "I'm angry the Government has done so little to raise awareness. "If they'd found it earlier he'd have had a better chance. It's great Anita Roddick is using her fame in such a positive way. By speaking out she will help so many. "* THE RISK FACTORSHEPATITIS C can be caught from the following: A blood transfusion carried out before 1991; medical or dental treatment abroad; a tattoo or piercing; unprotected sex; sharing a razor or a toothbrush; sharing drug equipment; exposure in the womb.

19 February 2007.Title: Laurence Picken;Lives Remembered;The Register
19 February 2007.Author: No author in byline
19 February 2007.chunks: Graham Wade writes: Laurence Picken (obituary, March 24) was my tutor at Jesus College, Cambridge, 1959-62, and from this grew a lifelong friendship. To visit his room was to move instantly to the 7th-century Tang dynasty, as he began to speak of travels and studies, offering ancient music so erudite it might well have originated on some distant planet. At the same time Laurence could be witty and caustic about those who held contrary opinions about how 7th-century music should be interpreted. His great energy diminished for a while when he contracted hepatitis in Mongolia and his recovery was slow. He was also upset to move from his rooms in college to a terraced house just outside the grounds. "They don't want us to die in our rooms!" he sighed. (c) Times Newspapers Ltd, 2007

19 February 2007.Title: Rusty van which supplies Gaza’s life-blood
19 February 2007.Author: Johann Hari in Gaza
19 February 2007.chunks: WORLD | THE INDEPENDENT CHRISTMAS APPEAL 2006 Dr Hassan Deed Suleiman stares at the three pieces of rickety machinery that stand between him and a meltdown in Gazas hospital network. We do not have back-ups for any of the essential components of our largest blood bank, he says, shaking his head. If when one of them breaks, we will not be able to do proper blood transfusions in much of Gaza. The flow of blood to our hospitals will stop. The effects will be terrible. Dr Suleiman is the director of Shifa Blood Bank, which supplies 60 per cent of the blood needed in Gaza, for everything from Caesarean sections to bomb victims to haemophiliacs. He talks over the low, unhealthy hum of the battered pieces of old equipment: the refrigerator that stores blood until it can be processed; the centrifuge that separates blood into its components; and the incubator that keeps the resulting platelets warm. All of these machines have been in continuous use since 1996, he says. How much longer can they last? Gazas blood banks have been crumbling for years. The Israeli siege made it extremely hard to get machine parts into this congested strip of land, home to one-and-a-half million people. Then the international boycott after the election of Hamas cut off the funds Shifa used to purchase even simple equipment, such as blood bags and testing kits. Earlier this year the blood bank ran out of hepatitis C testing kits. If things carry on deteriorating, Dr Suleiman warns, soon we will have to make a terrible choice stop screening blood for diseases like HIV and hepatitis, or stop putting out blood altogether. Blood has long been a bleak symbol of Palestinian life. The area has an unusually strong tradition of donating it. Dr Randa Khoudary of the Ministry of Health says: After an Israeli attack we invariably get a huge flood of donors at the hospitals. It is something even very poor people can do to show solidarity. But we have to turn away hundreds, because we do not have the capacity to process so much at one time. The Central Blood Bank Society collects a quarter of the blood for Gazas hospitals but its offices are being repossessed, the electricity is cut off and its staff go unpaid. Standing outside the offices, Bassim Shaban, the chief of the laboratory, says: We are deep in debt. We owe $150,000 and the Palestinian Authority has no money to bail us out because of the international boycott. Mr Shabbans offices in Khan Younis and Rafah have been sold. When the power supply was cut, the blood that the society collected warmed and went bad. Its mobile collection unit, which does have working, safe medical equipment, is rusting, its engine long since dead. Instead the society is forced to collect blood from the back of an old van. It is not safe, Mr Shabban says. One group has been trying to support the Palestinian doctors holding together their collapsing blood service: the medical agency Merlin, one of the three charities being supported by this years Independent Christmas Appeal. Christian Bunyan, head of the charitys projects in Gaza, says: Since the summer, Merlin has been working to ensure that the Ministry of Health is able to offer a more dependable service. That means shipping in key equipment like a refrigerated centrifuge, donor chairs and HIV test kits. As an international organisa-tion we are more able to get these supplies in and out of the Strip than Gazans, who face so many restrictions. Thanks to Merlin, the doctors in Gaza can continue collecting blood and screening it. It is providing parts to repair existing machinery and keep it running as long as possible. The charity hopes that by the new year it will be able to provide a new blood-collection vehicle, helping to increase safe collection throughout the Strip, a move that the doctors here say would be amazing, literally a life-saver. Back in the Shifa Blood Bank, Dr Suleiman adds: Blood is not an optional add-on to the funct ioning of our health system. It is a necessity. We have enough problems with blood in Gaza. We do not need this too. Charity auction: www.independent.co.uk/auction

23 April 2008.Title: Killer transfusions will be investigated at last
23 April 2008.Author: Vic Rodrick
23 April 2008.chunks: A3MILLION inquiry into why thousands of people were infected with killer viruses in blood transfusions was announced by the Scottish Government yesterday.Health Secretary Nicola Sturgeon described the scandalas"oneofthe most tragic episodes" in the health service's history.The announcement fulfils a key SNP manifesto commitment and represents a milestone victory for sufferers who have campaigned tirelessly for an inquiry for more than 15 years.An independent team chaired by Lady Cosgrove, a former judge and sheriff, will investigate how blood and blood products tainted with hepatitis C and HIV infected patients.It will also probe the deaths of Reverend David Black, 66, and Eileen O'Hara, 72, following a High Court ruling in February that Scottish authorities had breached human rights laws by not holding fatal accident inquiries.They both died in 2003 after becoming infected with hepatitis C following NHS treatment.Solicitor Advocate Frank Maguire, of Thompsons Solicitors, who has campaigned on behalf of the families for three years, said they were "delighted" with the decision.Ms Sturgeon said:"This tragedy has blighted the lives of a number of people in Scotland and we are committed to a thorough inquiry to get to the bottom of what happened." Lady Cosgrove's remit is expected to include the sources of blood used by the NHS in Scotland at the time and whether heat treatment sterilisation should been introduced earlier.Philip Dolan, chairman of the Scottish Forum of the Haemophilia Society, said it was tragic that several of the victims had died during the fight for an investigation.He added: "This is a battle we have endeavoured to fight for years.We've had so many obstacles put in our way." Brian Adam, MSP for Aberdeen North, has campaigned on the issue since the parliament was created in 1999.Hesaid: "These answers are long overdue and it has taken two terms of parliament and finally a change of administration to see it happen." Mary Scanlon MSP, Tory health spokeswoman, welcomed the inquiry but urged Ms Sturgeon to revisit the question of compensation payments.She added: "Nothing can undo the pain and suffering to individuals and their families, but this is an important step."

February 2009.Title: Free needles for drug users 'good use of NHS money'
February 2009.Author: No author found
February 2009.chunks:
Guardian.com 

February 19, 2009

Free needles for drug users 'good use of NHS money' 

LENGTH: 485 words


HIGHLIGHT: Medicine watchdog advocates combining needle exchange schemes with treatment 

Providing free needles and syringes to people who inject heroin and cocaine is a cost-effective use of NHS money, the government's medicines watchdog said today.
The National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (Nice) issued its first guidance on how harm reduction services for addicts should be run throughout England, suggesting combining non-judgmental needle exchange schemes with treatment to help users come off drugs. 
Prof Mike Kelly, director of the institute's public health division, said there are about 200,000 injecting drug users in Britain. He estimated about 25% of users share needles, putting themselves at a greatly increased risk of being infected with Hepatitis C or HIV.
Kelly said: "The cost to the NHS of caring for someone who injects drugs is around £35,000 over their lifetime. From a societal perspective, the average [lifetime] cost rises to an estimated £480,000 when you take into account the high cost of crime including criminal justice costs."
About 40% of drug users who inject are already infected with Hepatitis C and their risk of death is 10 times higher than among the population at large.
If needle exchange schemes are run well, they can provide an effective conduit for doctors, nurses and pharmacists to gain direct contact with hard-to-reach groups - the first step towards encouraging them to seek treatment.
Providing injecting drug users with extra years of healthy life was cost-effective for taxpayers, said Nice.
Kelly added: "Keeping in check the epidemic of Hepatitis and maintaining HIV at its relatively low levels is an important aim that this guidance will serve."
Needle and syringe exchange schemes have been provided throughout England for more than 20 years. They provide injecting drug users with sterile equipment, needle disposal bins and advice on safer injecting practices. Primary care trusts (PCTs) have had discretion on how to run services to meet local needs.
The Nice guidelines include advice on how PCTs should tailor the service to encourage injectors to seek treatment by offering more accessible opening times and locations.
Dr Mathew Hickman, chair of the Hepatitis C prevention working group at the Advisory Council for the Misuse of Drugs, said: "Needle and syringe programmes are a critical component of public health action to prevent Hepatitis C infections among injecting drug users.
"Evidence suggests that a combination of interventions is most effective. This means that staff need to use the opportunity they have with injectors actively to promote and refer people into treatment, such as opiate substitution programmes."
Dr David Sloan, vice-chair of the Public Health Interventions Advisory Committee, said: "Although HIV rates remain relatively low among injecting drug users in the UK, bad practice, such as the sharing of needles among multiple users, makes these individuals extremely vulnerable to any future outbreak."

March 2009.Title: Penrose again
March 2009.Author: Andrew Bolger
March 2009.chunks: Lord Penrose, the distinguished Scottish judge who five years ago chronicled how crisis engulfed Equitable Life, has started to untangle another murky tale.Now retired, he has launched a public inquiry into how Scots received blood contaminated with hepatitis C and HIV from the National Health Service in the 1970s and 1980s. Opening the inquiry last week, Lord Penrose stressed that his terms of reference from the Scottish government did not include compensation for the victims.One understands why his lordship was anxious not to raise false hopes. His 818-page report into Equitable was a lucid demolition of the performance of its executives, the inadequacies of its board and the failure of government regulators to prevent the world's oldest mutual life assurer from driving itself on to the rocks. But ministers, anxious to avoid offering compensation, chose to focus instead on his finding that Equitable was the "author of its own misfortunes".The UK government finally apologised to Equitable policyholders in January - but then asked another judge, Sir John Chadwick, to review claims under an "ex-gratia" compensation scheme.Does this mean senior judges are starting to usurp the politically-useful constitutional role of royal commissions, of which Harold Wilson once said: "They take minutes and waste years"?andrew.bolger@ft.com

March 2009.Title: INFECTED BLOOD VICTIMS 'DESERVE APOLOGY AND PROPER COMPENSATION'; SOPHIE GOODCHILD
March 2009.Author: No author in byline
March 2009.chunks: Thousands of victims of an NHS blunder involving contaminated blood today demanded an official apology from the Government.Treatment with imported blood that had not been properly screened exposed victims including children to viruses such as Aids and hepatitis C. The scandal which left more than 2,000 people dead and many terminally ill was described as a 'horrific human tragedy' by a long-awaited independent report published today.Lord Archer of Sandwell, who chaired the investigation, criticised ministers for failing to respond earlier to the disaster by halting imports of infected blood from countries including the US during the Seventies and Eighties. The former solicitor general said subsequent health crises such as variant CJD, the human form of mad cow disease, could have been avoided if officials had taken swift action.Lord Archer said at today's report publication: 'This matter is by no means closed. We are discovering viruses now that we didn't know existed. There could have been a system in place (if action had been taken earlier). And issues such as CJD might have been foreseen and even avoided. 'If you step on someone's foot on a crowded train then you may not yourself be to blame but you say 'sorry'. It (apologising) might help achieve closure. 'The Government is now under pressure to provide a new compensation deal for survivors.Evidence presented to the inquiry showed that widows and children have suffered as a result of inadequate financial settlements.One of the recommendations is that the existing settlement system is overhauled. No figure was given for possible new compensation levels, but Irish victims have already benefited by at least 100,000 from a similar scheme set up in their country.Lord Archer recommended that victims should also be entitled to health care not automatically available on the NHS such as counselling, home nursing and physiotherapy. They would gain access to this care through a special card-holder system.The report revealed that doctors and government officials knew as far back as the mid-Seventies that blood and blood products carried a danger of infection from viruses.But blood continued to be imported from countries such as the US where donors included paid prison inmates.The full scale of the contamination scandal only began to emerge at the height of Britain's Aids scare.Ministers have consistently refused funding for a formal public investigation and refused to provide any evidence to this inquiry.Campaigners said they welcomed the inquiry report and the 'tireless' work of the inquiry team.Chris James, chief executive of the Haemophilia Society, said: 'Successive governments have shamefully refused to fund a public inquiry and an independent inquiry held in public was the only way forward if the voices of those infected and the bereaved was ever to be heard. 'We are immensely grateful to Lord Archer and his inquiry team for their tireless endeavours to reveal the truth depth of this disaster.'

March 2009.Author: Stephen Wilkie
March 2009.chunks: MINISTERS were yesterday given a one-month deadline to arrange an inquiry into Scotland's tainted blood scandal.The move follows a judge's ruling which overturns a 2006 refusal to investigate the deaths of two Scots from hepatitis C.Relatives went to court to try to force the authorities to hold an inquiry into how Eileen O'Hara, 72, and Rev David Black, 66, contracted the virus while in NHS care.Both died in 2003. They were among the thousands of patients given contaminated blood in the Seventies and Eighties.After a judge ruled in favour of the families early last year, the Scottish Government promised a public inquiry, but eight months on, no date has been set and no judge appointed.Last February, at the Court of Session in Edinburgh, Lord Mackay ruled that relatives had the right to expect a reasonably prompt inquiry. He said: "Since the deaths of Mrs O'Hara and Mr Black, both the Lord Advocate and the Scottish ministers have acted in a manner incompatible with the European Convention of Human Rights of the deceased. "He quoted article two of the convention, which states "everyone's right to life shall be protected by law". He quashed the Lord Advocate's decision not to hold Fatal Accident Inquiries.Judge Lady Cosgrove was appointed to lead the inquiry but she pulled out and no replacement has been found.Yesterday, Lord Mackay said he was giving the Scottish Government and Lord Advocate Elish Angiolini four to five weeks to set up the inquiry.A Scottish Government spokesman added: "We are keen that the public inquiry should begin as soon as possible."

March 2009.Title: Blood scandal officials may be forced to testify
March 2009.Author: Severin Carrell Scotland correspondent
March 2009.chunks: Health officials involved in supplying blood products contaminated with hepatitis C and HIV could be compelled to give evidence in the first official inquiry into a scandal estimated to have so far cost 2,000 lives.Lord Penrose, a former high court judge appointed by Scottish ministers to head the inquiry, said yesterday he would use legal powers to force reluctant witnesses to appear and would formally investigate the conduct of UK ministers.The inquiry, expected to take three to four years, was set up by the Scottish Nationalist government in Edinburgh and given a pounds 3m budget after ministers in successive Tory and Labour governments refused a public or judicial inquiry.Nearly 4,700 people, chiefly haemophiliacs but also hospital patients given blood transfusions, became infected with Hepatitis C or both HIV and hepatitis C from the early 1970s. The Haemophilia Society said about 840 of the 1,200 people infected with both diseases had died, while about 1,200 infected solely with hepatitis C had since died. Another 63 wives and partners contracted HIV through secondary infections. Some of the contaminated blood had come from inmates in US prisons.Surviving victims have been able to claim pounds 20,000, and a further pounds 25,000 for the very seriously ill, in ex gratia payments under the government-backed Skipton fund set up in 2004. People infected with HIV have been given up to pounds 80,000 and monthly payments from another fund.Penrose said he and his team were aware their work "touches individuals and families who have suffered and continue to suffer, physically, mentally and emotionally [from] the consequences of treatment they were entitled to trust."

March 2009.Title: Compensation call for haemophiliacs
March 2009.Author: Andrew Jack
March 2009.chunks: The government should pay compensation and cover future health and insurance costs for the many hundreds of surviving haemophiliacs left infected by contaminated National Health Service blood products since the 1970s, an inquiry concluded .Ministers should also set up a committee to support haemophiliacs and manage their future treatment to the highest standards, says a privately funded report written under the chairmanship of Lord Archer of Sandwell, the former solicitor-general.The conclusions follow lengthy hearings demanded by haemophiliacs and convened unofficially two years ago after the government repeatedly refused to hold an official statutory inquiry into blood transfusions that led to HIV, hepatitis C and other viruses infecting nearly 5,000 people before tighter screening was introduced.Nearly 2,000 haemophiliacs have since died as a result of infection by blood bought from groups abroad at high risk of infection, including from inmates in US prisons. "Long after alarms had been sounded about the risks of obtaining paid-for blood donations . . . this practice continued," the report said. "It is difficult to avoid the conclusion that commercial interests took precedence over public health concerns. "The Department of Health said: "We have great sympathy for the patients and families affected by contaminated blood products in the 1970s and 1980s, and will study the findings of Lord Archer's report in detail. "The Scottish parliament has since established a statutory inquiry, while that covering England and Wales had no legal powers or official support.

20 May 2009.Title: Hepatitis victims lose battle for extra cash
20 May 2009.Author: No author in byline
20 May 2009.chunks: News | Britain in briefHEALTH Haemophiliacs who contracted HIV from infected blood will see payments they receive from the Government double but those infected with hepatitis C will get no extra cash, ministers have announced. Some 4,670 haemophiliacs who received blood transfusions in the 1970s and 80s were infected with hepatitis C, of whom 1,243 were also infected with HIV. 20 May 2009.Title: Outcry at NHS blood transfusion payouts: No extra help for people infected with hepatitis C Inquiry had called for improved compensation
20 May 2009.Author: Sarah Boseley Health editor
20 May 2009.chunks: The government was accused yesterday of putting budget constraints ahead of victims of the worst treatment scandal in NHS history after deciding not to increase compensation for people infected with hepatitis C during routine blood transfusions.An independent inquiry into the scandal, chaired by Lord Archer of Sandwell, in February recommended larger payouts for nearly 3,000 people with haemophilia who had been infected with hepatitis C and HIV, as well as help for widows and dependants.Their hopes were dashed yesterday by a response from the Department of Health offering an increase for the minority who had been infected with HIV but nothing more than a review in five years' time for the rest.Archer said the response was a "faltering step that only compounds the anguish of the afflicted and bereaved". He said: "It is difficult to avoid the conclusion that humanitarian impulses have come a bad second to Treasury constraints. "Archer branded the new funding for patients with HIV "paltry", and said that the failure to increase help for those with hepatitis C and to offer payment to their dependants was "sadly lacking in understanding and in compassion".In the 1970s and 80s about 4,670 people with haemophilia were given blood contaminated with hepatitis C and 1,200 were unwittingly infected with HIV. The blood products came from commercial companies in the US, whose paid donors included drug addicts and prisoners.The health minister, Dawn Primarolo, publishing the government's response, said: "We deeply regret that these events occurred following NHS treatment. "In addition to pounds 150m already shared out in lump sums and discretionary payments, financial help for those with HIV would rise to pounds 12,800 per year, she announced. She gave a commitment to review financial relief for the others within five years and announced pounds 100,000 for the Haemophilia Society, which recently had its government funding cut by pounds 70,000.Chris James, chief executive of the Haemophilia Society, said: "The government claims to accept the moral case for action but then, by not implementing the recommendations in full, shows its contempt for the victims of what Lord Winston has described as the 'worst treatment disaster in the history of the NHS'. "Lord Morris of Manchester, who was instrumental in getting the inquiry set up and who has raised the issues regularly in parliament, said: "This response will totally dismay the victims of an NHS treatment disaster that had already claimed the lives of 1,757 haemophiliac patients when I announced the setting up of the inquiry in February 2007. "Since then, he said, over 200 more patients had died.

20 May 2009.Title: Fears of whitewash over blood tragedy
20 May 2009.Author: Judith Duffy
20 May 2009.chunks: A DAMNING report into Britain's tainted blood scandal has condemned the "procrastination" that led to thousands of patients contracting deadly viruses including HIV and hepatitis C.A two-year investigation, led by Labour Peer Lord Archer of Sandwell, expressed dismay over the slow reaction by governments and scientific agencies that led to the scale of the "horrific human tragedy".In the UK more than 4,600 haemophiliacs who received contaminated blood products in the Seventies and Eighties were infected with HIV or hepatitis C.Nearly 2,000 have died as a result of what has been dubbed "the worst treatment disaster in the history of the NHS".The Scottish Government has pledged to hold a separate public inquiry north of the Border.But doubts were yesterday raised over whether the UK Government would provide vital information dating from before devolution. The independent Archer Inquiry, which cost 75,000, was privately funded and the Department of Health declined to give evidence.The inquiry's report said slow progress towards making the UK self sufficient in blood products had led to the NHS buying blood from America. But much of this had been taken from "skid row" donors, such as prison inmates, who were more likely to be infected with viruses.The report said: "It is difficult to avoid the conclusion that commercial interests took precedence over public health concerns. "Lord Penrose was appointed in January to lead the Scottish probe. Health Secretary Nicola Sturgeon pledged a "full and open" inquiry and said the UK Government had given assurances documents would be shared.She said: "No Scottish inquiry can compel that evidence, but we have received assurances from the Department of Health that they will cooperate fully. "But haemophiliac Andy Gunn, of Inverness, who contracted both hepatitis C and HIV from infected blood, said he expected the Department of Health to withhold evidence from a Scottish inquiry in "another whitewash". "Whilst we're grateful they're holding an inquiry it's no use really because they're stopping short and withholding crucial documents and witnesses, " he said.A spokeswoman for the Department of Health said they were examining Lord Archer's recommendations and added:"The Permanent Secretary Hugh Taylor has written to his counterpart in Scotland, and to Lord Penrose, to assure them of cooperation from the UK Department of Health."

20 May 2009.Title: Report into NHS tainted blood scandal urges payouts for families
20 May 2009.Author: Sam Lister
20 May 2009.chunks: A report into how thousands of haemophiliacs were infected with HIV, hepatitis and other conditions during NHS treatment will today condemn the inaction of successive governments and call for compensation for victim's families.The independent public inquiry into use of contaminated blood, which caused 1,756 deaths, will attack ministers' failure to investigate over the past 20 years. It has been referred to by Lord Winston, the leading medical expert, as "the worst treatment disaster in the history of the NHS".About 4,670 patients who received transfusions in the 1970s and 1980s were infected with hepatitis C of whom 1,243 were also infected with HIV through treatment with clotting products made from "bad blood".The two-year privately funded inquiry led by Lord Archer of Sandwell, a Labour peer and former Solicitor- General, received harrowing evidence from victims as well as testimony from families, former ministers and experts.The report will back calls for proper compensation and priority access for victims to a range of services. It will support evidence to the inquiry that commercial considerations were given priority over safety in the purchase of blood products. In the 1970s some were bought from US suppliers who used "Skid Row" donors, more likely to have HIV and hepatitis C.The inquiry will recommend more compensation for those who contracted viruses, many of whom have lived longer than expected because of advances in medication, as well as families of those who have died.Lord Archer is also expected to draw attention to the failure to learn lessons that might have been highlighted by a full public inquiry. As recently as 2004 an alert had to be issued to haemophiliacs on the danger they may have contracted the human form of mad cow disease from products administered between 1980 and 2001.This month the Health Protection Agency confirmed the death of the first haemophiliac to have contracted vCJD from contaminated blood, although this did not cause his death.Campaigners have also accused the Government of a cover-up over its decision to withhold more than 35 documents on confidentiality grounds.One woman told the inquiry that she had been given a "death sentence", while other witnesses said they felt haemophiliacs had been used as "guinea pigs" so doctors could study the progress of their diseases.Jenny Willott, Liberal Democrat MP for Cardiff Central, who gave evidence on behalf of constituents, said it was vital that the Government accepted failings highlighted by the inquiry and supported research into effective blood-screening technologies.Chris James, chief executive of the Haemophilia Society, said it was now incumbent on the Government to act on the findings.A Department of Health spokeswoman said: "The facts are now known around this distressing episode and we have introduced tough measures to protect patients." The Government had gone further than any other administration in making information available, she said..

20 May 2009.Title: Government 'must compensate the victims of HIV blood bungle'
20 May 2009.Author: Jo Willey Health Correspondent
20 May 2009.chunks: PRESSURE was mounting on the Government last night to compensate victims of the contaminated blood scandal of the 1970s and 80s.Nearly 5,000 haemophiliacs, including children, were left with Hepatitis C after being given contaminated blood from transfusions in the 1970s and 80s.A total of 1,243 of them were also infected with HIV.Almost 2,000 of those infected have since died.A two-year inquiry, led by Labour peer Lord Archer of Sandwell, yesterday called for compensation and condemned "procrastination" by Governments and scientifi c agencies that led to the scale of the "horrifi human tragedy". The study was privately funded by victims and their families after successive governments refused to investigate or admit any fault.Carol Grayson, 49, of Jesmond, Newcastle, whose haemophiliac husband Peter Longstaff died in 2005 aged 47, welcomed the report.Mr Longstaff had received a number of contaminated blood transfusions in the 1970s, given to him by the NHS and had contracted HIV and hepatitis.She said: "The Government must act quickly because many people are in a situation of quite severe poverty now."

20 May 2009.Title: Justice for haemophiliacs
20 May 2009.Author: No author in byline
20 May 2009.chunks: There could scarcely be a more appalling failure of the public health system than the fate inflicted upon thousands of haemophiliacs who relied upon the NHS for their supplies of blood, only to discover later that they were contaminated. This scandal began more than a quarter of a century ago, when the NHS imported large quantities of a blood product, known as Factor VIII, from America because there was not enough in this country, as there should have been. The blood had been collected from people at high risk of HIV and hepatitis C, notably intravenous drug users and prisoners. When it was given to haemophiliacs here, some 4,700 became infected and nearly half of them have died. Such a death toll might have been avoided had there not also been an attempt to deny knowledge of the contamination. Even more extraordinary has been the refusal over the years of any government to conduct a formal inquiry into what happened.An investigation that reported yesterday, under the chairmanship of Lord Archer of Sandwell, was privately funded and independently constituted. It has uncovered little that was not already known about how the disaster happened, but it has served to remind the country of a forgotten group of people and their families, who have often been treated with less sympathy and understanding than others who contracted HIV as a result of their lifestyle rather than purely by accident. The Archer report has proposed an improvement in the existing level of compensation for the victims and those who have to look after them, something the Government should address urgently. Just as important are the lessons to be learnt from this tragedy, foremost of which is that an inquiry should have been held many years ago to ensure that the same mistakes are not made again.

20 May 2009.Title: Blood scandal officials may be forced to testify
20 May 2009.Author: Severin Carrell Scotland correspondent
20 May 2009.chunks: Health officials involved in supplying blood products contaminated with hepatitis C and HIV could be compelled to give evidence in the first official inquiry into a scandal estimated to have so far cost 2,000 lives.Lord Penrose, a former high court judge appointed by Scottish ministers to head the inquiry, said yesterday he would use legal powers to force reluctant witnesses to appear and would formally investigate the conduct of UK ministers.The inquiry, expected to take three to four years, was set up by the Scottish Nationalist government in Edinburgh and given a pounds 3m budget after ministers in successive Tory and Labour governments refused a public or judicial inquiry.Nearly 4,700 people, chiefly haemophiliacs but also hospital patients given blood transfusions, became infected with Hepatitis C or both HIV and hepatitis C from the early 1970s. The Haemophilia Society said about 840 of the 1,200 people infected with both diseases had died, while about 1,200 infected solely with hepatitis C had since died. Another 63 wives and partners contracted HIV through secondary infections. Some of the contaminated blood had come from inmates in US prisons.Surviving victims have been able to claim pounds 20,000, and a further pounds 25,000 for the very seriously ill, in ex gratia payments under the government-backed Skipton fund set up in 2004. People infected with HIV have been given up to pounds 80,000 and monthly payments from another fund.Penrose said he and his team were aware their work "touches individuals and families who have suffered and continue to suffer, physically, mentally and emotionally [from] the consequences of treatment they were entitled to trust."

20 May 2009.Title: 'A horrific human tragedy': report criticises response to blood scandal: Government failed victims of infected product Haemophiliacs renew call for full and quick action
20 May 2009.Author: Sarah Boseley Alexandra Topping
20 May 2009.chunks: The full scale of the infected blood catastrophe that hit people with haemophilia after the UK supplies became contaminated with lethal viruses might have been averted if imports from the United States had been blocked, an independent inquiry report said yesterday.Lord Archer's report described the infection of thousands of haemophiliacs with hepatitis C and HIV as "a horrific human tragedy", adding: "Subsequent events have done little to alleviate the hurt of the victims or their families. "The inquiry was "dismayed at the time taken by governmental and scientific agencies to become fully alive to the dangers of hepatitis C and HIV infections and by the lethargic progress towards self-sufficiency in blood products in England and Wales". Ireland managed it in five years - in England and Wales it took 13.But in spite of a series of strong recommendations to government to renegotiate a fair, direct and more substantial compensation package with survivors and their families, the Department of Health offered only sympathy and a promise to look at the findings.Campaigners, who feel they have been rebuffed by the government at every turn, were left dissatisfied both with the report's inability to name the guilty men after all this time and with the government's non-committal response.Carol Grayson, whose husband, Peter Longstaff, died after being infected by HIV and hepatitis C, said she was pleased with the recommendations but disappointed that the inquiry could not hold anyone to account. The government response was "wishy-washy and insulting", she said. "We've already been waiting 20-odd years so it is essential the government implements the recommendations as people are dying as we speak. "Chris James, chief executive of the Haemophilia Society, welcomed the recommendations. "Many of our members would like an apology, but it is very clear from the report from Lord Archer that the apology will come in the form of the actions that the government now takes." It was "absolutely crucial" for the government to respond fully and quickly. "People have died waiting for answers; they can't wait any longer. "Some 4,670 haemophiliacs were given blood contaminated with the hepatitis C virus and 1,200 were later unwittingly infected with HIV in the 1970s and 80s. The blood products came from commercial organisations in the US, whose paid donors included injecting drug users and prison inmates. More than 2,000 haemophiliacs who received the tainted blood are now dead.Exactly who is to blame is now difficult to ascertain, the report says. Some critical documents have been destroyed. But even though the alarm over possible viral infections in blood donations was raised by 1970 in the US, it appears that UK officials did not appreciate the concerns until 1978. "If that is so, it represents a serious oversight in the department, or serious distortion of priorities," the report says.Archer said yesterday he was surprised ministers and officials from the Department of Health were unwilling to take part in the inquiry, "because there are things the government could have said in mitigation - things that weren't known about at that time".The report says a public inquiry should have been held much earlier to address the concerns of the haemophilia community. Government should set up an uncomplicated scheme to give direct financial relief to sufferers and families, which should be at least as generous as that which operates in Ireland.

20 May 2009.Title: Government procrastination blamed for HIV-contaminated blood tragedy
20 May 2009.Author: No author in byline
20 May 2009.chunks: Official lethargy led to reliance on US suppliers using 'skid row' donors who were more likely to be infected, an inquiry report saidGovernment procrastination led to thousands of patients becoming infected with HIV and Hepatitis C from contaminated blood, an inquiry report said today.The independent inquiry, led by Labour peer Lord Archer of Sandwell, said the infection of so many people was a "horrific human tragedy".The authors of the report said they were dismayed at the time taken by the government and scientific agencies to respond to the dangers of Hepatitis C and HIV infections.The report noted there was "lethargic" progress towards national self-sufficiency in blood products in England and Wales, where it took 13 years compared to five years in Ireland.As a result the NHS bought blood from US suppliers who used what became known as "skid row" donors, such as prison inmates, who were more likely to have HIV and Hepatitis C.The report said: "It is difficult to avoid the conclusion that commercial interests took precedence over public health concerns. "It added: "Whether the lack of urgency over much of this period arose from over-hesitant scientific advice or from a sluggish response by government is now difficult to assess. "Nearly 2,000 haemophiliacs have died as a result of exposure to the contaminated blood in what leading medical expert Lord Winston called "the worst treatment disaster in the history of the NHS".Some 4,670 patients who received blood transfusions in the 1970s and 1980s were infected with Hepatitis C, of whom 1,243 were also infected with HIV.Lord Archer's two-year privately funded inquiry was set up after decades of campaigning from victims and their families.His report noted: "The haemophilia community feels that their plight has never been fully acknowledged or addressed. "The authors said a full public inquiry into the scandal should have been held much earlier to address the concerns of haemophiliacs.In conclusion they said: "Commercial priorities should never again override the interests of public health. "The report made a series of recommendations, including:• the formation of a committee to advise the government on the management of haemophilia;• the testing of patients with haemophilia and their partners for any conditions with which they could have been infected;• the testing of all blood donors after they give blood;• those who were infected should be given cards entitling them to benefits not freely available on the NHS, including prescription drugs, counselling and home nursing;• compensation for those infected and for carers who have been prevented from working. This should be paid through the Department of Work and Pensions, and should not be means-tested;• a scheme to ensure haemophilia patients have access to insurance;• and an exercise to identify any people who were infected by contaminated blood but are still not aware of this.It emerged last week that a haemophiliac had contracted the human form of mad cow disease - Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (vCJD) - after being treated with a blood-clotting agent from an infected donor.The authors of today's report warned: "The problems surrounding vCJD are a reminder that new infections may yet arise, with serious results. "Lord Archer, asked if there should be an apology, said some advocated this approach as a means of recognising the human suffering that had been caused.He said: "It doesn't necessarily have to be construed as an admission that it was the government's fault. "If you tread on somebody's foot on a crowded train it may not be your fault but at least you say sorry, and I think probably it would help to achieve closure and help to alleviate feelings a bit if there was some kind of apology. "He added that he was "surprised" by the Department of Health's decision not to give evidence to the inquiry. "I am bound to say that in questions in which I have been involved if someone is giving evidence about it I have wanted to give evidence too. "I would like to say anything that could be said on my own behalf and I am surprised that the Department [of Health] did not take the same view.guardian.co.uk © Guardian News and Media 2009

20 May 2009.Title: Penrose again
20 May 2009.Author: Andrew Bolger
20 May 2009.chunks: Lord Penrose, the distinguished Scottish judge who five years ago chronicled how crisis engulfed Equitable Life, has started to untangle another murky tale.Now retired, he has launched a public inquiry into how Scots received blood contaminated with hepatitis C and HIV from the National Health Service in the 1970s and 1980s. Opening the inquiry last week, Lord Penrose stressed that his terms of reference from the Scottish government did not include compensation for the victims.One understands why his lordship was anxious not to raise false hopes. His 818-page report into Equitable was a lucid demolition of the performance of its executives, the inadequacies of its board and the failure of government regulators to prevent the world's oldest mutual life assurer from driving itself on to the rocks. But ministers, anxious to avoid offering compensation, chose to focus instead on his finding that Equitable was the "author of its own misfortunes".The UK government finally apologised to Equitable policyholders in January - but then asked another judge, Sir John Chadwick, to review claims under an "ex-gratia" compensation scheme.Does this mean senior judges are starting to usurp the politically-useful constitutional role of royal commissions, of which Harold Wilson once said: "They take minutes and waste years"?andrew.bolger@ft.com

20 May 2009.Title: INFECTED BLOOD VICTIMS 'DESERVE APOLOGY AND PROPER COMPENSATION'; SOPHIE GOODCHILD
20 May 2009.Author: No author in byline
20 May 2009.chunks: Thousands of victims of an NHS blunder involving contaminated blood today demanded an official apology from the Government.Treatment with imported blood that had not been properly screened exposed victims including children to viruses such as Aids and hepatitis C. The scandal which left more than 2,000 people dead and many terminally ill was described as a 'horrific human tragedy' by a long-awaited independent report published today.Lord Archer of Sandwell, who chaired the investigation, criticised ministers for failing to respond earlier to the disaster by halting imports of infected blood from countries including the US during the Seventies and Eighties. The former solicitor general said subsequent health crises such as variant CJD, the human form of mad cow disease, could have been avoided if officials had taken swift action.Lord Archer said at today's report publication: 'This matter is by no means closed. We are discovering viruses now that we didn't know existed. There could have been a system in place (if action had been taken earlier). And issues such as CJD might have been foreseen and even avoided. 'If you step on someone's foot on a crowded train then you may not yourself be to blame but you say 'sorry'. It (apologising) might help achieve closure. 'The Government is now under pressure to provide a new compensation deal for survivors.Evidence presented to the inquiry showed that widows and children have suffered as a result of inadequate financial settlements.One of the recommendations is that the existing settlement system is overhauled. No figure was given for possible new compensation levels, but Irish victims have already benefited by at least 100,000 from a similar scheme set up in their country.Lord Archer recommended that victims should also be entitled to health care not automatically available on the NHS such as counselling, home nursing and physiotherapy. They would gain access to this care through a special card-holder system.The report revealed that doctors and government officials knew as far back as the mid-Seventies that blood and blood products carried a danger of infection from viruses.But blood continued to be imported from countries such as the US where donors included paid prison inmates.The full scale of the contamination scandal only began to emerge at the height of Britain's Aids scare.Ministers have consistently refused funding for a formal public investigation and refused to provide any evidence to this inquiry.Campaigners said they welcomed the inquiry report and the 'tireless' work of the inquiry team.Chris James, chief executive of the Haemophilia Society, said: 'Successive governments have shamefully refused to fund a public inquiry and an independent inquiry held in public was the only way forward if the voices of those infected and the bereaved was ever to be heard. 'We are immensely grateful to Lord Archer and his inquiry team for their tireless endeavours to reveal the truth depth of this disaster.'

20 May 2009.Title: MINISTERS IN IMPORTED BLOOD BLUNDER ACCUSED OF COVER-UP; SOPHIE GOODCHILD
20 May 2009.Author: No author in byline
20 May 2009.chunks: THE Government was today accused of a cover-up over an NHS scandal involving thousands of victims infected by contaminated blood.Campaigners claim ministers withheld dozens of documents relating to the blunder that left nearly 5,000 patients with deadly diseases.The use of imported blood that had not been properly screened exposed victims to blood viruses including Aids and Hepatitis C more than 20 years ago. Nearly half, including children, have died as a direct result.But other terminally ill survivors of the scandal, called 'the worst treatment disaster in the history of the NHS', have spoken out before an official report into the case.Published on Monday, the findings of this two-year independent inquiry are expected to be hugely critical of how victims have been treated.Campaign group Tainted Blood told the Standard that Whitehall officials have still not released at least 30 documents to the inquiry panel chaired by former solicitor general Lord Archer of Sandwell.Spokesman Gareth Lewis said victims want an official apology, full compensation for their trauma, a full package of medical care and an admission that evidence of the disaster was ignored by successive governments. He said: 'My biggest concern is the evidence has been there yet successive governments have tried to hide it. 'It is only through freedom of information laws that we are in the situation we are. But there are still about 30 documents that have not been released that could help us find out the truth about what happened. We just want closure.' The full scale of the contamination scandal only began to emerge at the height of Britain's Aids scare. It was discovered that batches of imported blood and blood products had not been properly screened and were infected with viruses.Victims included those suffering from haemophilia, a condition in which sufferers lack a blood-clotting protein. This means they require regular blood transfusions.Those affected spent years battling for any financial settlement because it was difficult to prove exactly which batches of blood were infected.Eventually they were granted one-off payouts of up to 80,000 on the grounds they were not expected to live. But the development of antiviral drugs has meant many have survived.The fear now is that survivors are at risk of developing mad cow disease or CJD from the infected blood transfusions and products they received as far back as 20 years ago.This follows confirmation that an elderly haemophilia sufferer has died from the human form of mad cow disease after contracting it as the result of treatment with infected blood-clotting agent more than 20 years ago.The Standard has also learned that the US pharmaceutical companies which supplied tainted blood and blood products to the NHS have now agreed to settle with British victims.This will put pressure on the British Government to revise its compensation deals.

20 May 2009.Title: New deal urged for blood scandal victims: Infected patients' families need cash aid, says inquiry Ministers criticised for refusing to give evidence
20 May 2009.Author: Sarah Boseley Health editor Alexandra Topping
20 May 2009.chunks: The government will today come under pressure to forge a new compensation deal for thousands of people with haemophilia who were given blood tainted with HIV and hepatitis C, as a long-awaited report from an independent inquiry into the scandal is published.More than a quarter of those infected as a result of blood transfusions have died in what Robert Winston described as "the worst treatment disaster in the history of the NHS". Many are terminally ill. The inquiry heard that widows and children have suffered as a result of a financial settlement that fails to meet their needs.The report of the independent inquiry, set up two years ago by Lord Morris of Manchester and chaired by the former solicitor general Lord Archer, will be an exhaustive account of what went wrong in the 1970s and 1980s.It will criticise organisations, rather than individuals, for mistakes and for acting too slowly to halt importations of infected blood from paid donors in the US, some of whom were drug addicts and prisoners with hepatitis C infection from needle use.The inquiry heard evidence from Lord Owen, who called for Britain to become self-sufficient in blood while a minister in the 1970s and was dismayed by the lack of progress and also by the destruction of important documents after the scandal had become public.It will demand action to prevent future blood scandals, raising the issue of variant CJD - the human form of mad cow disease. It is known that vCJD entered the blood supply through donations from people who did not know they were infected. Last week it was confirmed that one haemophiliac with vCJD from contaminated blood had died, although not from the disease.Above all, the report will say that the government must now address the financial hardship of those with haemophilia and their families who have suffered as a result of tainted blood from the NHS. Compensation payments have been inadequate and some are living in poverty. People who became infected with hepatitis C, a potentially lethal liver virus, have been unable to get insurance except at prohibitive cost.Campaigners welcomed the publication of the report, calling it the only real attempt to reveal the full scale of the tragedy. Chris James, chief executive of the Haemophilia Society, said: "Successive governments have shamefully refused to fund a public inquiry, and an independent inquiry held in public was the only way forward if the voices of those infected and the bereaved were ever to be heard. We are immensely grateful to Lord Archer and his inquiry team for their tireless endeavours to reveal the true depth of this disaster. "He called for the government to create a National Haemophilia Committee, a body that would help patients to participate in their treatment, and full healthcare provision for survivors in addition to insurance and compensation. "There are vital lessons to be learned in ensuring that decisions are made in an open and transparent way that fully involves patients," he said.About 4,800 haemophiliacs were infected with hepatitis C through blood transfusions in the late 1970s and early 1980s, and around 1,200 of those were also infected with HIV. Most of the latter - more than 800 - have died. At the time of the inquiry's launch, in February 2007, there had been 1,757 deaths. The numbers are steadily rising. Some of those who gave evidence have since died.Carol Grayson, whose husband Peter Longstaff died after becoming infected with hepatitis C and HIV, hoped the report would provide closure for survivors. "It is going to be very emotional as there are lots of people who will not be there to hear the recommendations, but hopefully it will provide relief for some people who have campaigned for more than 20 years. "In spite of the scale of the tragedy, the government has consistently refused to hold its own public inquiry.Today's report is expected to point to new evidence of what went wrong from thousands of documents that were eventually handed over by the government. It will also criticise ministers for refusing to give evidence. Those involved in the inquiry believe it will be hard for the government to dismiss its findings because it was set up and conducted by respected parliamentarians and is independent of vested interests.

20 May 2009.Title: HIV TESTS ON 12,000 PATIENTS PUT AT RISK BY INFECTED WORKER
20 May 2009.Author: KIRAN RANDHAWA
20 May 2009.chunks: MORE than 12,000 patients treated by a hospital worker with HIV and Hepatitis C are at risk of having contracted the viruses, it was revealed today.All those who were treated by the healthcare worker have been contacted by the NHS trust this week and called in to take a blood test.Among the former patients at Lewisham Hospital is an 11-year-old boy who was treated by the employee when he had his appendix out last year. His father, from Downham, south-east London, said he received a letter from the hospital on Tuesday saying his son was at risk and should come in for a blood tests.He said: 'I was shocked to receive a letter like this and my first thought was how something like this could be allowed to happen. 'He is due to start secondary school in September and we don't want anything to upset him so we've had to lie to him about why he needs a blood test. Even though we know the chances of him having anything are slim, we are very worried. 'The letter read: 'You may already be aware that we have been conducting an investigation into the case of a healthcare worker in Lewisham who has been found to be infected with HIV. 'The investigations have revealed that the healthcare worker is also infected with hepatitis C. Records suggest that your child may have been cared for by this healthcare worker in the past. 'The parents of the child took him to Blackheath Hospital the following day for a blood test and expect the results within a month.Dr Donal O'Sullivan at Lewisham Hospital, said: 'We are very much aware of how concerned patients will be. It is important to emphasise, however, that any risk to patients is likely to be low. 'There has never been a case of HIV infection in the UK which has occurred because of transmission from a healthcare worker to a patient. The risk of spread of hepatitis C in this way is slightly greater, but is still regarded as low. 'More than 100 staff have been preparing for the testing and a helpline is set up. The infected employee is no longer at the hospital.--LONDON needs a teen sex tsar to cut levels of pregnancy and disease in young people, the capital's top sexual health experts have warned. Doctors told the London Assembly that sexual health services are fragmented and of variable quality across the capital. Hong Tan of the London Sexual Health Programme said: 'We need a senior strategic London leader in sexual health.'

20 May 2009.Title: Blood products victims 'failed by official delays'
20 May 2009.Author:
Rebecca Smith
Medical Editor
20 May 2009.chunks: HAEMOPHILIACS became infected with hepatitis and HIV through contaminated blood products while the Government procrastinated, an inquiry into the "catastrophe'' has claimed.It concluded that imported blood products continued to be used despite concerns they could be contaminated. Procrastination by officials during the Seventies and Eighties meant that many people became needlessly infected with the viruses.The fiasco, which saw 4,670 people infected with hepatitis C and one quarter of those also infected with HIV, was the "worst treatment disaster in the history of the NHS'', according to Lord Morris of Manchester, who organised the inquiry.Of those infected, 1,757 have since died.Blood products were imported from America where donors were paid, so they often came from prisoners and drug addicts, which increased the likelihood of contamination.The companies which processed the blood also made a profit. Lord Archer of Sandwell, the chairman of the inquiry, said commercial priorities must never again override the interests of public health.The inquiry recommended that those affected should receive compensation equal to that given in a similar case in Ireland, thought to be around pounds 350,000, and should receive free care.The report concluded: "The procrastination in achieving national self-sufficiency to avoid the use of high-risk blood products from overseas had disastrous consequences. Had self-sufficiency been achieved earlier the scale of the catastrophe would have been significantly reduced. ''However Lord Archer said: "It is a bit late and a bit pointless to say 'who is to blame?' What is important now is to try to remedy the condition of people who have suffered. ''Dr Charles Hay, the chairman of the UK Haemophilia Centre Doctors' Organisation, said that it was a misconception that the hepatitis C risk would have been lower if patients were given British products instead of American.He added that if self-sufficiency had been achieved then a larger proportion of haemophiliacs would have been exposed to blood from donors who developed vCJD. He said: "The patients were managed according to the best information available at the time. ''The Department of Health said: "Steps to safeguard blood products against HIV and hepatitis C have been in place since 1985. In addition, every reasonable step to minimise risks from blood transfusion has been taken.''

20 May 2009.Title: 2,000 LIVES - THE PRICE PATIENTS PAID IN INFECTED BLOOD SCANDAL
20 May 2009.Author: JENNY HOPE MEDICAL CORRESPONDENT
20 May 2009.chunks: THOUSANDS of patients contracted fatal infections from contaminated blood because commercial interests took priority, an independent inquiry claims.Delays by official bodies in dealing with risky imported blood products led to almost 5,000 people contracting HIV and Hepatitis C.The inquiry, led by Labour peer Lord Archer of Sandwell, said the procrastination was a 'horrific human tragedy'.Official action to make England and Wales self-sufficient in blood products took more than twice as long as elsewhere - 13 years compared with five years in Ireland.As a result, the NHS bought blood from U.S. suppliers which used 'skid row' donors who were more likely to have deadly diseases.The report said: 'It is difficult to avoid the conclusion that commercial interests took precedence over public health concerns. 'The inquiry said, however, that it was impossible to apportion blame. It concluded: 'Whether the lack of urgency over much of this period arose from over-hesitant scientific advice or from a sluggish response by Government is now difficult to assess. 'Nearly 2,000 of the more than 4,600 haemophiliacs infected with Hepatitis C have died.And just 345 of the 1,243 who contracted HIV have survived. Many victims were youngsters when infected in the 1970s and 1980s. Lord Archer's two-year privatelyfunded inquiry was set up after decades of campaigning from victims and their families.They were denied an official inquiry but eventually granted oneoff compensation of up to 80,000. Most suffered from haemophilia, a condition in which sufferers lack a blood-clotting protein and require regular blood transfusions.The Archer report made a series of recommendations, including free prescriptions, access to insurance and further compensation.It emerged last week that a haemophiliac had contracted the human form of mad cow disease after being treated with a clotting agent from an infected donor.The report warned: 'The problems surrounding vCJD are a reminder that new infections may yet arise, with serious results. 'Chris James, of the Haemophilia Society, said: 'We've said for some time that the current level of [compensation] payments are inappropriate. 'A Department of Health spokesman said officials would study the report's findings. 'Every reasonable step to minimise risks from blood transfusion has been taken and robust screening measures are in place,' she added.j.hope@dailymail.co.uk'WE WERE USED AS GUINEA PIGS'ROBERT Mackie contracted HIV and Hepatitis C after receiving contaminated blood products in 1984.But it took doctors three years to tell him he had HIV that had developed into full-blown Aids.Mr Mackie, from Melrose in the Scottish Borders, told the inquiry that he and other infected haemophiliacs were used as guinea pigs in Aids research at Edinburgh Royal Infirmary-Mr Mackie, 58, said it was only 'by the grace of God' that his wife Alice was not infected too. 'They endangered my wife's life for three years by not informing me I had Aids - that's not acceptable by any standards,' he added.He saw two uncles, one cousin and many haemophiliac friends die in the 1990s from a single batch of contaminated blood.

20 May 2009.Title: 12,000 FACE TESTS OVER HEALTH WORKER'S HEPATITIS
20 May 2009.Author: DANIEL MARTIN
20 May 2009.chunks: THOUSANDS of patients are being called for blood tests after a health worker who treated them tested positive for HIV and hepatitis C.The health trust in Lewisham, South-East London, insists the risk of anyone contracting either disease is very small - but has written to 12,000 people advising them to come in for tests.All those the worker came into contact with will be tested for the potentially fatal liver disease hepatitis C, but the trust said the risk of people getting HIV was so low that tests were not needed. People can have the tests if they request them.Lewisham primary care trust would give no details about the health worker, including which job he performed. Tests showed he had the diseases late last year and he no longer works with patients.HIV is usually transmitted through unprotected sex, while hepatitis C is usually caught by drug users who share needles.NHS bosses say the risks of any of the health worker's patients getting either disease is very low, as some of his blood would have needed to enter their bloodstream.Many patients on the list have already been tested but must now wait for up to a month to be sure the result is negative.So far, there is no indication that anyone has suffered ill health as a consequence of the incident.Dr Donal O'Sullivan, a public health consultant, said: 'We are very much aware of how concerned patients will be at this news. It is important to emphasise, however, that any risk to patients is likely to be low. 'There has never been a case of HIV infection in the UK which has occurred because of transmission from a healthcare worker to a patient. 'The risk of spread of hepatitis C in this way is slightly greater, but is still regarded as low. 'Healthcare workers are not routinely tested for hepatitis C. It is an inflammation of the liver caused by a virus with symptoms including fatigue, weight loss, nausea, flulike symptoms, abdominal pain and sometimes jaundice. It can lead to complications such as liver cancer.Despite the very small risk of infection, the PCT sought advice from experts on the UK advisory panel for healthcare workers infected with blood-borne viruses.The panel told the PCT they should recommend a hepatitis C test to all patients treated by the healthcare worker at a time when there was any risk.It said that in terms of HIV, the risk was so small that no tests were needed.The PCT said it had taken until April to send the letters out because of the huge task of going through everybody's medical files.
